cia-0000119205:
A November 1968 CIA document reports on American, Thai, and Philippine prisoners of war held in Laos. The heading misspells Filipino as Philippino, and it breaks off before finishing the list of places. Even so, the core fact stands: men from three allied nations were held in camps in Laos.

Prisoners in Laos were among the hardest to account for, since the war there was secret and the camps remote. Knowing where allied prisoners were held shaped rescue plans and later accounting work. The document records the locations as the agency understood them late in 1968, one piece of a search that would continue for decades after the fighting ended.
cia-0000132205: Situation report 522, from January 1991, reports a Czech team finding traces of nerve gas in Saudi Arabia, the place name breaking off in the heading. Chemical weapons were the war's most feared wild card. The report records that alarming finding. Nerve gas reports were checked against wind, symptoms, and soil samples, since a false alarm could shift gas mask policy for hundreds of thousands of troops.
cia-0000132305: All quiet is the headline of Situation Report 615 in the CIA's Iraq-Kuwait series. The report is dated January 4, 1991. It covers military developments on a front whose name is cut short in the title. The wording echoes a famous war novel, likely on purpose. Quiet sectors in January 1991 rarely stayed quiet for long. The short report records a calm day inside a fast-moving crisis file.
cia-0000132605: Guatemalan exiles in contact with the Cuban government fill item 6 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated July 1, 1960. Exiles were the raw material of Havana's plan to export its revolution. Cuba was gathering the region's displaced fighters and planners that year. The short item tracks those contacts and the people involved in them.
cia-0000135605: Spanish-language papers of the 2506 Brigade fill a CIA record dated October 3, 1960. The record keeps the Spanish text of one or more brigade papers. Spanish papers formed part of the paper trail of the coming invasion. Brigade 2506 was the exile force then training to land in Cuba. The short record keeps the text as it was filed.
cia-0000135805: Men who might defect are the subject of a CIA cable dated May 5, 1954. Defectors were prized goods in the Guatemala mission that spring. Each man who crossed over struck a blow at the Arbenz government's nerve. The cable itself is short, but the hunt behind it ran for months. It weighs the chances offered by the men named inside it.
cia-0000136005: Dated 6 February 1954 and now declassified, a CIA cable records air strip information, the landing grounds the invasion planes would need when the day came. Lincoln was where PBSUCCESS staff worked the Guatemala operation day to day, under code names, in 1953 and 1954. Nothing in the heading promises drama, yet the sheet adds one more firm date and subject to the coup record.
cia-0000136305: LINCOLN's summary of radio material from 0800 to 1700 on 24 June 1954 records a hard day around Chiquimula. Castillo reported entering the town, urged planes to pursue enemy troops toward Zacapa to block a counterattack, and noted his shock troops had no gasoline. Other messages describe smoke bombs requested so positions could be marked, and fuel failing to reach Esquipulas. The cable is a running log of the PBSUCCESS ground fight.
cia-0000137005: Mexican newspaper editorials are quoted at length in this July 1954 cable on using reports of communists hiding in embassies. One editorial, in Spanish, denounces those who arrived in Mexico dripping blood and crimes, pockets full of looted Guatemalan money, and cries let them go to Russia among their own. Another calls sheltering an enemy of Mexico's friends solidarity with that enemy, and a Mexican ruler's inescapable obligation to put Mexico first. The cable mines the press for the asylum fight.
un-ga-res-505:
China's charge against the Soviet Union fills Resolution 505, adopted by the General Assembly on 1 February 1952. The Republic of China held that Moscow had broken the Sino-Soviet Treaty of Friendship and Alliance of 14 August 1945. That pact bound both sides to respect each other's land and rule, and to keep out of each other's home affairs. It also pledged Soviet moral backing and arms aid to China.

The Assembly frames the case as a threat to China's freedom and to peace in the Far East. Breaches of treaty pledges, it holds, strike at the trust world law must rest on. The charge came at a Cold War peak, with Chinese and UN forces at war in Korea.
un-sc-res-205: Among the formal acts of the United Nations Security Council sits Resolution 205, which the catalog dates to 1965. The Council is the UN body charged with world peace and security, and it speaks formally through texts like this one. For students of the UN, the record offers the Council's language itself rather than a summary written later.
un-sc-res-305: Security Council Resolution 305 survives in the official record, and the catalog dates it to 1971. Resolutions are the way the Council states its decisions, and member states are expected to take them seriously. Preserving the text in this form keeps a small piece of diplomatic history open to any reader. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-405: From the Council's official record comes the text numbered 405, catalogued here at 1977. Behind each numbered text lies a meeting, a draft, and a vote, even when the final wording runs to a few lines. Read in sequence with its neighbours, it helps trace how Council practice grew across the postwar decades. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-1905: Resolution 1905, adopted in 2009, survives here as a formal act of the Security Council in record form. English Wikisource made the copy this collection holds. Inside, the Council's well-known pattern turns once more: past decisions are named, the facts of the day are weighed, and new orders are set down in numbered form. The entry keeps one full turn of that pattern.
cia-0000132505:
President John F. Kennedy had been in office only weeks when this CIA briefing on Cuba was written on February 4, 1961. Cuba sat near the top of the new team's agenda. Planning for an invasion by Cuban exiles was already underway inside the government.

The paper belongs to the intelligence flow feeding that planning: short, frequent updates meant to keep decision-makers current on the island. Read now, it shows how much of the new presidency's early attention went to one small country ninety miles away. The CIA released the declassified text through its Reading Room decades later.
cia-0000135705: This Spanish document, dated 2 January 1961, is filed in the CIA's declassified 2506 Brigade collection. The brigade spent that month in training camps, preparing an invasion its members expected to free Cuba. The catalog gives the item no individual subject. Dated pieces like this one, in the brigade's own language, are the raw material from which the operation's daily history is built. The record is presented as released.
cia-0000136705: This Spanish-language item from the 2506 Brigade papers carries an estimated date of 1 January 1961, the estimate flagged in the catalog. The brigade was then in its final winter of training for Cuba. No subject is recorded for the document. It is preserved in Spanish in the declassified release, one of the cluster of brigade records placed at the New Year by the reviewers' estimate.
plos-pone-0000005:
John Ioannidis turned his lens on science itself in a 2006 PLOS ONE study of citation patterns. A citation is one paper crediting another, and citations steer careers, funding, and fame. Ioannidis asked where the most-cited papers in science actually appear, and how tightly they bunch in a few journals.

He describes journals as ecosystems, with top papers clustered in a small set of elite outlets. That clustering shapes what gets read and rewarded. The study feeds a long debate: does prestige follow quality, or does the journal's name inflate a paper's reach? Ioannidis, known for questioning research habits, gives that debate hard numbers.
aquinas-rickaby-of-god-and-his-creatures:
Thomas Aquinas wrote the Summa Contra Gentiles in Latin in the 1200s, setting out Christian belief through reasoned argument. Joseph Rickaby, an English Jesuit, turned it into English in 1905 with notes and some cuts, and his version is the text given here. Aquinas aimed the work at readers who did not share his faith.

Four books move from God and his nature, through creation and the care of the world, to human acts and last things. The last book treats the Trinity, Christ, and the sacraments. Rickaby's notes flag hard points and dated science. For English readers this was long the most usable door into Aquinas's great summary.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d105: Roosevelt replied to Winant on November 8, 1943, the same day the ambassador's letter in this series was written. The reply is Document 105 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Guidance to London mattered in those days, with two conferences to staff and steer. The record names the parties and the date only. The letter is printed in the Foreign Relations volume beside its companion dispatch.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d205:
Admiral William Leahy, the President's chief of staff, sent President Roosevelt a memorandum on 10 November 1943. It reports the Joint Chiefs of Staff's view on the Soviet request for Italian naval and merchant ships, which Secretary of State Hull had raised in a message of 3 November.

The chiefs draw a careful line. Since the Soviet Union had accepted Italy as a co-belligerent, no Italian ships should change ownership or registry. But Soviet use of the ships to help the war effort is acceptable, so long as title stays Italian. Leahy recommends that the vessels Moscow asked for be made available on exactly those terms.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d305:
Mike Reilly, supervising agent of the United States Secret Service, telegraphed the agent at Cairo from Tehran on 24 November 1943 with travel and security findings for the President's journey. The message was to be shown to Roosevelt himself, along with Hopkins, Watson, and Admirals Brown and McIntire.

Reilly reports the American legation is adequate and a mile from the adjoining British and Russian missions, with no security problems on the route between. He lays out a slow option by air to Abadan and then by rail, crossing the Karun river by small boat, and warns the railroad holds many dangerous security problems. His urgent advice is to fly direct, leaving Cairo at half past seven and reaching Tehran the same afternoon. He asks for the President's decision that night.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d405:
President Roosevelt sent Ambassador Steinhardt a secret instruction from Tehran on 1 December 1943, carrying the invitation to Turkey's president. Having met Marshal Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill will be in Cairo on Saturday and Sunday, 4 and 5 December, with a Soviet representative, and they greatly value a meeting with Inönü.

Steinhardt is to pass the message to Inönü at once, hand it over in person if possible, and impress its extreme secrecy on him. The British and Soviet ambassadors are being told to deliver matching invitations, and the three are to concert a simultaneous presentation. Inönü may consult his parliament in secret session about leaving the country if he feels he must. Roosevelt adds that it would be useful if Steinhardt could accompany the Turkish president to Cairo.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d505:

dunsany-gods-of-pegana-1905:

hyslop-science-future-life-1905:

todd-hydesville-1905:

oliver-dweller-two-planets-1905:

teed-cellular-cosmogony-1905:

warren-eolithic-flints-1905:

jewish-encyclopedia-rothschild-1905:

halevi-kuzari-1905:

wilde-de-profundis-1905:

kuprin-duel-1905:

Hakluyt had saved many; Purchas, holding Hakluyt's own leavings, saved many more.

This volume's narratives show the method at work, testimony printed before its only copy could perish. The tellers are sailors, merchants, and envoys of the early 1600s, speaking close to their journeys. Together they made the Pilgrimes the seventeenth century's great sequel to Hakluyt. Halfway through the modern set, the supply of such voices shows no sign of failing.

Volume eleven opens the second half of the MacLehose Purchas His Pilgrimes, Glasgow, 1905 to 1907. Samuel Purchas first published his collection in 1625, naming it Hakluytus Posthumus for Richard Hakluyt. From Hakluyt's papers and his own searches, Purchas raised the broadest archive of travel his century produced.

The narratives here keep the family character: first-hand, urgent, and close to salt water. Merchants price their goods, captains log their storms, and envoys describe strange courts. Dozens of the texts in the full set survive only in Purchas's print. Volume eleven carries that rescue forward, proof that his net caught what single copies could not hold.

Purchas His Pilgrimes, volume twelve in the twenty-volume MacLehose edition of 1905 to 1907, descends from Samuel Purchas's folio of 1625. Purchas was an Essex clergyman who made himself the heir of Richard Hakluyt. He bought Hakluyt's remaining papers and spent years turning them, with much more, into print.

Readers of this volume meet the same rich traffic as in the rest: voyages, embassies, and trades across the known world. The accounts speak in the words of the travelers, near the hour of their return. Many would be lost today if Purchas had not set them in type. The Pilgrimes still stands as the great sequel to Hakluyt.

Volume thirteen of the MacLehose reprint, Glasgow, 1905 to 1907, continues Samuel Purchas's Purchas His Pilgrimes. The work of 1625 grew from a desk piled with other men's adventures. Purchas, who stayed home, coaxed journals out of sailors and companies until he held the largest voyage hoard of the age.

Printed here, those journals keep the dust of the road and the roll of the deck. The set preserved dozens of narratives that single manuscripts could not have saved. Purchas meant the Pilgrimes as Hakluyt carried on past the grave, and the scale proves the claim. Volume thirteen adds its own voyages to that crowded, seaworthy shelf.

Samuel Purchas's Purchas His Pilgrimes reaches volume fourteen in the MacLehose edition, Glasgow, 1905 to 1907. The original collection of 1625 was a publishing event: four great folios of travel under one editor's name. Purchas had taken Richard Hakluyt's unpublished remains and built outward in every direction.

This volume's share follows the set's rule, testimony first and polish second. Sailors, factors, and missionaries report what they saw, in words set down near the time. Scores of accounts in the Pilgrimes live nowhere else in print or script. For students of the early modern world, that survival is the book's first claim on their shelves.

The fifteenth volume of the MacLehose Purchas, Glasgow, 1905 to 1907, keeps Purchas His Pilgrimes under full sail. Samuel Purchas published the work in 1625 as the heir and rival of Richard Hakluyt. Where Hakluyt had gathered England's voyages, Purchas ranged wider still, printing the travels of many peoples and trades.

Bound in this volume are narratives that Purchas alone preserved from loss. Their tellers write as participants, with a participant's pride, error, and wonder. The whole twenty-volume set forms the standard complete edition of the Pilgrimes. Volume fifteen is no appendix or afterthought: it is main cargo, first-hand and irreplaceable, from the great age of sail.

Volume sixteen continues Purchas His Pilgrimes in the MacLehose reprint of 1905 to 1907, from Samuel Purchas's original of 1625. Purchas edited at a distance, but his sources did not: they are journals and letters written on the spot. The book's full title, Hakluytus Posthumus, declares its descent from Richard Hakluyt's famous collection.

Here the descent shows in method as much as in matter. Purchas prints whole accounts where he can, trusting the traveler's words over his own summary. Dozens of narratives across the set owe their survival to that trust. The Pilgrimes became the largest voyage collection of the seventeenth century, and this volume keeps its decks crowded.

Purchas His Pilgrimes, volume seventeen in the MacLehose edition, Glasgow, 1905 to 1907, nears the end of a twenty-volume voyage. Samuel Purchas began the work with Richard Hakluyt's papers in hand and published it in 1625. He was a clergyman-editor of endless appetite, and the Pilgrimes fed a nation's hunger for news of the world.

The accounts in this volume share the set's plain virtue: they were written by men who were there. Their reports cover trade, discovery, and the meeting of peoples across great distances. Many such texts exist only because Purchas printed them before their copies perished. Volume seventeen keeps the rescue late, full, and seaworthy.

Volume eighteen of the MacLehose reprint, Glasgow, 1905 to 1907, carries Samuel Purchas's Purchas His Pilgrimes of 1625 toward its close. Purchas built the work as Hakluyt's posthumous heir, and said so in his title. The labor took years of gathering from sailors, merchants, and the families of dead travelers.

What that labor saved fills this volume: narratives in the first person, rough with real weather and real risk. The Pilgrimes grew into the largest voyage collection of its century because Purchas refused to let such papers die. Modern readers meet the early global age here without a middleman's polish. Volume eighteen delivers its share of that direct witness.

The nineteenth volume of Purchas His Pilgrimes, in the MacLehose edition of 1905 to 1907, stands one step from the end of the set. Samuel Purchas published the original in 1625, having inherited Richard Hakluyt's papers and Hakluyt's mission with them. That mission was rescue: print the voyages before time eats the manuscripts.

This volume's narratives show the mission still at work near the finish. Travelers tell their own tales of coasts, courts, markets, and storms, in words close to the events. The full set preserves dozens of accounts found in no other source. Volume nineteen holds its place in that archive with undiminished, first-hand weight.

Volume twenty completes the MacLehose reprint of Purchas His Pilgrimes, Glasgow, 1905 to 1907. Samuel Purchas's original work of 1625 closed with the bulk of a small library. In twenty modern volumes, the Pilgrimes stands as the standard complete edition of the seventeenth century's great sequel to Hakluyt.

The final volume keeps the set's character to the last page: voyage narratives told by the men who lived them. Purchas, a stay-at-home clergyman, gave those men a print afterlife that manuscripts could not promise. Dozens of their accounts survive through him alone. To close volume twenty is to finish the largest gathering of travel testimony its age ever made.
cabeza-de-vaca-journey-bandelier-1905:
Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca survived a wrecked expedition and spent eight years crossing North America on foot. His Relación of 1542, given here in Fanny Bandelier's 1905 translation as The Journey of Alvar Nuñez Cabeza de Vaca, tells that passage from Florida to Mexico. He began as a royal officer and ended as a wanderer, trader, and healer among native peoples.

No European had yet described the peoples of the American Southwest, and Cabeza de Vaca did it first. His account mixes hunger and wonder, fear and hard-won respect for those who fed him. The journey stands as one of the great survival stories of the age. It also records a rare, humane meeting of worlds.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol05:
Volume V of the Journal of Discourses, issued at Liverpool in 1858, keeps the sermon record rolling. Brigham Young and his fellow speakers address a people still new to their mountain home. Their words, caught in shorthand and printed abroad, traveled back across the ocean to the very congregations that heard them.

Teaching here is practical as often as it is lofty: how to live, work, worship, and endure. The set's value lies in that closeness to the spoken moment. Volume V adds its year to the running doctrinal record of nineteenth-century Mormonism, one discourse at a time.
lazzarelli-crater-hermetis-1505:
Lodovico Lazzarelli staged a Hermetic dialogue in Crater Hermetis, printed at Paris in the landmark edition of 1505. Mercury instructs his student Tat on the Crater, the divine mixing-bowl in which souls are reborn. The little work rode in great company: Lefèvre's edition joined it with Ficino's Pimander and the Asclepius.

That 1505 volume fixed the Hermetic canon for the Renaissance, and Lazzarelli's dialogue shows the teaching turned toward poetry and vision. The Latin text sings of a second birth granted to those who plunge into the bowl of mind. Readers meet Hermetic thought here at its most ardent and strange.
swanton-haida-texts-and-myths-1905:
Swanton's 1905 bulletin gathers texts and myths he recorded in the Skidegate dialect of Haida, spoken on Haida Gwaii off the British Columbia coast. Like his Tlingit volume, it prints the native words beside English versions, from the Bureau of American Ethnology.

Raven stands at the center of many stories, shaping the islands and outwitting gods and men. Other texts tell of the potlatch, the great feast of giving, and of shamans, spirits, and voyages to the world of the dead. Haida storytellers were famed for long, polished tales, and this book preserves that art in the original tongue.
russell-on-denoting-1905:
On Denoting, published in the journal Mind in 1905, is a paper of barely fifteen pages that founded modern philosophy of language. In it Russell presents his theory of descriptions, and analytic philosophy has lived off the idea ever since.

The puzzle: sentences about things that do not exist, like the present king of France, seem meaningful yet cannot point to anything. Russell shows such phrases are not names at all but structures that dissolve into quantifiers and predicates. The analysis cleared famous tangles in logic and metaphysics at a stroke. Philosophers still teach this paper as the model of their craft.
santayana-life-reason-vol-1-1905:
Reason in Common Sense, published in 1905, opens The Life of Reason, Santayana's five-volume account of how reason grows within human life. This first volume traces the birth of reason in common sense and the imagination.

Santayana describes how the mind, pressed by need and chance, builds a world of objects, selves, and causes out of flux. Common sense is honored as a hard-won achievement, not a naive error. Philosophy begins, for him, by understanding this natural achievement before judging it. The prose is lucid and quietly poetic. It introduces the most graceful philosophical system America produced.
santayana-life-reason-vol-2-1905:
Reason in Society, published in 1905, is the second volume of The Life of Reason. Santayana follows reason out of the single mind into the life men build together: love, the family, industry, government, and war.

Each of these is judged by one standard: how far it serves the harmony of human interests and the life of reason. Santayana praises and blames with an even hand, a Spaniard's eye on Anglo-Saxon pieties. His chapter on love and the family remains much quoted. The volume shows his method at its best, cool appraisal in beautiful sentences.
santayana-life-reason-vol-3-1905:
Reason in Religion, published in 1905, is the third volume of The Life of Reason and Santayana's most famous treatment of faith. He reads religion as poetry and myth: the imagination's picture of man's fate, true as poetry even where it fails as fact.

Trouble comes, he argues, when myth is taken literally, made literal at our peril. He treats prayer, piety, and dogma with sympathy and without belief, being himself an atheist who loved Catholic forms. The book offended the devout and charmed the skeptical. Its balance of reverence and detachment remains unmatched in the philosophy of religion.
santayana-life-reason-vol-4-1905:
Reason in Art, published in 1905, is the fourth volume of The Life of Reason. Santayana turns from religion to art, asking how the love of beauty fits the rational life he has been tracing through mind, society, and faith.

Art, for him, is reason in the realm of sense: the plastic arts, music, and poetry give feeling a formed and shareable shape. He treats fine art and useful craft on one scale, judging both by the harmony they achieve. The writing is measured, aphoristic, and quietly sensuous. The volume completes his survey of man's great pursuits before the final word on science.
chesterton-heretics-1905:
Heretics, published in 1905, is G. K. Chesterton's rejoinder to the fashionable heresies of his day, a book of essays on the writers and doctrines then thought most modern. Shaw, Wells, Kipling, and others are his targets, each honored and opposed.

Chesterton's method is paradox: he agrees that his opponents matter, since heresy means a truth taken seriously, and then denies their conclusions. Behind the fun stands his claim that a philosophy must be livable as a whole. The book made his name as a controversialist. It also prepares the ground for Orthodoxy, its sequel and his most famous book.
perry-approach-philosophy-1905:
The Approach to Philosophy, published in 1905, is Ralph Barton Perry's introduction to philosophy from the standpoint of the new realism. Perry, a Harvard philosopher and James's student and biographer, wrote it to clear the ground for beginners crowded by systems.

He distinguishes philosophy from science, religion, and common sense, and sets out the problems each method can and cannot solve. His manner is patient, exact, and quietly argumentative for the realist cause. The book served as a doorway for students in Perry's generation. It remains a clean specimen of Harvard philosophy in the age of James and Royce.
devries-species-varieties-mutation-1905:
Hugo de Vries, a Dutch botanist, was one of three men who brought Mendel's lost work back to light in 1900. His Species and Varieties, from 1905, sets out his own theory of how new species begin. It rests on years of plant breeding.

De Vries argues that new forms arise by sudden jumps, which he calls mutations. Watching evening primroses throw off new types, he saw change happen at once, not by slow creep. Genetics soon reshaped his idea, but the word mutation stayed. The book marks the birth of modern genetics. Lectures given in America form the core of the text.
plos-pone-0003405:
Jennifer M. Curry and co-authors traced how tumors raise new blood vessels in this 2008 paper. A signal called M-CSF draws scavenger immune cells into tumors. Those cells can help tumors grow vessels, a process called angiogenesis. The team followed the chain from that signal to vessel growth.

M-CSF switched on VEGF, a strong vessel growth factor, in the cells. The switch ran through the MAPK/ERK pathway and a protein named Sp1. In living tissue, that chain led to new vessel formation. Each link in the chain is a point where drugs might cut supply lines.
plos-pone-0003505:
Mathieu Brodeur and co-authors probed illusory shapes with brain waves in this 2008 study. Kanizsa figures make viewers see edges where none are drawn. Studies usually flash the full set of inducer shapes at once. A newer method, the notch mode, builds the inducers bit by bit.

Two early brain waves, P1 and N1, marked stages of that processing. Comparing modes clarified what each wave means for illusion building. The visual system fills in missing contours in steps. Timing those steps helps separate sensing from true perception. Illusions are prized because they reveal the steps normal sight keeps hidden.
plos-pone-0003605:
Adam T. Szafran and co-authors built an imaging platform for hormone signaling in this 2008 paper. The androgen receptor answers male hormones and drives several diseases. Its function shifts with steroids, growth factors, and small molecules. Knowing those shifts matters for prostate cancer and androgen insensitivity syndrome.

High throughput imaging let them analyze receptor function at scale. They could separate effects tied to ligand, cell cycle, and mutations. Automated pictures turn single tests into systematic maps. Such maps speed the search for drugs that tune this receptor. Prostate cancer is one of the most common cancers in men worldwide.
plos-pone-0003705:
Fatemeh Heidary, Mohammad Reza Vaeze Mahdavi, Farshad Momeni, and colleagues published this animal study in PLOS ONE in 2008. People of lower social status die earlier and suffer more disease in many studies. Controlled experiments on inequality itself are rare, for plain ethical reasons. The team used rabbits to model it.

Rabbits fed under unequal food conditions showed worse cardiac health than better-fed peers. The gap in diet stood in for the gap in social standing. The study models in animals how food inequality might wear down the human heart over time.
plos-pone-0003805:
Eisuke Chikayama, Michitaka Suto, Takashi Nishihara, and colleagues published this metabolism methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. Metabolic phenotyping gives a bird's-eye view of an organism's chemistry. The team applied NMR spectroscopy to mixtures of metabolites labeled with stable isotopes.

Their analysis works across plant and animal systems alike. It reads the labeled mixtures to sketch whole metabolic pathways at a coarse grain. In the post-genomics era, such views of chemistry in action complement what gene and protein data alone can show. One shared method serves both kingdoms of life in this work, plant and animal alike.
plos-pone-0003905:
Virginie Rigourd, Caroline Chauvet, Sonia T. Chelbi, and co-authors tested a disputed gene for preeclampsia in 2008. Preeclampsia is a blood-pressure disorder of pregnancy rooted in the placenta. It affects up to one in ten pregnancies. Changes in a gene called STOX1 had been proposed as a cause in 2005.

Later groups doubted that claim, so the question stayed open. The authors raised STOX1 levels in choriocarcinoma cells, a placenta-like cell line. Gene activity in those cells shifted in ways seen in preeclamptic placentas. The match keeps STOX1 in play as part of the disorder's story.
plos-pone-0004005:
George J. Milne, Joel K. Kelso, Heath A. Kelly, and co-authors modeled school closure during flu pandemic in 2008. With little direct evidence, models guide pandemic planning for governments. The team built a model of one small community in detail. It captured exact household structures and daily contacts.

Their PLOS ONE article compares school closure inside individual-based models. Closing schools cuts contacts among children, who spread flu fast. The small community model shows where that helps and where it does not. Planners can use such tests before committing to disruptive closures. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004105:
Susana Campino, Julian Forton, Srilakshmi Raj, and co-authors validated gene control variants in 2008. Finding regulatory variants that tune gene expression challenges genome research. Several studies had tied non-coding variants to expression differences. Those links relied on statistical signals that need confirmation.

Their PLOS ONE article applies allele-specific expression tests to HapMap populations. The method checks whether one gene copy outproduces the other in a person. A real imbalance proves a nearby regulatory variant exists. Validated variants can then be tested for disease roles. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004205:
Timothy Hospedales and Sethu Vijayakumar published this theory paper in PLOS ONE in 2009. Our senses work together to build one accurate picture of the world. The leading framework treats perception as ideal observer inference, weighing each sense by how much it can be trusted.

The authors recast multisensory oddity detection, spotting the one stimulus that differs from the rest, as Bayesian inference. Their model works out what an ideal observer should conclude from combined senses. In plain terms, it asks what a perfect observer would pick. The work gives scientists exact predictions to test against human results in multisensory tasks.
plos-pone-0004305:
Francesca Corlazzoli and colleagues published this epigenetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Chromatin, the packaging of DNA, adapts and responds to cues from inside and outside the cell. The authors hypothesise that inherited abnormal chromatin states in cancer and ageing are caused by genetic or environmental factors. Their earlier work showed that mutation or loss of the retinoic acid receptor RARα disrupts these states.

Here they argue that a derangement upstream of RARα triggers repression of a broad epigenetic network. One broken controller, in their account, can silence many genes at once, a pattern seen in cancer.
plos-pone-0004405:
A checkpoint molecule best known in cancer may also guard the brain. Antje Kroner, Nicholas Schwab, Chi Wang Ip, and co-authors study PD-1 in this 2009 PLOS ONE article. They used a mouse model where oligodendroglia drive inflammation and nerve damage.

In that model, CD8 lymphocytes mediate the immune response. The team asked how the co-inhibitory molecule PD-1 modulates the damage. A brake on immune attack could limit neural injury. The work points to immune regulation as a lever in inflammatory brain disease. Mouse models let the team test checkpoint effects that human studies cannot isolate.
plos-pone-0004505:
Laboratories around the world measure HIV-killing antibodies in different ways, and Eva Maria Fenyo, Alan Heath, Stefania Dispinseri, and co-authors report a joint effort to compare them, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Neutralizing antibodies are central to HIV vaccine research, because a vaccine should raise antibodies that block the virus. Yet it was unclear which assay, or mix of assays, gives a reliable measure of protection.

An international collaboration, called NeutNet, ran the same samples through many labs and methods. Their report compares how the assays agree and where they differ. Vaccine trials cannot be judged if every lab's ruler is different. This kind of shared yardstick is quiet work, but vaccine science depends on it.
plos-pone-0004605:
Creatine supplements did not add to the benefits of weight training in people with HIV. Giorgos Sakkas, Kathleen Mulligan, Makani DaSilva, and co-authors found that in a controlled trial reported in PLOS ONE in 2009. Progressive resistance exercise training improves physical functioning in patients with HIV infection. Creatine can augment training benefits in athletes and improve muscle function in patients with muscle wasting, so the combination looked promising.

The study was randomized, double-blind, and placebo-controlled, the strongest design for such a question. Patients trained, with creatine or a dummy supplement. Creatine failed to augment the benefits, as the title plainly states. A solid negative result saves patients money and hope spent on a supplement that, in this setting, does not deliver.
plos-pone-0004705:
Glyn Elwyn and colleagues built a tool to grade aids that help patients choose care, for PLOS ONE in 2009. Decision aids can be leaflets, videos, or web tools that lay out options and trade offs. Patients and doctors need a fair way to tell good aids from weak ones.

The team built a scale through draft, test, and check stages with other raters. They report how the scale was built and how well raters agree when they use it. A shared scale can lift the quality of aids in clinics. It also helps buyers pick tools they can trust.
freeman-debtor-1905:
Banbridge, the town in Freeman's 1905 novel The Debtor, sits close enough to the great City to see its glow. Trains speed between them, and half the men commute to wrestle for daily bread. Harper issued the book with pictures by W. D. Stevens.

Banbridge keeps its own season of luncheons, teas, dances, and clubs through the winter. Women there run a whist club and a strong club for study and fitness. Against that bright surface, a family slides into debt. Freeman tracks what owing money does to pride, marriage, and standing, in a shrewd study that refuses easy blame.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-05:
Quebec in 1632 and 1633 fills Volume 5, issued by Thwaites in 1897. The mission starts again after an English spell in control of Quebec. Paul Le Jeune's famed Relation stands at the heart of the book.

Le Jeune gives a classic account of Montagnais life in these years. He also sets out the Jesuit plan for winning converts, step by step. Hunting camps, winter cold, and sharp debates fill his long report. Many call his text the key document of early Canadian history. It opens the long St. Lawrence phase of the whole Relations series.
journal-of-discourses-vol-05:
The Move South dominates Volume Five, covering the tense year 1858. Salt Lake City stands empty as the Saints flee before the army. Then, the crisis past, the people return to find their homes intact.

Sermons manage an exodus of thirty thousand people with calm order. Young directs camps, herds, and hope from the pulpit week by week. Relief and thanks mark the return, yet warnings stay sharp too. The army camps nearby, and trust between foes stays thin here. Faith under pressure, at a whole people's scale, fills this striking volume. Later Saints told the Move South as a founding miracle of order.
treaty-of-portsmouth-1905:
Russia and Japan ended the Russo-Japanese War with the Treaty of Portsmouth in 1905. The talks met at Portsmouth, New Hampshire, where President Theodore Roosevelt had pressed both sides to negotiate. Japan's armies and navy had shocked the world by beating a great European power, but both nations were worn out and short of money.

Under the terms, Russia accepted Japan's leading position in Korea and gave up the southern half of Sakhalin Island. Russia also handed Japan its leases and rail rights in southern Manchuria, though it paid no money damages. Roosevelt won the Nobel Peace Prize for his part in the settlement, the first American to receive it.
commons-trade-unionism-labor-problems-19:
Commons edited Trade Unionism and Labor Problems in 1905, early in his career as a labor scholar. Rather than write a treatise, he gathered the essential documents and essays of the young labor movement. The volume was meant for students and readers who wanted the raw material of industrial conflict at first hand.

Selections cover union rules and aims, strikes, boycotts, and the legal fights that surrounded organized labor. Employers, union leaders, and investigators all speak in their own words. Commons adds framing that helps a reader see the labor question whole, as his generation called it. The sourcebook taught a generation of students what unions wanted and why employers resisted, and it remains a useful entry into the debates of 1905.
haitian-constitution-1805:
Haiti proclaimed its first constitution in 1805, a year after winning independence from France. Jean-Jacques Dessalines, leader of the slave revolt that freed the colony, now ruled as emperor of the new state. The charter was the freed people's answer to the world that had held them in chains.

The text declares Haiti free and indivisible, abolishes slavery forever, and bars white men from owning land or property in the country. In its boldest article, it declares all Haitians black by law, whatever their skin, making blackness a badge of citizenship rather than of bondage. The first founding law of a free Black nation stands as the most uncompromising claim of liberty ever written into a constitution. Its defiance shaped Haiti's hard, proud first century.
cia-0000008005:
Looking toward mid-1952, CIA analysts issued another forecast on Indochina in February of that year. The French war against the Viet Minh had settled into a grinding contest for towns, roads, and rice land. Washington watched closely, fearing a communist win in Southeast Asia.

The estimate weighs how much ground each side might hold by summer and what could change the balance. Papers in this series were updated as facts shifted, so each one freezes a moment of judgment. Historians compare them to see how American views hardened over time. This forecast sits early in a long, grim sequence.
cia-0000009805:
Location and description of a prisoner of war camp in Ha Tay province fill a July 1971 CIA report. Ha Tay province surrounds Hanoi on its west and south, hosting several known prison sites. A full description meant layout, guard routine, and prisoner numbers as known.

Descriptions at this detail level served planners who might raid, watch, or one day inspect the site. They also gave debriefers a baseline when freed men described the same walls. Building them took many small reports merged with care. This file is the merged product for one Ha Tay camp, kept current as of 1971.
cia-0000009905:
Two American prisoners, and food stores with them, were moved by the Viet Cong in Tan Uyen district, a November 1966 report states. Tan Uyen lies north of Saigon, in country the Viet Cong contested for years. Prisoners and supplies traveling together show captivity's logistics in plain view.

A prison system is also a supply problem: guards must feed men who cannot feed themselves. Watching food move could reveal where camps sat and how large they were. The pairing of men and stores in one report is therefore no accident. This file preserves that small, telling movement in the southern system.
cia-0000012205:
Syria's Baath party had seized power in stages, and by September 1966 its most radical wing ruled in Damascus. A CIA paper that month, titled Syria's Radical Future, weighs where the revolution would go next. The new rulers preached Arab socialism, feuded with their own party's founders, and leaned toward Moscow.

The paper judges how far the radical course might run at home and abroad. It weighs the regime's hold on a country used to coups and sudden turns. The study captures Damascus at the start of a hard-line era that reshaped Syria's role in the region.
cia-0000012305:
A November 5, 1961 memo from Helms to the DIA director rounds out the year's thickest run of traffic. Its quoted title concerns deployment and breaks off in the file at 'The Deplo...' Soviet writing on how forces deploy was exactly what American planners craved. Deployment speed decided warning time in any war's opening hours, so such pieces were gold.

The correspondence's drumbeat held across twelve months of memos. Formality stayed brisk; the stakes stayed grave throughout. For readers, the page closes the year's survey of a paper mountain, with the new year's dangers already visible on the horizon.
cia-0000023005: Luis Felipe Bellorin was arrested, and the CIA kept the record, with a cover sheet, in a file dated in 1954. The title gives no charge or country, so neither is stated here. Cover sheets routed such items through the right desks at headquarters. An arrest report on a named man was basic field output in the agency's Latin America watch.
cia-0000027105: The situation in Cuba is surveyed in a CIA paper dated in 1958. That year Batista's government was losing its grip as Castro's rebels gained ground in the hills and cities. By New Year's Day 1959 the old order had fled the island. A 1958 situation paper thus catches Cuba on the edge of a change that reshaped the whole Cold War.
cia-0000028305: The Shah's increasing assurance is the subject of a CIA paper dated in 1968. Assurance here means self confidence, and the Shah of Iran had much to feed it: oil wealth, a strong army, and American backing. Judging a ruler's mood was real intelligence work, since his choices steered a whole state. The paper catches that confidence near its high water mark.
cia-0000042705:
An ecumenical council condemned the killing of the Jesuits, in a CIA record dated October 6, 1989 in the catalog. An ecumenical council speaks across church lines, not for one church alone. Its voice carried weight with governments as well as believers.

Inside, the council's condemnation of the murders is preserved as issued. Church bodies rarely speak with one voice, which gave this statement force. The file shows faith communities entering the political fight over the killings. Their verdict was moral rather than legal in form. It reached audiences that no Salvadoran court or party could command on its own.
cia-0000045205:
Guillermo Ungo was interviewed on the kidnapping, in a CIA record dated August 1, 1985. Ungo led the FDR, the political front allied with the guerrillas. His view of the crisis came from outside the government entirely.

Inside, the opposition leader's answers on the case are preserved. He voiced suspicion of the government's handling at every turn. The left had its own strong reasons to keep its distance from the crime. A kidnapping of a president's daughter could stain every cause it touched that autumn. The file holds his voice from the crisis's first weeks, sharp with the distrust that divided El Salvador's politics at every level.
cia-0000049005: The extreme left planned armed actions in El Salvador in late 1980. Its plans included pressure on workers to join the December 3 funerals, and a CIA item holds the report. The funerals were for the murdered FDR leaders, and the left meant them as a show of force. The item shows protest, grief, and armed struggle being planned as one campaign.
cia-0000049105: An allegation named Roberto D'Aubuisson in the assassination of Archbishop Romero, and a CIA item from 1985 preserves the naming. D'Aubuisson, the far right's leader, was the man the left blamed for the murder from the first day. The item survives in the Truth Commission files, where the charge waited for judgment.

plos-pone-0004805:
Iñigo Ortiz de Mendíbil, José Vizmanos, and Francisco Novo studied signatures of selection in fusion transcripts from chromosomal translocations in human cancer, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Recurrence and non random distribution of translocation breakpoints in tumors are usually attributed to local sequence features near breakpoints. However, functional constraints might also delimit the positions and partners of fusions that survive in cancer cells over time.

The team looked for selection signatures in resulting fusion transcripts. Evidence of selection would mean fusions are not random accidents alone. Surviving fusions likely confer growth advantages. That insight helps prioritize fusions as drug targets.
plos-pone-0005405:
Growing nerve fibers steer with a tip called the growth cone, which reads guidance cues and directs the cytoskeleton. Tubulin, the building block of microtubules, carries chemical modifications that affect that steering. Marcos and colleagues tested one modification in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Tubulin tyrosination, the addition of the amino acid tyrosine, proved required for proper growth cone organization. It was also required for pathfinding, the cone's choice of route. A tiny tag on a building block thus helps wire the developing brain correctly. One wrong turn by a growth cone can wire a sense to the wrong place for life. So the small tags that steer it are worth the close care this work gives to each one in turn.
plos-pone-0005505:
Cecilia Gonzalez Campo and colleagues studied a brain protein called reelin in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Reelin is released outside cells and helps build the layered structure of the young brain. It has also been linked to schizophrenia.

The team showed that certain brain cells that calm other cells release reelin in the adult brain. There, reelin helps keep the receptors that receive glutamate, a key excitatory signal, in balance. That balance matters for clear thinking, and its loss may play a part in mental illness. Loss of that balance has been tied to poor thinking in several brain disorders, which gives the work a wider reach.
plos-pone-0005605:
Angela Schoolmeesters, Teresa Eklund, and Devin Leake profiled small RNAs in stem cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Mesenchymal stem cells from bone marrow can be guided to become bone, fat, or other tissues. That makes them strong candidates for repairing injured tissue.

The team mapped which microRNAs change as the cells commit to the bone pathway. Certain microRNAs proved vital to that choice of fate. Knowing the switches helps labs grow the right cell type reliably for therapy. Bone repair after fracture is one clear use, and the microRNA switches may be druggable in time. Reliable control of cell fate is what turns stem cells from a promise into a treatment that clinics can use.
plos-pone-0005705:
Hui Li and colleagues studied mice missing a proton-sensing receptor in 2009, and found effects on both bone and tumors. The receptor, OGR1, reacts to acid levels around cells. In lab tests it had already shown power to slow the spread of prostate cancer when boosted.

Mice without the receptor formed bone-eating cells in abnormal ways. They also grew fewer tumors in the team's tests. That double effect makes OGR1 a puzzle: it touches bone health and cancer at once. Sorting out both roles could point to new treatments for bone loss and cancer spread.
plos-pone-0005805:
Andrea Byrnes and co-authors searched in 2009 for a blood gene signature of chronic fatigue, using identical twins who differ in the illness. Chronic fatigue has no known cause and no lab test, leaving patients in limbo. Twins discordant for the illness control for genes and upbringing at once.

The team scanned gene activity in white blood cells from forty-four evaluated subjects, including the twin pairs. No signature separated the ill from the well, they report. That null result still counts: it rules out an easy blood biomarker of this kind. Research can shift to other tissues or triggers.
plos-pone-0006405:
Stress experienced by parents can echo in the behaviour of their offspring. Daniel Naett and colleagues tested cross-generation effects in chickens in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. They hypothesised that chronic unpredictable food access would make chickens feed more conservatively, and that such adaptations might be inherited.

The study tracked both acquired behaviour adaptations and brain gene expression across generations. Offspring of stressed birds showed matching shifts in habits and brain genes. Inherited stress tuning challenges simple gene-only views of heredity. Farm animal welfare research gains a long-term dimension from such effects.
plos-pone-0006505:
Lucia Talamini and Martijn Meeter modeled a thinking problem in schizophrenia in PLOS ONE in 2009. A large body of evidence suggests impaired context processing in schizophrenia. People with the illness struggle to use setting and background to guide responses. The authors propose that this impairment arises from defective integration in mediotemporal lobe circuits.

Their model gives objects dominance over context. In a healthy brain, context shapes how an object is read; here, the object wins. A working model lets researchers test ideas that are hard to probe in patients. It also ties a symptom pattern to a specific circuit fault.
plos-pone-0006605:
Tita Ritsema and co-authors asked how plants turn sugar into stored fructan in PLOS ONE in 2009. Sugar from outside the cell starts the making of fructan, a stored form of carbohydrate. The cell steps that link sugar to fructan were still obscure. Past work had shown that a step with calcium is part of the chain. The team now asked about small GTPases, a set of protein switches used in many cell paths.

They asked if these switches act as signal hubs in the sugar-driven start of fructan making. Hubs would be prime control points for plant breeders to use. Fructans help plants cope with stress and are also used in foods. The study maps one more part of this sugar sense system.
plos-pone-0009405:
Claude Saegerman and co-authors published this animal disease investigation in PLOS ONE in 2010. Bluetongue virus serotype 8 was first reported in northern Europe in August 2006. It swept through herds in 2007 and 2008, hitting sheep and cattle hard. Where and when the virus first entered remained unknown.

The team worked backward from herd records and outbreak data. They estimated the most likely time and place the virus entered Belgian ruminants. Pinpointing an introduction helps officials understand how the disease crossed into new territory. That knowledge sharpens surveillance at the borders where the next incursion may land.
plos-pone-0009505:
Stephanie Soscia and colleagues offered a new view of a protein tied to Alzheimer's disease in PLOS ONE in 2010. The protein, amyloid beta, builds up in the brains of patients. It is often treated as waste with no normal job. Yet it binds to many partners in the body. The team tested whether it can act against microbes.

In their tests, amyloid beta killed a range of germs, much like known defense proteins do. That suggests the protein has a real role in the brain's defenses. Plaques might then be the leftovers of an immune fight gone too far. The idea reframes how Alzheimer's damage may begin.
plos-pone-0009605:
Amber Hartman and a large team published a full genome in PLOS ONE in 2010. The microbe is Haloferax volcanii, strain DS2. It belongs to the archaea, the third domain of life beside bacteria and eukaryotes. It thrives in very salty water where most life cannot. Labs use it as a model for archaeal biology.

Sequencing its complete genome gives the full list of its genes. Researchers can now plan experiments against a known map instead of guessing. The genome also supports comparisons with other salt loving microbes. Such comparisons show how life adapts to extreme salt, heat, and dryness.
plos-pone-0010405:
Eric Blalock and co-workers tracked aging markers in mice given a diabetes drug long-term, for PLOS ONE in 2010. Pioglitazone helps restore insulin response in type 2 diabetes. It works through a master switch for fat and sugar handling. Reports had suggested such drugs might also slow brain aging in Alzheimer's models. The team measured aging signs in both body and brain after long treatment.

Long use lets benefits and harms both show up honestly. The study read out many markers rather than one, giving a broad picture. Drugs taken for years by millions deserve that kind of checking. Results here inform debates about repurposing diabetes drugs for brain protection. Aging, the authors remind us, is a whole-body process worth measuring widely.
plos-pone-0010505:
Rong Lu and co-workers tracked long-term effects of a Salmonella protein inside living animals in PLOS ONE in 2010. Salmonella infection is common and can linger, raising risks of bowel disease and cancer. One bacterial protein it injects into our cells is AvrA. Evidence suggested AvrA does many jobs, from calming inflammation to altering cell growth. Most studies, though, were in dishes rather than whole animals.

Studying chronic effects in vivo shows what months of exposure do to the gut. That timescale matches the human risks under debate. If one bacterial protein nudges tissue toward disease, it becomes a target for prevention. The study extends AvrA research into realistic, long-term settings. It bridges infection biology and chronic disease research.
plos-pone-0010605:
Orlaith Fraser and Thomas Bugnyar watched ravens after fights, in PLOS ONE in 2010. After a conflict, an uninvolved bird sometimes approaches the loser and stays close. In primates, that kind of contact is often read as comfort.

The ravens did approach recent losers more than other flock members. The contact also seemed to lower later stress and further attacks. The authors weigh comfort against simpler explanations, like seeking safety. Even with care, the pattern looks much like consolation. Finding it in birds suggests concern for others runs deeper in evolution than once thought.
plos-pone-0010705:
Hans Supèr, August Romeo, and Matthias Keil modeled how the brain separates objects from backgrounds, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Seeing a mug on a table feels instant, yet the brain must decide which edges belong to the mug. That border assignment is a core step in vision.

Their model solved the task in one forward pass, without signals looping back. Local edge cues fed a network that assigned borders and split surfaces. The output matched key features of human perception. A forward-only design is simpler to build into machines, so the model interests both brain science and computer vision.
plos-pone-0010805:
Preethi Srikanthan and colleagues combined national survey data on muscle, fat, and blood sugar, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sarcopenia, the loss of muscle with age, often occurs in the same bodies as obesity. Each condition alone is tied to insulin resistance, the core fault of type 2 diabetes. Whether the pair is worse than the sum was the open question.

In the third National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, people with both low muscle and obesity had the worst insulin resistance. Their blood sugar control was also poorer than in either condition alone. Muscle is not just for strength; it is a sugar sink. Keeping muscle while losing fat may matter more than weight alone suggests.
plos-pone-0011005:
Vyacheslav Gurevich and Yona Kassir published this yeast development study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Meiosis, the cell division that makes spores in yeast and eggs and sperm in animals, runs on a cascade of gene regulators switching each other on in sequence. The authors asked a basic control question: does completing the program require each regulator to reach a strong level?

Surprisingly, meiosis tolerated drastic changes in the amounts of its three consecutive positive regulators. The timing of early gene activity did not set when DNA copying began. But the timing of the middle activator did set when nuclear division started. Switching it on early forced division early. That broke coordination with DNA copying. Gurevich and Kassir uncover a design switch, from judging amounts to judging timing, that makes a developmental program run robustly.
plos-pone-0011105:
Hubbe, Neves and Harvati tackled human origins in PLOS ONE in 2010. How and when people first settled the Americas is still argued over. The authors tested rival ideas about migration routes, timing and the spread of early groups across the New World.

By weighing those scenarios against the available evidence, the study shows which accounts fit best. The question matters because this was one of the last great moves of humans across the globe. A clearer picture helps link skull form, genes and climate in one story. It also guides where future digs and studies should look.
plos-pone-0011205:
Drumond, Nieto, Trigo and colleagues traced Brazilian rainfall in PLOS ONE in 2010. The dry northeast of Brazil depends on seasonal rains that begin far from the region itself. Using a method that follows air parcels backward, the team identified the main sources of moisture for both the pre rainy and rainy seasons.

Ocean and land sources fed the region in different shares across the seasons. Knowing where rain water comes from improves drought forecasts. Millions of farmers plan planting around those forecasts. The study links distant seas and forests to the fate of a semi arid region's harvests.
plos-pone-0011305:
Gawlik, Remacle, Shiryaev and colleagues built an ultra sensitive sensor in PLOS ONE in 2010. Furin is an enzyme that cuts proteins, including some used by anthrax toxin to enter cells. The team built a light based sensor able to report furin at extremely low levels on cell surfaces.

Such sensitivity reveals enzyme activity that older tests would miss entirely. Tracking furin could matter for following how anthrax protective antigen is processed. The sensor also suits studies of other diseases where furin plays a part, including some viral infections. Biodefense gains a sharper tool for detecting a key step in toxin action.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1305:
General Groves, who commanded the Manhattan District Project, wrote to Secretary of War Stimson on 18 July 1945. Groves had built the atomic bomb in secret, at sites across America. His message reached Stimson at Potsdam two days after the first test in New Mexico.

A report from Groves at that date could only carry one kind of news: how the new weapon had performed. Stimson waited on exactly that word to brief the president. This entry is the bomb entering the summit's record. Few papers in the volume carry more weight per line, or were read by fewer eyes at the time.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1405:
Another Caffery report to the acting secretary of state bears the date 7 August 1945. The volume prints pairs of Caffery cables for both 6 and 7 August. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

Paired cables across two days give readers a short, dense window into the Paris embassy's work. France's leaders were digesting the Potsdam results and pressing their own claims for a zone and a voice in Germany. Caffery stood between that pressure and a Washington eager to move on. His reports from these days show the squeeze plainly. They close the volume's main run of French papers before the exchange turns to formal notes.
frus-1945-50-intel-d105:
The Fortier Committee sent a memorandum to Director of Central Intelligence Sidney Souers on 14 March 1946. Committees of officers did much of the new group's early design work. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

A committee paper to the director shows the CIG being built by study and report, the Washington way. The Fortier group's work fed the decisions by which the group took over the SSU's operations and set its own shape. Readers can use this memorandum to see the transfer from the receiving end. The remnant is not pleading to survive here. The new body is planning what to take and how to run it. The shift of viewpoint is the story of 1946 in one paper.
frus-1945-50-intel-d205: A text titled "Memorandum for the Record" bears the date 25 January 1947. Readers meet it as document 205 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The first peace-time setup paired the National Intelligence Authority at the top with the Central Intelligence Group below it. Notes to the file look minor, but they fix dates and facts that bigger papers leave vague.
frus-1945-50-intel-d305:
On 29 October 1948, the Director of the Policy Planning Staff (Kennan) sent a memorandum to the Under Secretary of State (Lovett). The Office of the Historian kept it as document 305 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. An outside survey team led by Allen Dulles was then reviewing the CIA, and its findings would drive a round of reform debate.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d405:
One entry in the 1949 record is a Central Intelligence Agency memo dated 21 December 1949. It stands as document 405 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The State Department's Office of the Historian published the volume.

Most papers in the volume name a writer and a reader, but an agency memo speaks for the CIA as a whole. Two years after its birth, the agency was setting its views down in formal papers for the rest of the government. The memo lets readers hear that new corporate voice. The paper's plain heading fits a season when the agency was still learning to speak with one voice.
frus-1861-d105:
On 11 November 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams as the Trent storm gathered. The letter is document 105 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Three days before, a Union captain had seized two Confederate envoys from the British ship Trent. Seward's November letter to London went out as that storm gathered. The whole tie with Britain now hung on the words men like Seward and Adams chose in the weeks ahead. The envoys, Mason and Slidell, were bound for London and Paris when their ship was stopped. Their names, Mason and Slidell, would soon be on every tongue in two capitals.
frus-1861-d205:
On 1 May 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Bradford Wood, his new minister to Denmark. Wood was the new American minister to Denmark. The letter is document 205 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Denmark was a small post, but its straits guarded the Baltic sea road. Seward filled even minor posts with care that spring. His May letter to Wood shows the whole map of the service being set in order at once. Even minor posts closed the gaps through which Southern agents might have slipped. Gaps closed at small posts kept the whole fence sound around the South.
frus-1861-d305:
Writing home was Mr. Bigler's duty, and his letter of 2 August 1861 went to Seward. Congress received it as Document 305 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. The date falls in the first summer of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d105:
Seward heard from Charles Francis Adams on 11 July 1862, in a dispatch sent from abroad. Congress received it as Document 105 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. It belongs to the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d205:
On 14 January 1862 Lord Lyons sent Secretary of State William H. Seward a note printed as Document 205 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It answered into a stream of notes the two men traded through that month.

Lyons prided himself on plain, even dealings with Seward, whom he found changeable but workable. Their written exchanges in January 1862 rebuilt a working tie strained by the Trent crisis weeks before. A single note may treat a small matter; the run of them shows two governments learning to live with a war neither could ignore. The British legation stood a short walk from the State Department, and messengers passed between them daily.
frus-1862-d305:
Three Seward dispatches to Paris are dated 23 August 1862, and the first is Document 305 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. All three went to William L. Dayton, the American minister to France.

A three-letter day at the Department usually meant a steamer sailing and a full desk. The topics across such a set could span the whole Paris brief, from the war to Mexico to trade. For the reader, the trio of 23 August is a snapshot of everything Washington wanted in front of its Paris envoy. It was taken as the summer campaign peaked. A steamer's sailing day set the legation's week, and Dayton wrote against that clock.
frus-1862-d405:
At the height of a hard summer for the Union, on 31 July 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Horace J. Perry in Madrid. The dispatch is Document 405 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

July 1862 brought the Army of the Potomac's retreat from Richmond and fresh fears that Europe might step in. Seward worked to keep foreign courts from reading Union setbacks as collapse. His orders to Madrid in this season carried the government's case to Spain. That court's Cuban ports and Mexican venture made it one the Union could not afford to lose or to provoke.
frus-1862-d505:
On 11 June 1862 James Shepherd Pike wrote from The Hague to Secretary of State William H. Seward. His report is Document 505 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

Pike's June report reached Washington in July, by which time the news it answered was history. That delay shaped all Civil War diplomacy: ministers had to be trusted with wide discretion. Pike used his to keep the Dutch ministry well disposed and well informed, and to report frankly when they were neither. His letters from The Hague, plain and sometimes tart, were among the files Seward could read for Dutch opinion without discounting the writer. The dispatch sustains that run into the summer.
frus-1862-d605:
Dated 21 March 1862, this letter comes from the Spanish commander in Mexico. It is addressed to Admiral Jurien de la Gravière. It answers the French admiral's note of the day before. It is Document 605 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

The catalog heading prints the Spanish general's name as Trim. He is evidently the Prim of the companion papers. Prim's despatch carried the admiral's letter as an annex. The exchange between the two commanders belongs to the allied quarrel that ended with Spain's withdrawal from Mexico within weeks. Read as a pair, Documents 604 and 605 show coalition diplomacy failing in the field. The failure is written in polite, exact language. It is the language officers used when they were parting company.
frus-1862-d705:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles N. Riotte on 6 October 1862. Riotte was the American minister in Costa Rica, and the letter is document 705 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862. A second letter to Riotte followed three days later.

Outward letters in a pair often split one post's business into two short notes. Seward's October letters kept Riotte stocked with word from Washington as the war news turned. They show the State Department's habit of close guidance. It was kept up even for a small legation in Central America, while the Union's fate hung in the balance at home.
frus-1863p1-d105:
Charles Francis Adams received this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward under date of 2 March 1863. It is the ninth of twelve Seward letters to Adams dated that day in the volume. Adams was the American minister in London; the letter is document 105 in part one of the 1863 volume.

By the ninth sheet, Seward had covered the great heads of the London brief and was at its finer points. The batch shows a secretary who knew his file cold and meant his envoy to know it too. This letter is a late piece of that day's work. Its worth is in the set: twelve sheets that reset the brief for spring.
frus-1863p1-d205:
The State Department's mail for London dated 23 May 1863 carried this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 205 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

After emancipation became official policy in January 1863, Seward could argue that aiding the South meant aiding slavery. That argument runs under much of the year's diplomacy. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d305: Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to Charles Francis Adams, his minister in London, on 5 October 1863. It is document 305 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, within the orders that steered American policy toward Britain during the Civil War. Through such letters Washington told its man in London what to press, protest, or let pass.
frus-1863p1-d405:
From the British legation in Washington on 1 March 1863, Lord Lyons sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as document 405 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

London watched for any sign that Washington meant to widen the war. Lyons's job was to read American intentions and report them home faithfully. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d505:
A letter of 9 May 1863, from Lord Lyons to William H. Seward, stands as document 505 in the printed record. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the spring of 1863. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d605:
On 8 August 1863, William H. Seward, the Secretary of State wrote to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
plos-pbio-0020005:
Yoav Gilad, Victor Wiebe, Molly Przeworski, and others compared smell genes and color vision in primates for PLOS Biology in 2004. Primates with full three-color vision tend to have lost more of their smell receptor genes. Those genes are the largest gene family in mammal genomes.

The pattern points to a trade-off in evolution. As some primate lines gained rich color sight, keen smell may have mattered less, so broken smell genes could pile up. The authors test that idea by counting working and broken genes across species. Their result is a clear case study in how senses evolve. It shows how a gain in one system can leave marks across the whole genome.
plos-pbio-0020405:
Vardhman K. Rakyan, Thomas Hildmann, Karen L. Novik, and their team piloted an epigenome study in PLOS Biology in 2004. DNA methylation is a chemical mark that can silence genes without changing the DNA code. The team profiled those marks across the human major histocompatibility complex, a dense region packed with immune genes.

A pilot study tests whether a big project is worth doing. Here it showed that methylation maps of this key region can be built and read. Marks varied by tissue and by gene, as a working control system should. The work helped launch the Human Epigenome Project, which aimed to do for these marks what the genome project did for the code itself.
plos-pone-0000105:
Yan Li, Peter Roycewicz, Evadne Smith, and their team studied flowering time in the plant Arabidopsis in PLOS ONE in 2006. When a plant flowers decides its seed yield and its fit to local seasons. The team bred plants under mixed conditions to find the gene regions, called QTL, that set flowering under both place and season effects.

Local adaptation means each population's timing fits its own home. Lab tests that include varied conditions reveal more of the genes behind that fit than single-condition tests. The work shows adaptation is built from several regions acting together, not one master gene. That lesson guides crop breeding for new climates, where timing must be retuned as seasons shift.
plos-pone-0000205:
Ana G. Popa-Lisseanu, Antonio Delgado-Huertas, Manuela G. Forero, and colleagues published this bat ecology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Its title frames the finding: bats have conquered a formidable feeding niche, the myriads of songbirds that migrate at night. Some bats hunt those birds on the wing, in darkness, high above the ground.

Catching birds in flight at night demands sharp echolocation and bold behavior. The authors present evidence for how bats exploit this seasonal flood of prey. The study redraws part of the night sky's food web, adding bats as serious predators of migrating songbirds.
plos-pone-0000305:
Jasmine I. Daksis and Glen H. Erikson published this diagnostics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It presents a heteropolymeric triplex-based genomic assay, a DNA test design, for detecting pathogens or single-nucleotide polymorphisms, one-letter variants, in human genomic samples. The assay uses triple-stranded DNA structures to recognize its targets.

A single platform that can flag either an infection or a genetic variant is versatile for labs. The authors describe the assay and its detection principle. Work of this kind fed the growth of DNA-based testing that now underpins much of clinical diagnostics.
plos-pone-0000405:
Jianmin Zhong, Algimantas Jasinskas, and Alan G. Barbour treated ticks with antibiotics and measured the cost, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The tick Amblyomma americanum carries bacteria and spreads several diseases to people. The team asked what happens to the tick itself when its resident bacteria are hit with antibiotic treatment.

The authors report that treatment reduced the ticks' reproductive fitness, meaning treated ticks produced fewer or weaker offspring. If a tick depends on its microbes to thrive, those microbes become a target. Hitting them could be a way to control the tick and the diseases it carries. The study links microbiology to pest control through the tick's own body.
plos-pone-0000505:
Ute Becherer and colleagues paired two lab methods to count single release events in hormone cells, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Chromaffin cells release adrenaline in tiny packets. The packets fuse with the cell's outer skin and spill their load out, a step called exocytosis. One method reads the cell's surface electrically as each packet fuses. The other films the packets under a special microscope.

Each method alone leaves gaps. The readings lack pictures, and the pictures lack exact timing. Used side by side, they watch the same event in two ways at once. Tools that can track single packets help research on all kinds of release, from insulin in diabetes to signal release in the brain.
plos-pone-0000605:
Tamar Geiger and Alexander Levitzki tracked how skin cells become dependent on a growth signal as they transform, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Human papilloma virus 16 can drive keratinocytes, the skin's main cells, toward cancer. During early transformation, the cells show loss of robustness and addiction to IGF1, a growth factor they increasingly cannot live without.
