Addiction to a signal is a vulnerability: cut the signal and the transformed cell dies while normal cells cope. Loss of robustness means the cells also lose backup pathways, narrowing their options. Together these changes describe how a virus narrows a cell's life until one growth factor holds the key, a pattern drug developers look for.
plos-pone-0000705:
Laurent Gillet, Janet S. May, Susanna Colaco and colleagues described a viral decoy in a mouse herpesvirus, for PLOS ONE in 2007. Herpesviruses stay infectious for the long term without changing their surface antigens much. So they must evade neutralization, the blocking of virus by antibodies, by other means. Immune sera block this virus in fibroblasts, yet fail in other cell types, sometimes even enhancing infection.

The title names the trick: the viral protein gp150 acts as an immunogenic decoy that limits neutralization. A decoy soaks up the antibody response where it does least harm. Understanding decoys matters for vaccine design against herpesviruses, which have frustrated vaccine makers for decades.
plos-pone-0000805:
Rajnish Joshi, Samir Patil, Shriprakash Kalantri and colleagues X-rayed health care workers who carry silent tuberculosis infection, in PLOS ONE in 2007. More than half of health care workers in high-incidence, low and middle income countries are latently infected with TB. The team determined radiological lesions in a cohort of such workers in India, and their association with T cell immune responses.

Latent infection is supposed to be quiet, so abnormal radiological findings raise questions: old scars, or early disease? Correlating images with immune response could sort harmless findings from warning signs. Health workers are both at risk and essential to TB control, making their silent infections a policy problem, not just a medical one.
plos-pone-0000905:
Wayne Dawson, Kazuya Fujiwara and Gota Kawai offered a practical way to predict knots in RNA folding, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Predicting how an RNA strand folds is often the first step toward knowing its structure. Most tools skip pseudoknots, folded loops that cross each other, because searching for them is slow and complex.

Skipping them, though, leaves real structures out of reach. The authors use heuristic modeling, guided shortcuts, with mapping and step by step folding to make the search workable. Better folding guesses help everyone who studies RNA viruses, gene control and RNA based drugs. The paper is aimed at users who need answers in real time.
plos-pone-0001005:
Leslie Wolf, Alexis Donoghoe and Tim Lane examined how state law affects routine HIV testing, in PLOS ONE in 2007. In 2006, US health officials recommended HIV testing for everyone aged thirteen to sixty-four as a routine matter. That plan would drop separate written consent and required pretest counseling.

State laws, written earlier, often demand exactly those steps. The authors map the clash between the new guidance and standing law. Routine testing aims to catch infections early, since many people learn their status late. Whether it can happen depends on legal details as much as medical ones. The paper is a guide for states weighing updates.
plos-pone-0001105:
Paolo Fabene, Flavia Merigo, Mirco Galie and colleagues studied brain damage in rats given a seizure triggering drug, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Hippocampal sclerosis, scarring in a memory area, marks many temporal lobe epilepsy cases. The neuron loss there was thought to come from excitotoxic injury, overexcited cells burning out, rather than ischemic injury from lost blood flow.

Using pilocarpine to induce status epilepticus, prolonged seizures, in rats, the team assessed vessel structure, gene expression and the time course of neuron damage. Their title says both mechanisms are involved. Splitting the blame changes what protection researchers should try during prolonged seizures.
plos-pone-0001205:
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS, gradually destroys the spinal cord's motor pathways. Svitlana Garbuzova-Davis and colleagues looked for damage to the barrier protecting the spinal cord. Their study, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article, used mice that model the disease. The blood-spinal cord barrier normally controls which molecules and cells pass from blood into cord tissue.

The authors present evidence that this barrier is compromised in both early and late symptomatic SOD1 mice, the standard ALS model. Barrier failure has also been reported in ALS patients. A leaky barrier could let harmful blood components reach motor neurons, making it a possible target for treatment.
plos-pone-0001305:
To prepare for a possible flu pandemic means re-checking old licensed drugs, in case the virus adapts to humans. Dennis Morrison and colleagues ran a randomized crossover study of two such drugs. Amantadine and oseltamivir were given alone and together. The study came out in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The combination pairs an ion channel blocker with a neuraminidase inhibitor.

The study checked how the body handles the combination: how it absorbs and clears each drug when both are present. Combination therapy only makes sense if the drugs do not clash. Their results inform pandemic stockpiling and treatment plans for avian H5N1 infection.
plos-pone-0001405:
Jana van Vliet-Ostaptchouk and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a gene called TUB and body weight. The gene is active in the brain area that steers hunger. In mice, faults in it cause late onset weight gain, insulin issues, and loss of sight and hearing. The team asked whether common variants matter in women.

They checked variants in the gene against body makeup and eating habits in middle aged women. Links found there would tie a mouse lead to human traits. Even weak links help map the gene web behind weight. The study adds one more piece to the search for why bodies store fat so unlike.
plos-pone-0001505:
Simon Overduin and Philip Servos wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE brain scan study on the sense of touch. Scans had been used to map how touch is laid out in the human cortex. Such maps often lean on what was found in monkeys. The pair probed whether human touch maps mirror each other across body sides.

Their scans show a neat mirror layout for touch sense in the cortex. That layout fits a symmetric plan for the two body halves. A clear map helps brain surgery and stroke care, where touch zones must be spared. It also frees human maps from sole reliance on monkey data.
plos-pone-0001605:
Jeffrey Alten and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on collapse from blood loss after trauma. Half of trauma deaths come from this collapse of blood flow. The team built a rat model that pairs a mild wound with grave blood loss. In that model, heart output fell by half and death loomed.

They show a signal protein, switched on before the shock, can ward off the collapse. The protein acts through a known cell switch in the liver and vessels. A ward that works when given ahead of time fits planned surgery and high risk care. It also names a path for drugs to copy.
plos-pone-0001705:
Oumaya Bouchabke and co-authors used natural variation in a weed to study drought responses in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The plant is Arabidopsis thaliana, the standard lab plant. Wild accessions, lines collected from different places, differ in their genes. The team asked whether those differences could reveal the genetic basis of drought response.

They characterized a set of accessions, most from a core collection chosen to capture the species' genetic diversity, under dry conditions. The full text gives the accessions' traits and how their drought responses differed. Natural variation is a free experiment run by evolution, and mapping it can find drought genes that breeding could later move into crops.
plos-pone-0001805:
David Vallenet, Patrice Nordmann, Valérie Barbe, and their co-authors compared the genomes of three Acinetobacter bacteria in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Acinetobacter baumannii causes many hospital infections in humans. Strains resistant to many drugs, or even to nearly all drugs, were reported more and more worldwide. To study its way of life, researchers need relatives that live differently for contrast.

The team compared two new genomes with a third, covering three ways of life in one study. The full text gives the genome maps and the gene gaps tied to each way of life. Genes unique to the hospital germ are leads for drugs and tests against a germ that resists nearly all drugs.
plos-pone-0001905:
Takahiro Suzuki and co-authors checked a chemical mark on DNA in cloned mice, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Cloning by moving a body cell's nucleus into an egg can make animals that match the donor in genes. Yet clones often show odd traits and odd gene activity, so something beyond the gene code must go wrong.

The team scanned the whole genome for faults in acetylation, a mark that helps switch genes on, at a site called H3K9. They looked for spots where clones depart from normal mice. Such faults may explain why clones grow in odd ways. The work also bears on stem cell care, where cloning is hoped to yield spare tissue.
plos-pone-0002005:
Sandra Kuhlman and Josh Huang shared a method to label and steer chosen neuron types in the mouse brain, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The brain mixes many neuron types, and testing the job of one type calls for tools that act only on that type, at fine detail. Their method pairs Cre-knockin mice, in which a gene switch sits in one cell type, with viruses that carry genes.

The viruses were built to express a green glow protein, a red one, or channelrhodopsin, a light-gated channel, only where the switch is on. The kit lets labs both see a neuron type and drive it with light.
plos-pone-0002105:
Liran Shlush and co-authors read the genes of the Druze as a window on the old Near East, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Mitochondrial DNA haplogroups, sets of variants passed down the female line, are usually strongly partitioned by global region. The X haplogroup is a unique exception, spread widely with no clear home region.

The team examined variation in mitochondrial DNA among the Druze, a small, close-knit community of the Near East. As the title frames it, the Druze act as a population genetic refugium, a refuge where old lineages persist. Such refuges preserve patterns erased elsewhere by mixing.
plos-pone-0002205:
Ahmed Moustafa, Adrian Reyes-Prieto, and Debashish Bhattacharya counted genes that one ancient cell passed to the ancestors of plants, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The plastid, the green compartment that runs photosynthesis, began when an early cell captured a cyanobacterium and kept it. That event seeded the line leading to red algae, green algae, land plants, and glaucophytes.

The team traced genes from Chlamydiae, a separate bacterial group, into the plant line. They found at least 55 such genes, most of them now serving the plastid. The count shows the plastid's origin story involved more donors than the textbook version suggests.
plos-pone-0002305:
Marisa Mazari-Hiriart and co-authors assessed water quality where treated wastewater is reused for farming near Mexico City, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Recycling wastewater for irrigation is common in developing countries and can expose people to microbes through water, soil, and crops. The balance of benefit and risk needed local evidence.

The team ran a longitudinal study in a periurban agricultural area, sampling water over time and weighing the health implications. Their data show what residents and farm workers actually face. Findings like these help cities reuse scarce water with clearer eyes about treatment and hygiene.
plos-pone-0002405:
MacKenzie and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Julia J. MacKenzie, Noé D. Gómez, Souvik Bhattacharjee, among others. Its subject is a Plasmodium falciparum Host-Targeting Motif Functions in Export during Blood Stage Infection of the Rodent Malarial Parasite Plasmodium berghei. Plasmodium falciparum sends hundreds of proteins, including major virulence proteins, into the host red blood cell.

To reach the host cell fluid, most of these proteins carry a short host-targeting motif of 11 amino acids. The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002505:
Mutalima, working with fellow researchers, published a study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Nora Mutalima, Elizabeth Molyneux, Harold Jaffe, among others. Its subject is associations between Burkitt Lymphoma among Children in Malawi and Infection with HIV, EBV and Malaria. The title goes on to note results from a Case-Control Study. Burkitt lymphoma, a childhood cancer common in parts of sub-Saharan Africa, has been linked to Epstein Barr Virus (EBV) and malaria.

The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002605:
Kalita and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Mridul K. Kalita, Umesh K. Nandal, Ansuman Pattnaik, among others. Its subject is cyclinPred: A SVM-Based Method for Predicting Cyclin Protein Sequences.

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work. Each claim is tied to the work the team did, and the text keeps facts apart from the views of the authors.
plos-pone-0002705:
In 2008, Rui Wang and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was identification of a regulatory t cell specific cell surface molecule that mediates suppressive signals and induces foxp3 expression. Authorship is credited in the record to Rui Wang and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Regulatory T (T reg ) cells control immune activation and maintain tolerance. A further point appears in the abstract. How T regs mediate their suppressive function is unclear. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002805:
In 2008, Kathryn E. Reif and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was prevalence and infection load dynamics of rickettsia felis in actively feeding cat fleas. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Kathryn E. Reif, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Rickettsia felis is a flea-associated rickettsial pathogen recurrently identified in both colonized and wild-caught cat fleas, Ctenocephalides felis . A further point appears in the abstract. We hypothesized that within colonized fleas, the intimate relationship between R. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002905:
David Miles, Marianne van der Sande, David Jeffries and colleagues revisited Gambian infants two years after cytomegalovirus infection in 2008. Their earlier study had found large groups of mature CD8 T cells soon after infection in young infants. Those groups stayed in place through the first year that followed.

The follow-up, published in PLOS ONE, asks whether such large subpopulations of these immune cells are still maintained at two years. That matters because cytomegalovirus is caught very early in life in the Gambia. The results inform how lasting effects of infant infection shape the growing immune system.
plos-pone-0003005:
Konstantinos Kostarakos, Manfred Hartbauer and Heiner Römer linked matched filters, mate choice, and trait evolution in 2008. Understanding communication means studying both variation in signals and how receivers respond to it. Receiver preferences in turn shape how signals vary over generations.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the authors examine how a receiver tuned like a matched filter affects the evolution of sexually selected traits. A matched filter responds best to one signal form. The framework helps explain why some courtship signals stay narrow and stereotyped instead of drifting widely. Anyone can read the full text free of charge through the journal's open access site.
plos-pone-0003105:
Wubei Dong, Xiaojia Tang, Yihai Yu and co-authors modeled the biological clock of the fungus Neurospora crassa in 2008. Their model-driven process, called Computing Life, identifies ensembles of genetic networks describing the clock. The mechanism involves the genes white-collar-1 and white-collar-2, which encode a transcriptional activator.

Systems biology here means fitting network models to data rather than testing one gene at a time. Published in PLOS ONE, Neurospora is a classic clock model, and an ensemble approach admits several networks may fit. That honesty about uncertainty can guide sharper experiments. The complete article sets out the methods and data behind each claim in full.
plos-pone-0003205:
Olena Morozova, Vyacheslav Morozov, Brad G. Hoffman and colleagues present a visualization approach for gene expression data in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Serial Analysis of Gene Expression, or SAGE, is a DNA sequencing-based method for large-scale profiling that offers an alternative to microarray analysis. Most analyses of SAGE data aimed at finding co-expressed genes had used various versions of clustering.

The authors offer a seriation approach for visualization-driven discovery of co-expression patterns in SAGE data. Readers get a method that orders data so patterns become visible to the eye. Visual discovery can reveal gene groups that rigid clustering rules might split apart.
plos-pone-0003305:
Tu-Anh Tran, Marie-Ghislaine de Goër de Herve, Houria Hendel-Chavez and colleagues study resting T cells as an HIV reservoir in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In HIV-infected patients on long-term effective therapy, virus persistence in resting long-lived CD4 T cells is a major barrier to curing the infection. Cell quiescence, by favouring HIV latency, reduces the risk of recognition and destruction by cytotoxic lymphocytes.

The authors characterize resting regulatory CD4 T cells as a site of HIV persistence in patients on long-term therapy. Readers learn which quiet cells shelter the virus from drugs and immunity. Cure research must reach exactly such reservoirs.
plos-pone-0007405:
Catalin Vasilescu, Simona Rossi, Masayoshi Shimizu, and colleagues searched blood microRNAs for sepsis prognosis markers in 2009. The physiology of sepsis remains poorly understood. Despite advances in management, sepsis is life-threatening with poor outcomes, and earlier warning of deterioration could save lives in intensive care units worldwide.

New diagnostic markers tied to sepsis mechanisms could enable specific therapies. The authors build microRNA fingerprints from patient blood. They identify miR-150 as a plasma prognostic marker in sepsis patients. A blood marker that forecasts outcome could help doctors triage care and test treatments.
plos-pone-0007505:
Yih-Horng Shiao and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 reporting an unusual RNA found in lung cancer cells. Between genes, the team detected a non-coding RNA related to ribosomal RNA. Ribosomal RNA is the core of the cell's protein-making factories. A stand-alone relative sitting between genes was unexpected. The authors measured how its levels relate to the cell's normal rRNA output.

The molecule's levels tracked with how much regular rRNA the cells produced. They also tracked with how often a single-letter variant appeared in the rRNA gene. Those correlations hint that this overlooked RNA takes part in managing the protein factories. Lung cancer cells push protein production hard, so such a manager could matter. The study flags a molecule most surveys would have ignored. It invites a closer look at what intergenic RNAs do.
plos-pone-0007605:
Louise Strandberg and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on sepsis, the body's dangerous overreaction to infection. Sepsis is often caused by gram-positive bacteria, especially Staphylococcus aureus. Few effective therapies exist, so knowing what predisposes patients matters. Obesity was their suspect. The team fed mice a high-fat diet for a long period, then induced sepsis and compared the outcomes with lean mice.

The chronically fat-fed mice died more often. Their immune response to the infection was disturbed as well. Chronic overeating thus does more than strain the heart and metabolism. It rewires immunity in ways that show up when infection strikes. That link helps explain worse sepsis outcomes in obese patients. The study gives the clinic a mechanism to think with: diet history as immune history.
plos-pone-0007705:
Matthew Hirsch and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It describes a method for editing genes with a virus called AAV. Short pieces of single-strand DNA, called oligonucleotides, can guide precise changes. The virus triggers a brief DNA damage response in the cell it enters.

During that response, the cell's repair tools rebuild the viral genome into circular forms. The authors harness that moment to steer small, targeted edits into DNA. The technique, called recombineering, offers a gentle way to rewrite short stretches of genetic code. Such tools matter for gene therapy research.
plos-pone-0007805:
Jingxian Liu and Jianxing Song published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It finds a new way to study proteins that clump together. Protein aggregation inside the body is linked to many human diseases. Yet clumped proteins will not dissolve, which blocks close study of the process.

The authors took insoluble mutants of the SH3 domain, a common protein part. They dissolved them in salt-free water, against expectations. Then they used NMR to read the proteins' structure in detail. The trick opens aggregation itself to high-resolution study. That could reveal how clumps form and how to stop them.
plos-pone-0007905:
David Mutch and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It profiles body chemistry after a common weight-loss operation. Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery brings weight loss and better insulin sensitivity. It also cuts related illnesses such as diabetes and heart disease.

The many metabolic adaptations behind those gains are still being mapped. The team used metabolite profiling on patients after surgery. They identified candidate markers that reflect the clinical adaptations. Such markers could tell doctors which patients are responding well. They may also reveal how bypass surgery resets metabolism, beyond simple restriction of food.
plos-pone-0008005:
Rodrigo Suarez and colleagues mapped smell wiring in a small Madagascan mammal for PLOS ONE in 2009. The lesser tenrec uses a vomeronasal system to read scent signals from its own kind. In most mammals, two cell groups in that system send their wires to strictly split zones of the brain.

In the tenrec, the two groups' wires mix and even swap zones, ending together in single target balls. That merged map breaks a rule long thought fixed for mammals. Odd wiring like this is a gift for science: it shows which parts of the smell map can bend as species evolve.
plos-pone-0008105:
Vijaya Kolachalama and colleagues modeled drug flow from stents at artery forks in PLOS ONE in 2009. Stents that leak drugs are now standard for propping open clogged arteries. Forks, where one artery splits in two, are the hardest spots to dose evenly.

Their model showed blood flow itself boosts how much drug settles from the stent into the fork walls. Flow, long treated as a mere carrier, is an active part of dosing. Stent designs that work with the flow, rather than ignoring it, should coat forks more evenly and heal them better.
plos-pone-0008205:
Hannah E. Jones and colleagues examined bacteria in fetal membranes in a PLOS ONE study from 2009. Infection inside the womb may help trigger early labor. It may also play a role when membranes rupture too soon. Many bacteria linked to early birth are hard to grow in the lab. So the team turned to molecular methods instead.

They compared membranes from very preterm births with those from births at term. Both the frequency and the mix of bacterial species differed between groups. Such data help clarify how hidden infection relates to early delivery. They may guide efforts to prevent preterm birth.
plos-pone-0008305:
Deverick Anderson and his team wrote in PLOS ONE in 2009 about wound germs that resist drugs. Some germs that infect a wound after surgery can shrug off a key drug, methicillin. These germs are called MRSA, a form of the germ Staphylococcus aureus. What MRSA itself adds to harm and cost was not well known. Past work gave mixed answers on that point.

The team ran a matched study of 659 surgical patients in more than one center. Each sick patient was matched with a like patient for a fair test. They weighed both health results and money costs tied to the drug-proof germs. Clear counts help wards judge how much it is worth to stop such germs.
plos-pone-0008405:
Alan C.-N. Wong, Thomas J. Palmeri, Baxter P. Rogers, and colleagues asked how the way a person learns about an object changes the brain's picture of it, in PLOS ONE in 2009. That experience reshapes object representations in the visual cortex was already known. What was not known is whether the kind of learning matters. Learning can take many forms, and each might leave a different mark on the cortex.

The team used contrasting training programs to teach people about objects, then measured the cortical patterns that followed. How the objects had been learned changed how the visual cortex represented them. Two people can thus look at the same object while their brains file it differently. The result matters for teaching and for retraining vision after brain injury.
plos-pone-0008505:
James Thomas and co-authors study a fertility gene in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The gene is PRDM9, also called Meisetz. In mice, mismatched forms of PRDM9 can cause hybrid male sterility. That sterility can isolate populations and may help form new species. Mice lacking PRDM9 are sterile in both sexes. Their meiosis, the cell division that makes sperm and eggs, stalls early.

The author traces how fast PRDM9 has evolved across species. Its change is described as extraordinary in speed and pattern. Rapid change fits a gene caught in an evolutionary arms race. The paper helps explain hybrid sterility and speciation.
plos-pone-0008605:
Sarah Huber and co-authors study immunity in Darwin's finches in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Invasive parasites are a major threat to island animal populations. Darwin's finches of the Galapagos face introduced pox virus and nest flies. The fly Philornis downsi harms nestlings in their nests. The team developed assays for parasite-specific antibody responses in the medium ground finch. That finch is Geospiza fortis, a classic Darwin species.

They find invasive parasites trigger acquired immunity in the finches. Birds exposed to the parasites mount antibody defenses. Such ecoimmunity may help finches persist under new parasite pressure. It also shows island species can adapt immunologically, not just genetically.
plos-pone-0008705:
Ronan Murray, James Robinson, Jodi White, and colleagues reported a dangerous pairing seen during the flu pandemic. Their 2010 PLOS ONE article describes pneumonia caught outside hospitals. The culprits were pandemic H1N1 flu together with MRSA, a drug-resistant staph germ. Bacterial lung infection has long been a known flu complication. Resistant staph made that complication harder to treat.

The authors describe the co-infected patients and their illness course. Two germs at once can turn a flu case fatal fast. Quick recognition matters because standard antibiotics may fail against MRSA. The report warns clinics to suspect this pairing early.
plos-pone-0008805:
Davide Corti, Johannes Langedijk, Andreas Hinz, and colleagues mined HIV patients' immune memory for rare antibodies. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. A vaccine against HIV remains a central unmet goal. A few infected people make antibodies that neutralize many viral strains. Those rare antibodies mark weak spots on the virus. Memory B cells store the recipes for them.

The team screened memory cells and isolated new monoclonal antibodies. Some neutralized a broad range of HIV-1 strains. Each broad antibody teaches vaccine designers what shape to imitate. The work brings an antibody-guided vaccine closer to reality.
plos-pone-0008905:
Hui Yang, Chao Liu, Yongwang Zhong, and colleagues showed the Huntington protein jamming a cell disposal machine. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Huntington disease comes from an overlong repeat inside the huntingtin protein. How that change kills brain cells remains uncertain. Expanded huntingtin stresses the cell's protein-folding compartment. The disposal system, which shreds worn proteins, may be part of the story. An enzyme called gp78 tags proteins for that shredding.

Huntingtin bound a domain of gp78 and blocked its work. It stopped gp78 from gripping both ubiquitin tags and the p97 helper. A jammed disposal route could poison neurons over years. The block names a fresh target for Huntington therapy.
plos-pone-0009005:
Mohammed Ali and co-authors tested a suspected helper in HIV's escape from human cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Human cells fight HIV with tetherin, a protein that pins new virus particles to the cell surface. HIV answers with its protein Vpu, which defeats tetherin somehow. The protein CAML was a candidate partner in that counterattack.

The team removed or added CAML and watched virus release. Tetherin worked the same with or without CAML present. So CAML does not tune the restriction on HIV-1 particles. Ruling out a plausible suspect narrows the search for how Vpu really works.
plos-pone-0009105:
Brian Layden and co-authors surveyed a huge family of cell receptors in embryonic stem cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. G protein coupled receptors are the largest receptor family in the body. They had barely been studied in embryonic stem cells. Knowing which signals steer these cells is vital for cell replacement therapy.

The team focused on Gs-alpha signalling, one arm of the family. That pathway proved to play a real role in stem cell behaviour. Mapping active receptors shows which chemical levers labs can pull. Such levers could guide stem cells into the tissues doctors need.
plos-pone-0009205:
Lin Chen, Wanliang Shi, Hui Li, and co-authors published this infection study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It brings together two public health problems: opioid use and tuberculosis. Both can harm the lungs, but how they do so was unclear. The study asks how the two insults interact inside the body.

The team gave mice long-term morphine and infected them with the tuberculosis bacterium. They report that a sensor protein called Toll-like receptor 9 plays a critical role in what followed. With both insults present, lung cells died by apoptosis, a tidy form of cell suicide. The finding ties an immune sensor to the extra damage seen when the two problems combine.
plos-pone-0009305:
Carmen Blanco-Aparicio and co-authors published this breast cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2010. A signaling protein called AKT shows up at high levels in many human breast cancers. That rise usually follows faults in the PTEN/PI3K pathway, a control circuit for cell growth. How extra AKT actually pushes tumors to form was the open question.

Using mouse models, the team explored what stronger AKT activity contributes to mammary tumors. Their work separates AKT's own push from the effects of the broken pathway around it. Knowing which part drives growth matters, because drugs that block AKT are judged by exactly that. The study maps AKT's share of blame in tumor formation.
plos-pone-0011405:
Simon Zeller and co-authors grew genetically modified wheat under varied conditions in 2010 to measure how genes and environment interact. A wheat line carrying an added gene may thrive in one field and disappoint in another, because soil, weather, and pests all change what the gene does. Regulators often judge such wheat from trials in a narrow set of conditions.

Their field work showed that the added gene's effects on the plant shifted with the environment in which it grew. The same line could look beneficial in one setting and neutral or costly in another. That variability carries a clear lesson for approval and farming alike. A transgene should be judged across the range of conditions where farmers will actually grow it, not from a single favorable trial.
plos-pone-0011505:
Dineke Frentz and co-authors compared in 2010 the rulebooks doctors use to read HIV drug resistance. HIV mutates to dodge drugs, and genotypic tests read the virus's DNA changes to predict which drugs will still work. Several interpretation systems translate the same DNA into advice, and they sometimes disagree, leaving doctors unsure which to follow.

The team tested how well each system predicted patients' actual viral outcomes over time on treatment. A head-to-head comparison on real outcomes, not opinion, tells clinics which rulebook best forecasts whether a drug combination will hold. Choosing the better interpreter can mean fewer failing regimens and less resistance built by trial and error. The study serves everyday HIV care directly: the test is only as good as the rules that read it.
plos-pone-0011605:
Erica Larson and Alexander Idnurm traced the history of a fungal gene in PLOS ONE in 2010. The gene, called leuA, makes an enzyme fungi need to build leucine, an amino acid that humans and animals cannot make. Because people lack this pathway, it has been proposed as a target for antifungal drugs.

Larson and Idnurm found the gene in a group of early fungi and compared its history across species. The evidence points to two separate origins for the same enzyme in fungi. Finding that nature arrived at the same tool twice reshapes how researchers read fungal evolution and judge drug targets.
plos-pone-0011705:
Sean Rands modelled how effort by single animals sharpens what a whole group knows, in PLOS ONE in 2010. By foraging carefully or scanning for predators, an animal improves its own picture of the surroundings. Group members can also tap the shared pool of information that others gather.

Rands asked how much private effort is worthwhile when public information is also available. His model shows when extra individual work pays off for the group as a whole and when it does not. The result helps explain how social animals balance doing their own work against copying neighbours.
plos-pone-0011805:
Daniel Casasanto and Kyle Jasmin analysed the hand gestures of politicians speaking, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Body-specificity theory holds that people with different bodily traits form different mental representations, even for abstract ideas. An earlier test found right- and left-handers associate good things with their dominant side.

The authors tracked spontaneous gestures during positive and negative political speech. Speakers' hands added their own commentary, favouring one side for good content and the other for bad. The pattern links handedness, gesture and abstract value, suggesting the body quietly shapes how politicians, and voters, frame good and bad.
plos-pone-0011905:
Christopher Record and colleagues compared in 2010 the three-dimensional structures of the four human MST kinases. These enzymes, related to the yeast Ste20 kinase, help control cell death, cell growth, and cell polarity. Their faulty regulation has been linked to prostate and colorectal cancer, yet the four family members are switched on in different ways.

A side-by-side structural comparison shows where the four enzymes match and where their shapes part company. Those differences explain how one family can serve several control jobs without mixing signals. For drug design, the map highlights which pockets are shared and which are unique enough to target a single member.
plos-pone-0012005:
Kerstin Johannesson and co-workers examined in 2010 the indiscriminate mating of male marine snails. In promiscuous species, males gain from mating often, since each mating may add offspring. Females gain little past an optimal number of matings, and extra ones can cost them, setting up a sexual conflict.

The study asks whether male snails' refusal to be choosy, mating with partners of little benefit, reflects that conflict compromising their behavior. Males that cannot afford to pass up chances may waste effort or even mate with the wrong targets entirely. The snails make a tidy test of how far selection pushes males toward quantity over judgment.
plos-pone-0012105:
Seiichi Kanzaki, Akira Yamaguchi, Kayoko Yamaguchi, and co-authors examined the thymus gland in mice with a storage disease, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The mice model Sandhoff disease, in which a missing enzyme lets fatty material build up in cells, slowly harming the brain. The thymus, a small gland that trains immune cells, had drawn the team's interest in earlier work on these mice.

They describe how the gland changes as the disease advances in this model. Immune changes are easy to overlook in a disease known for nerve damage, yet they may shape how the illness unfolds. Mapping them gives researchers a fuller picture of the disease and more places to look for ways to slow it.
plos-pone-0012205:
Rea Tschopp, Abraham Aseffa, Esther Schelling, and co-authors surveyed cattle tuberculosis where herds, wildlife, and herders meet in southern Ethiopia, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The disease is well documented in Ethiopia's highland cattle but had never been studied among the pastoralist herds of the South Omo region. There, cattle, wild animals, and people live in unusually close contact.

Their survey measured how common the disease is at that busy crossroads. Bovine tuberculosis can pass to people through milk and close contact, so the number sets the risk for herding families too. First measurements in an unstudied region are what control programs, and honest advice to herders, are built on.
plos-pone-0012305:
Owen Woodward, Yun Li, Shengqiang Yu, and co-authors identified a cut piece of the polycystin-1 protein in PLOS ONE in 2010. The inherited disease behind this protein fills kidneys with cysts until they fail, and it traces to faults in either of two genes. Polycystin-1 is a huge membrane protein, and the team found it is clipped to release a fragment with a job of its own.

The fragment, called P100, controls how calcium enters cells through a store-operated route, by working with the calcium sensor STIM1. Calcium mishandling is a leading theory for why cysts form. Each piece of this pathway clarified brings the disease's first cause closer to a druggable step.
plos-pone-0012405:
David Rosen, Santosh Putta, Todd Covey and colleagues profiled single leukemia cells to map how they answer DNA damage, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Acute myeloid leukemia varies hugely between patients, and drug response varies with it. Using a method that reads signals inside many single cells, the team compared damage responses with each sample's growth pathway profile.

Distinct patterns of damage response and cell death lined up with Jak/Stat and PI3 kinase pathway states. Those links suggest which patients' leukemias might yield to which drugs. Single-cell profiling of this kind moves leukemia care toward matching treatment to the signaling habits of each patient's cancer.
plos-pone-0012505:
Erum Khan, Mehreen Kisat, Nabil Khan and colleagues reviewed dengue fever cases in Pakistan across 2003 to 2007, in a 2010 PLOS ONE retrospective study. Dengue's pattern in Pakistan had changed greatly over two decades, and small local studies disagreed with each other. A pooled national picture was needed to plan hospital and mosquito control responses.

The team assembled patient records to describe who fell ill, where, and with what clinical features. Their profile shows the age and seasonal patterns outbreaks followed in those years. Solid baseline data like this let health officials spot when a new season breaks pattern and demands a faster, bigger response.
plos-pone-0012605:
Carpaneto, Koepsell, Bamberg and co-authors examined a protein that moves sugar through maize plants. Most higher plants ship sucrose, a sugar, from leaf to root and grain. The gate for that trip in maize is a transporter named ZmSUT1, driven by protons crossing the cell membrane.

Their 2010 study measured tiny electric charges that shift as the gate opens and closes. Both sugar and protons changed those charge movements, revealing steps in how the transporter works. Understanding this gate matters for crop science, because sugar flow sets how well a plant fills its grain.
plos-pone-0012705:
Huo, Yao, Wang and co-authors shrank tumours in mice with a virus cocktail carrying part of the telomerase gene. The fragment, hTERTC27, comes from the tail end of human telomerase, an enzyme most cancers switch on. Earlier work showed the fragment curbs HeLa cell growth and tumour formation.

Their 2010 study gave the cocktail under the skin of mice with melanoma and saw growth held back. Using a piece of the cancer's own machinery against it is an elegant trick. The result supports more work on this fragment as a cancer treatment base.
plos-pone-0012805:
Reitzel, Behrendt and Tarrant watched daily clock genes respond to light in a sea anemone. Circadian rhythms run the day-night cycles of behaviour and body function in most animals. Nematostella vectensis, a simple anemone, sits near the root of the animal family tree, making its clock a clue to the clock's origin.

Their 2010 study found rhythmic gene activity tied to light in this simple animal. A working clock in such an early branch suggests the animal clock is truly ancient. That reshapes the story of how timekeeping evolved.  Daily cycles were tested under changing light schedules too.
pmc-2633005:
Bursac, Gauss, Williams, and co-authors discuss purposeful selection of variables in logistic regression. Logistic models predict a yes-or-no outcome from many possible factors. Builders must choose, from a large set of candidate factors, which ones belong in the best model.

Choices may rest on clinical sense or on statistical strength, and several selection methods compete. The authors argue for a purposeful approach that mixes both grounds and checks each step. Better variable choice yields models doctors can trust for risk prediction, rather than models that merely fit one dataset by chance.
pmc-3176805:
Song, Dong, Long, and co-authors present REST, a toolkit for processing resting-state brain scan data. Resting-state fMRI records brain activity while a person lies still and does nothing in particular. Interest in the method had grown fast, since resting patterns reveal how brain regions connect.

No publicly available, well-integrated, and easy-to-use tool for this data yet existed, the authors say. REST fills that gap with a systematic processing pipeline. Easy tools widened the resting-state field, letting smaller labs study brain networks in health, ageing, and mental illness.  Group studies of meditation and sleep adopted the toolkit for resting data.
pmc-3436805:
Rausch, Zichner, Schlattl, and co-authors present DELLY, a tool for discovering structural variants in genomes. Structural variants are large gains, losses, or rearrangements of DNA. Finding them with high sensitivity and specificity is essential for describing natural variation and disease-causing changes in personal genome sequencing.

DELLY integrates two kinds of evidence: paired reads spaced oddly along the genome, and split reads that cross a breakpoint. Combining both signals catches variants either signal alone would miss. The tool became a standard choice for genome studies of rare disease and cancer.  Clinical genome services use it when hunting the cause of rare disease.
pmc-3557905:
Jinek, East, Cheng, and co-authors show that CRISPR-Cas9 editing can be programmed with RNA inside human cells. In bacteria, type II CRISPR systems use a dual RNA guide to direct the Cas9 enzyme to cut foreign DNA at specific sites. The team asked whether that system could be rebuilt for human cells.

They show Cas9, assembled with hybrid guide RNAs, cutting DNA inside human cells at a chosen matching site. That result helped turn a bacterial defence system into a general genome editing tool, with wide effects across medicine and biology.
pmc-4708105:
Okonechnikov, Conesa, and García-Alcalde presented Qualimap two in 2016. Finding random errors and systematic bias is a crucial step in any sound pipeline for high-throughput sequencing data. Tools for this quality control task existed, but multi-sample work needed more.

Qualimap two gives advanced checks across many samples at once. Users can compare quality metrics side by side and spot a bad run before it poisons an analysis. That early warning saves costly re-sequencing and false findings. The tool covers both general sequencing data and targeted types, making it a standard checkpoint in genomics pipelines.
pmc-4934905:
Hill, Fatoba, Oke, and their colleagues estimated the global prevalence of chronic kidney disease in 2016. Kidney disease is a global health burden with high costs to health systems. It is also an independent risk factor for cardiovascular disease, the world's leading killer.

Their systematic review and meta-analysis pooled studies from around the world. All stages of kidney disease carry higher risks of heart problems, early death, and reduced quality of life. A single global estimate helps governments plan dialysis, transplant, and prevention services. It also underlines how often kidney disease goes undetected until late stages.
pmc-4967105:
Loboda, Damulewicz, Pyza, and their team reviewed the Nrf2 and HO-1 system in 2016. Nrf2 is a switch that turns on genes which guard cells. Those genes fight oxidants, calm inflammation, and clear toxins from the body.

The pair is found, in some form, in a wide range of species, from worms to humans. That long shared past points to a core role in how life deals with stress. The review also covers how this system shapes growth and how long a species lives, and its part in disease. The work helps labs see where drugs that boost this guard might help.
pmc-5717805:
Janus Jakobsen, Christian Gluud, Jorn Wetterslev, and coauthors wrote this practical guide in 2017. It covers missing data in randomized clinical trials, a problem that can bend results if handled badly. How much bias appears depends on why the data went missing.

The guide explains when filling in missing values by multiple imputation is a sound choice. Flowcharts walk readers through checks on the trial design and the pattern of missing values. Worked examples show the steps in real trials. Trial teams can use the guide to plan analyses that reviewers and readers can trust more.
pmc-6095905:
Chaithanya Chelakkot, Jaewang Ghim, and Sung Ho Ryu reviewed the gut barrier and its breakdown in 2018. The gut lining does far more than digest food. Together with mucus and immune cells, the cell layer keeps microbes and toxins out of the body.

The review explains the seals between gut cells and the signals that tighten or loosen them. Stress, alcohol, and disease can open gaps that let harmful material through. Such leaks are tied to bowel disease, liver trouble, and wider inflammation. Readers see why a quiet barrier failure can echo through the whole body.
pmc-6227505:
Kyle Foreman, Nicholas Marquez, Anne Dolgert, and coauthors forecast future health for many countries in 2018. Long-term planning needs a view of how life expectancy and causes of death may change. Earlier forecasts covered only part of that picture.

The team models future mortality for a large set of causes under a reference path and under better and worse paths. Rising incomes, education, and risk control drive most gains in the better path. Some causes, tied to obesity and mental health, worsen even then. Governments use such scenarios to test whether today's investments fit tomorrow's burdens.
pmc-7049905:
Boris Bikbov, Caroline Purcell, Andrew Levey, and coauthors estimated the global burden of chronic kidney disease in 2020. Planning care for kidney disease needs solid counts, yet many countries have none. The study fills that gap with modeled global estimates.

Coverage runs from 1990 to 2017 for nearly two hundred countries. Kidney disease proves common, affecting roughly one in ten adults in their global estimate. Deaths tied to it have risen as populations age and diabetes spreads. The authors press for screening of high-risk groups and cheaper access to dialysis and transplant where needs are unmet.
pmc-7190605:
Romano Lugano, Mohan Ramachandran, and Anna Dimberg reviewed tumor angiogenesis in 2019. Tumors grow new blood vessels through several distinct processes. These vary by tumor type and site and can run side by side in one tumor.

Secreted factors, above all VEGF, orchestrate the sprouting and remodeling of vessels. The resulting network is leaky and chaotic, which feeds resistance to therapy. Anti-vessel drugs help some patients but often lose effect. The review maps causes and consequences and points to combinations that might finally normalize tumor blood flow. Combination strategies that pair vessel drugs with immunotherapy are reviewed as the most hopeful direction.
pmc-7369905:
Fei He, Xiaoli Ru, and Tao Wen reviewed in 2020 the roles of NRF2, a protein that acts as a master switch for cell defense. When switched on, it raises the production of genes that help cells withstand poisons and oxidative stress, the chemical wear caused by reactive oxygen. It also helps cells clear drugs and ride out other kinds of damage.

The review ranges well beyond that core defense role, covering how this switch affects inflammation, metabolism, and diseases such as cancer. The authors explain the signals that turn it on and off, and why both too little and too much activity can cause harm. Their account frames a target that drug developers watch closely, since nudging it could protect tissue or, done wrong, shield tumors.
pmc-8371605:
John Jumper and a large team at DeepMind reported in 2021 that their AlphaFold system could predict protein structures with high accuracy. Proteins do the work of life, and knowing a protein's folded shape helps explain how it functions. Experiments had solved the shapes of roughly one hundred thousand proteins, a small share of those known to exist.

AlphaFold instead computes the shape from the protein's sequence alone, and the team shows it matching experimental results closely across many test cases. They describe how the system reasons about the sequence and its evolutionary relatives. The work reshaped structural biology almost at once, putting a reliable predicted shape within reach for nearly any protein a researcher cares about.
plos-pone-0360005:
Tharun Tom Oommen and a large clinical team studied in 2026 a blood signal that may help predict outcomes for patients hospitalized with cirrhosis, advanced scarring of the liver. The signal is interleukin-6, a messenger of inflammation, measured on admission. The authors describe it as a time limited and cause dependent prognostic signal: it carries information about the near future, and its meaning shifts with what caused the liver disease.

Their cohort study analyzes the data two ways, with standard frequentist statistics and with Bayesian methods that weigh prior knowledge openly. A cheap admission blood test that sharpens prognosis could help doctors triage scarce intensive care and speak more honestly with families about what lies ahead.
plos-pone-0359405:
Zihui Liu and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on esophageal cancer. The cancer studied is squamous cell carcinoma of the food pipe, tested in cell cultures and in TE-1 xenografts, tumors grown in animals. The treatment under study is Shenling Qige Granules, a traditional Chinese medicine preparation.

As the title states, the granules inhibit the cancer's progression in these models by acting on a chain of molecular signals that runs from DCN through TGF-β to Smad. Showing a mechanism, not just an effect, helps judge whether a traditional remedy deserves clinical testing. Researchers working where traditional and modern cancer medicine meet are the audience.
plos-pone-0357605: Danilovich and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE trial on walking as a cure for frailty in older adults. One group walked at a brisk pace; the other walked at a casual pace. Whole clusters of people were assigned together in this randomized trial. If brisk walking reverses frailty better, a cheap daily habit could help older adults stay strong and independent longer.
plos-pone-0359105: Heron and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a urine test tied to a risky pregnancy condition. Preeclampsia raises blood pressure and can harm mother and baby. The team analyzed bits of DNA in urine that come from kidney cells. If kidney DNA in urine flags the condition early, a simple sample could help doctors watch high-risk pregnancies more closely.
plos-pone-0356305: Fielder and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE review on vaping during pregnancy. As a scoping review, it maps studies in both people and animals. The outcomes cover the mother, the unborn child, and the infant after birth. Pregnant people get mixed messages about vaping, so a clear map of what is known and unknown can guide honest advice.
plos-pone-0359205: Islam and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on what people eat in Bangladesh at each stage of life. They mapped food consumption patterns from childhood to old age. They also checked whether diets at each stage supply enough nutrients. Gaps found at a given age can guide food aid and advice aimed at that stage rather than at everyone at once.
plos-pone-0357905:
Vigneswaran Ravi and three colleagues describe a computer model of the Hall effect in a 2026 PLOS ONE article. The Hall effect is the small voltage that appears across a conductor in a magnetic field, and it sits at the heart of many magnetic sensors. Exact formulas struggle once a device's shape, material, and metal contacts all matter at once, which is where their model comes in.

Working in the free program FreeFEM++, they simulate the effect with the finite element method and check the output against known analytical solutions. They then show how physical defects, which formulas cannot handle, change the readings, using a cross shaped graphene sensor as the worked example. The shared script doubles as a teaching aid and a research tool.
plos-pone-0358705:
Tekle Gebremeskel Ygzaw leads a team of eight following children treated for severe pneumonia in Tigray, Ethiopia, reported in PLOS ONE in 2026. Pneumonia remains one of the biggest killers of young children, and Ethiopia carries a heavy share of that burden. Knowing how long recovery takes, and what slows it, helps hospitals plan beds and follow up care. Prospective local data from Tigray's public hospitals were lacking.

The team tracked just over three hundred admitted children across two months, recording when each recovered. About eighty-five percent recovered, with the typical child well again in five days. Statistical models then separated the factors tied to faster or slower recovery from background noise. Findings like these let regional clinicians counsel families realistically and flag the children who need closer watching during admission.
plaw-109-148-2005: Congress passed this federal law, the Support Our Scouts Act, in 2005. The short title states its purpose; the enrolled text holds the binding details. It stands as Public Law 109-148 of the 109th Congress. The library keeps it as part of the public record.
europmc-pmc8885505: Stenberg and co-authors published this research paper in 2022 on guidelines (official advice) for perioperative care in bariatric surgery: boosted recovery after surgery society recommendations: a 2021 update. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Results like these feed the work that turns lab findings into future treatments.
plaw-109-36-2005: Passed in 2005, this federal law designates the facility of the United States Postal Service located at 301 South Heatherwilde Boulevard in Pflugerville, Texas, as the. Designations put names on the official map and into federal records. The library keeps it in the public record of how federal laws get made.
europmc-pmc8227405: Published in 2021, this research paper takes on the SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein and its role in viral structure, biological (from living things) functions, and a target. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. If later work backs it up, the finding could open a new path for treating the illness.
europmc-pmc7694805: Published in 2020, this research paper takes on VIRIDIC-A new tool to calculate the intergenomic similarities of prokaryote-infecting viruses. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. A tested new tool like this gives doctors a steadier way to measure what they see in patients.
plaw-109-151-2005: Passed in 2005, this federal law amends title I of the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974, title XXVII of the Public Health Service Act, and the Internal Revenue Code. Amendments like this fine-tune existing programs without rewriting the whole law. It stands as Public Law 109-151 of the 109th Congress.
europmc-pmc8618305: A fresh look at 3D cell culture systems: tumor application (use), advantages, and disadvantages arrived with this 2021 research paper. The traditional two-dimensional (2D) in vitro (in lab dishes) cell culture system (on a flat support) has long been used. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
plaw-109-10-2005: Congress passed this naming law in 2005 for the facility at 501 I Street in Sacramento, California, now the "Robert T. Matsui United States Courthouse". Congress uses designations to etch names and places into the official map. The library keeps it in the public record of how federal laws get made.
plaw-109-8-2005: Congress passed this federal law, the Bankruptcy Abuse Prevention and Consumer Protection Act, in 2005. The short title states its purpose; the enrolled text holds the binding details. The library keeps it in the public record of how federal laws get made.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-1005: GAO published its findings on defense Infrastructure: Opportunity to Improve the Timeliness of Future Overseas Planning Reports and Factors Affecting the Master Planning Effort for the Milit in 2008. plos-pone-0356905:
You Tang and coauthors published a 2026 proteomics study in PLOS ONE on a tobacco relative used to manufacture proteins in leaves, called plant molecular farming. Yields often disappoint because the plant's own protein-cutting enzymes chew up the product. Using deep protein measurement, they separated three stresses leaves face: infiltration, the bacteria delivering genes, and the burden of making a foreign protein.

Even plain buffer infiltration, usually treated as a neutral control, triggered cell-wall remodeling and oxidative stress on its own. Filtering that background out revealed a core bacterial response marked by a growth-versus-defense trade-off. Making a virus capsid precursor provoked a stronger, distinct wave of protein-cutting enzymes than making a simple glowing marker protein did. They also expanded the plant's known enzyme catalog to about fifteen hundred entries The cargo itself shapes the plant's defenses, they conclude, so strategies should be tuned per product.
plos-pone-0357805:
Jessica Chen and colleagues published a 2026 qualitative study in PLOS ONE on what happened to people displaced by the huge 2022 floods in Lismore, in regional Australia. The study draws on online news coverage over the following two years. Rather than interviewing survivors, the team analyzed seventy-one news articles and then checked how closely the coverage matched the wider research literature on flood displacement and health.

The reporting tied displacement to trauma, distress, and a gnawing feeling of being in limbo while housing stayed unresolved. Articles traced families through emergency shelters, short-term fixes, and the hunt for long-term homes, including informal arrangements that official systems never record, and showed how each stage shaped health. Yet the most severely affected groups received little attention. The authors conclude the media captured the broad harm accurately but underplayed the worst cases, which matters because coverage steers where help and sympathy flow.
plos-pone-0357405:
Md Sadiq Iqbal and Mohammod Abul Kashem published a 2026 paper in PLOS ONE arguing that asking whether a text is human or machine-written is the wrong question. Forensics wants to know which model wrote it; universities want to know whether a human collaborated. Their system, SiBot, treats detection as source attribution across many classes. They built and released two benchmark corpora. One spans more than twenty AI sources; another models pure and human-AI hybrid writing.

On the harder many-source corpus, the best classical combination reached only middling accuracy, showing how tough attribution is. On the ten-class corpus, their hybrid design, blending word-frequency features with a transformer's contextual embeddings, scored above ninety percent, beating the strongest transformer alone by a wide margin. The framework is publicly deployed. Detectors, they say, must move from binary verdicts to graded, source-aware answers among hybrid drafts.
plos-pone-0356605:
Jason Johnson-Peretz and a large team report what patients and clinic staff thought of a flexible HIV care model in rural Kenya and Uganda. Their 2026 paper draws on the SEARCH trial, which served people whose work and travel make regular clinic visits hard to keep. The model let patients choose longer refill gaps, community pickup, and help when moving between clinics.

Interviews with patients and providers found every option welcome, with a discreet travel pack of medicine and supplies liked most. Longer gaps freed patients to focus on taking doses rather than chasing appointments. Poverty and hunger still blocked steady treatment, so participants asked for wider services, food or job help, and stronger supply chains.
plos-pone-0356205:
Ai Cui and colleagues lay out a trial plan, published in 2026, for testing whether a lung-scarring drug can prevent radiation harm in lung cancer care. Patients with advanced lung tumors that cannot be removed often receive combined drug treatment and radiation, and the radiation itself can inflame and scar the lungs. The drug nintedanib already treats one scarring lung disease, so the team asks whether it can also protect these patients.

Under the plan, a small group of patients at three centers in China will be split by chance. Half will take the drug around their radiation course. Half will receive standard care alone. Doctors will track lung injury, safety, and quality of life. Because no results exist yet, the value here is the careful design future findings will rest on.
plos-pone-0357005:
Md Ahosanul Haque Shahid and colleagues isolate and sequence the bacterium behind fowl cholera, a major killer of poultry, from layer birds. Knowing the local strain's resistance pattern and danger genes guides control. From dozens of suspect field samples the team confirmed a small set of type A isolates. Culture and gene tests did the confirming. The isolates then faced a panel of common antibiotics. One representative genome was sequenced in full.

The sequenced genome held the usual two thousand or so genes. It also held a set tied to sticking to hosts and dodging immunity. A predictor flagged possible risk to people. Isolates resisted several front-line drugs yet stayed sensitive to a handful of others, including common fluoroquinolones. Shahid and colleagues offer the profile for surveillance and vaccine planning.
plos-pone-0357205:
Irtaza Tahir and colleagues publish the plan for a systematic review asking whether adding immune therapy to radiation before surgery raises danger for patients with removable solid tumors. The combination is spreading fast in cancer care, and harm data are scattered across small studies. Their protocol searches major databases, trial registries, and conference records from the past decade for studies reporting severe side effects, treatment stops, deaths, and surgical complications.

Where studies allow, results will be pooled with random-effects models and split by tumor site and radiation style. The entry here is the protocol itself: no results yet, but a fixed, public recipe meant to keep the later review honest. Tahir and colleagues aim to give surgical teams a clear harm ledger for a popular new combination.
plos-pone-0355505:
Tahir Hussain and colleagues derive new exact solutions of Einstein's equations for cylinder-shaped universes filled with an imperfect, uneven fluid. Exact solutions are rare treasures in relativity because the equations resist direct solving. The team uses scaling symmetries of different sizes to organize the search. Then it reads off the matter content each geometry demands. It checks which solutions are empty. It checks which carry flowing matter, and which ripple like waves.

The family they build connects to classic models, including cylindrical waves, older static cylinders, and expanding models of Kasner type. Hussain and colleagues present the catalog as raw material for testing ideas about cosmic strings, gravitational waves, and how lopsided matter shapes spacetime over time.
plos-pone-0356505:
Likai Wu, Meina Zhang, and Wenzhe Wang combined two control ideas to make a cheap four-legged robot walk well. The first idea is biological rhythm generators that set each leg's beat. The second is a team of learning agents, one per leg, that nudge the rhythm to fit the ground. Their 2026 framework deliberately keeps the robot's onboard brain tiny. All four legs share one small policy network, run from simple body sensors.

In simulation and on a real low-cost robot, the system crossed obstacles, ramps, stairs, and rough ground. It did so more stably and efficiently than baseline controllers. Cameras, torque sensors, and motion capture stayed in the lab, not on the robot. The design points toward inspection and rescue robots that schools and small firms can actually afford.
plos-pone-0352705:
Amy Palmer and seven colleagues check whether a widely used child mental health questionnaire makes sense to Indian teenagers, in this 2026 study from Karnataka. India urgently needs trustworthy youth mental health data, but the anxiety and depression scale in question was written for other cultures and had never been culturally validated there. Twelve adolescents aged thirteen to seventeen thought aloud as they answered each item, revealing where the wording stumbled.

Fourteen of the forty-seven items caused problems for at least three teenagers, with the obsessive-compulsive section faring worst. The authors discuss why particular phrases misfire, covering unfamiliar concepts and awkward phrasing, and propose reworded versions. This think-aloud step is the first stage of full validation, and the authors frame it as essential groundwork before the scale's scores can be trusted in Indian prevention programs.
plos-pone-0355405:
Emily Zabor, Yağmur Seda Yeşiltaş, and Arun Singh ask how often doctors should scan the livers of patients treated for melanoma inside the eye, in this 2026 study. This cancer, uveal melanoma, tends to spread first to the liver, and catching spread early matters. At their center, a gene test sorts patients into low and high risk, with higher-risk patients scanned more often or with stronger imaging. The team modeled schedules from monthly to yearly against real outcomes.

Among roughly three hundred fifty patients, about one in five developed spread during follow-up. The analysis found yearly scans optimal for low-risk patients and scans every nine months optimal for high-risk patients, balancing detection delay against scan burden. Longer gaps were tied to larger lesions at detection. The authors offer the risk-tailored schedule as a framework for designing surveillance that is neither lax nor wasteful.
plos-pone-0356105:
Saba Desta Tessema and six colleagues test a color-coded early warning chart for mothers in Ethiopian hospitals, in this 2026 quasi-experimental study. Most maternal deaths in Ethiopia are preventable if deterioration is caught early, yet warning charts are used inconsistently. More than eleven hundred obstetric inpatients at four public hospitals were split between two kinds of monitoring. One group used the chart, which grades vital signs, consciousness, bleeding, and other signs green, yellow, or red. The other received standard monitoring.

Charted patients triggered alerts nearly five hours sooner on average, were seen by a physician faster, and received interventions faster. They needed fewer ultrasound scans, left hospital about half a day earlier, and faced a meaningfully lower risk of severe maternal outcomes. The authors support wider use while calling for larger multi-cluster trials to confirm the effect across settings and risk groups.
plos-pone-0356005:
Yi Li and colleagues tested a simple blood-count score for predicting outcomes in advanced throat cancer behind the nose. Chemoradiation often suppresses blood cell production, but the combined effect across cell types was unclear. Their 2026 study scored several hundred patients by how many of three blood lines fell below normal.

Higher scores tracked with clearly worse survival and more spread of disease during about six years of follow-up. Patients with all three lines low faced far higher risks of death and distant spread than those with none low. The score added modest sorting power on its own. Li and colleagues suggest it can sit beside standard staging when judging a patient's risk.
plos-pone-0355605:
Ali Yalçın and co-authors address in 2026 how shoulder motion should be reported for children born with brachial plexus injury. Clinicians use a set of standard arm movements, yet labs describe the joint angles in different ways. The team rechecked motion sensor data from the uninjured arms of ten children.

Three common ways of ordering angle calculations were compared for jumps and for match with expected clinical values. One order caused locking problems in several movements, and no single order suited every movement best. The authors argue for movement specific reporting rules, so results from different studies can be compared with more trust.
plos-pone-0355305:
Yinda Long and co-authors build in 2026 a physics based model that forecasts how long a phone battery will last. They used an open source phone as their test case and built the model in parts, covering the screen, chip, radio, and other uses. Heat effects on the battery were built in as well.

Across six common patterns of use, predicted run time ranged from about an hour under heavy load to more than a day when light. Chip use and room temperature drove fast drain most. Simple steps such as easing workload and screen use stretched heavy use time a lot in the model.
plos-pone-0351305:
Jauharah Khudzari and colleagues compare in 2026 the fire risk of heated tobacco devices and lit cigarettes in Malaysia. A heat camera recorded surface warmth while products ran alone and while resting on common burnable materials. Tests took place under normal room conditions, with and without simulated puffing.

Lit cigarettes grew extremely hot and left burn marks on fabrics and dry matter. Heated devices stayed far cooler, well below the point where the tested materials would catch fire, and left no visible damage. Puffing raised cigarette heat but barely changed device heat. The authors still limit their claim to the products and conditions they tested.
plos-pone-0354905:
Kyla Lee, Anna Gagliardi, and colleagues present in 2026 a study plan on how Korean immigrants in Canada share health decisions with family doctors. Earlier work on East Asian patients gave mixed results and rarely sampled with this group in mind. The planned interviews will be held in Korean or English, as each person prefers.

Twelve adults who moved under the economic stream and who see one doctor regularly will take part. Analysis will look for shared themes about care and about sharing choices, reported only in grouped, unnamed form. Recruitment was still open, so the document describes aims and methods rather than findings.
plos-pone-0355105:
Duyen Nguyen, Taehyeong Kim, and Junyoung Park combine in 2026 live experiments and computer simulation on how groups of mice escape under stress. Electric stimulus strength, an obstacle near the exit, guide walls at several angles, and group size were all varied. Escape time, speed, and spacing between mice were measured, and a validated agent model replayed and widened the conditions.

Obstacles and walls helped when groups were dense and stimulus was moderate, smoothing flow and cutting escape time, but hindered when groups were sparse or stimulus was extreme. Wide enough spacing between mice kept flow stable and prevented clogging at the narrow exit. The joined method validates well.
plos-pone-0355205:
Zhoujun Zhu and co-authors study in 2026 the pollen of a woody oil tree valued in Guizhou, China, building reliable tests for whether its pollen is alive and can sprout. Fruit yield and oil quality depend on good pollination, yet pollen testing for this tree lagged. Microscope work described pollen shape across family lines, and nine staining methods plus sprouting recipes were compared across two breeding lines.

Pollen kept a shared genus shape with clear variety between lines. Two stains separated living from dead grains best, and each line had its own best sprouting recipe in a growth mix. A two tier plan is proposed: one stain for precise lab work, another for quick field checks.
plos-pone-0352905:
Amadeusz Jacek Miązek and Justyna Światowiec-Szczepańska published this 2026 study of how chief executives take risks. They measured whether bosses focus on gains or on avoiding losses by analyzing the language of shareholder letters from Warsaw-listed firms over a decade. They then matched that mindset to company risk choices and pay structures.

Gain-focused chief executives steered their firms into bolder risks, while loss-focused ones played safer. Pay design shifted both tendencies: steady salary cooled the bold, and bonuses pushed the cautious. The pair suggest boards tune pay packages to the individual chief executive's mindset.
plos-pone-0354705:
Guanglong Bao and six colleagues published this 2026 study of level design in Metroidvania games, where players explore large maps and unlock new routes. They turned the maps of three well-known games into networks, then measured where save points, teleport points, and boss encounters sit and how central those spots are.

The three games used their special points very differently. Save and travel points shifted from spread-out support toward late-game travel efficiency, while bosses stayed off to the side everywhere. Bao suggests network measures give designers a concrete way to judge and tune map layouts.
plos-pone-0354605:
Ghalia Khoder led a team of eight authors on this 2026 laboratory study of a possible stomach cancer drug. The compound, NSC 57774, blocks SHP2, a signaling switch that stomach tumors often run at high levels. Using a stomach cancer cell line, the team tracked growth, movement, and several cancer signaling pathways after treatment.

The drug slowed cell growth and migration while sparing ordinary fibroblast cells, and it outperformed a commercial blocker and a standard chemotherapy drug in these dish tests. Khoder calls it a promising candidate that still needs animal and clinical testing.
plos-pone-0354305:
Reema Al-Daraiseh led a team of six authors on this 2026 study building a questionnaire about how mental health service users view artificial intelligence. More than four hundred people attending clinics in Jordan answered structured interviews while the team developed the tool and checked its consistency.

The result is a twenty-item questionnaire that measures perception of artificial intelligence reliably. Al-Daraiseh intends it for finding what shapes readiness to accept AI tools, so policymakers can see adoption barriers through patients' eyes. The team notes the same tool can now be tested in other populations and health systems.
plos-pone-0320105:
Saha Roy and colleagues, in a 2026 study, ask how filling in missing values in medical data changes what artificial intelligence models learn. Gaps are common in health records, and the way they are filled can tilt results. The team compared six ways of handling missing data across common prediction methods.

Two tasks were tested: spotting COVID-19 and predicting which patients would get worse. In a general screening group, a method that fills gaps by chained estimates gave the best results, lifting detection and revealing hidden viral coinfections. In an intensive care group, using only complete records looked stronger at first, but that edge came from bias: sicker patients were tested more, so their records were fuller. The authors warn that the right fix for missing data depends on the care setting, and the wrong one can mislead doctors.
plos-pone-0354805:
Usama and colleagues, in a 2026 computer study, test whether chemicals made by a salt-loving bacterium could help maize grow under drought. Maize feeds much of the world, and dry spells cut its growth badly. Some soil bacteria help plants cope, but how their chemicals act inside the plant is poorly mapped.

The team docked bacterial chemicals, in simulation, into a maize enzyme that helps manage plant growth signals. Two bacterial compounds gripped the enzyme more tightly than two well-known plant hormones used as yardsticks. A long motion simulation, lasting two hundred nanoseconds of model time, showed the pairings stayed stable, held together by steady bonds. The authors are clear that this is all in silico, meaning done on a computer. The results nominate these bacterial chemicals for greenhouse and field tests, which alone can show whether they truly help crops in dry soil.
plos-pone-0353505:
Zhang, in a 2026 paper, designs a search engine for archive images that contain text, such as stamped official documents. Archives hold mountains of such pages, and finding one page by its content is hard when seals cover text, print blocks are tiny, and scans are noisy. Plain text reading misses how words and pictures relate.

The proposed system has five layers, from cleaning the image to matching a query. A scene graph step maps the elements on the page and how they relate. An attention step then fuses three kinds of features: the graph, the text, and links between image and text.
