On test data, the first returned result was right far more often than with a classic text-only method, including on pages with seal cover and tiny print. Each search answered in a small fraction of a second. Zhang presents the design as support for archives going online.
plos-pone-0353105:
Zhai and colleagues, in a 2026 study, link exercise to the wish for children in China, where birth rates have fallen below replacement level. Money worries get most attention, but anxious minds may also hold people back. Drawing on a large national social survey from 2021, the team asked whether people who exercise more also want more children, and why.

More exercise went with stronger fertility intentions. Tracing the paths, exercise was tied to better mental well-being and to more social engagement, and both of those were tied to wanting children. The link was strongest among single people and among those with more education and income. The authors are careful to speak of association, not proof of cause, since the data are a one-time snapshot. Still, they suggest that public health support for body and mind belongs in any serious answer to low fertility.
plos-pone-0354205:
Yang and Feng, in a 2026 study, use tracking data from four men's World Cups to see how the physical demands on footballers changed from 2010 to 2022. Two hundred twenty-five matches were analyzed, covering players from the five world confederations. Measures included total distance, top speed, sprinting, and low- and high-intensity running.

Top speed, sprint distance, and low-intensity running all rose across the period in every confederation, a shared global shift toward a faster game. Total distance and high-intensity running told regional stories instead. Total distance rose late in the period in Asia, Europe, and the Americas, but not in South America. High-intensity running fell in several confederations while barely changing in Africa. The authors conclude the modern World Cup asks more speed of everyone, while how much ground players cover still depends on regional styles of play.
plos-pone-0324305:
Schepisi and colleagues, in a 2026 study, track emergency department visits for mental health crises across three large Italian areas before and during COVID-19. More than five million residents were followed from 2018 to 2021. The question was not only whether visits changed, but whose changed most, since the pandemic hit the poor hardest and services shrank at the same time.

Before the pandemic, first crisis visits were more common among the most deprived residents, women, the youngest and oldest, and immigrants. When COVID arrived, visits fell, and the fall grew steeper with deprivation: the worse off the area, the bigger the drop. Age gaps in visit rates narrowed as middle-aged groups fell most. The authors read the pattern as unmet need, not improved health: those with the greatest barriers stayed away most, a warning for how services should reopen after a crisis.
plos-pone-0353605:
C. K. Revathi and H. Santhi combine several layers of computer optimisation to sharpen heart-disease prediction, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Coronary artery disease, the narrowing of the heart's own arteries, is a leading killer, and deep-learning image models can spot it — if their settings are tuned well. The authors hybridised an optimiser inspired by hunting hawks with an automated tuning library, and adjusted the settings dynamically during training.

Applied to four image networks, the framework lifted accuracy sharply over the conventional version of the optimiser. One network reached the highest score, near ninety-eight percent, on their artery-narrowing dataset. Better-tuned models could one day support faster, more reliable screening of heart scans.
plos-pone-0349805:
Mekuriaw Dereje Tekele and five colleagues publish a protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026 for a trial testing whether pharmacists can teach asthma patients their way to better control, in Ethiopia. The trial will run at a large specialised hospital's chest clinic. Patients will be assigned at random to usual care or to a structured education package: teach-back conversations, illustrated leaflets, and follow-up by phone and text message.

After three months, assessors who do not know the assignments will measure medication knowledge, inhaler technique, adherence, and asthma control. The design uses intention-to-treat analysis and explores whether some patient groups benefit more. Pharmacists are an underused teaching force in asthma care, and this trial tests their value rigorously.
plos-pone-0350905:
Ye and colleagues tested a skin cream made from DNA fragments on sun-damaged skin in a 2026 study. Sunlight breaks down the skin's support network, causing wrinkles and sagging. The team traced how the cream enters skin, which cell pathways it switches on, and how it performed against a standard retinol cream in a split-face trial.

Treated skin samples grew thicker surface layers and more collagen and elastic proteins. In the face trial, the new cream improved wrinkles, thickness, and eye bags about twice as much as retinol, with good tolerance. The results support the cream as a repair option for sun-aged skin, pending larger trials.
plos-pone-0353205:
Wenfang Li, Xingchen Zhang, and Sen Cao present this 2026 PLOS One study on what makes a traffic crash in Changsha, China, likely to injure someone. Using nearly ten thousand crash records from 2017 to 2019, they combined built-environment features, grouped into five dimensions such as density and transit access, with crash-context factors like lighting. Three machine learning models were trained and the best was pried open to rank its influences.

Models using both kinds of information beat models using either alone, with the combined approach discriminating best. Distance to the nearest metro station, lighting, road density, and land-use mix ranked among the strongest factors. Farther metro access generally raised injury risk, while denser, more mixed neighborhoods lowered it. The authors frame built environment and crash circumstances as partners, not rivals, in explaining injury risk.
plos-pone-0350505:
Byron Hernández-Ortiz and three colleagues hunt for bird species linked to avian influenza outbreaks in Brazil. Their 2026 study uses nationwide surveillance records gathered up to July 2025. The data cover more than eleven hundred records, one hundred twenty-seven species, and hundreds of municipalities. Finding the riskiest species helps officials aim limited monitoring effort.

Terns stood out sharply. Four tern species showed strong positive links with the highly pathogenic H5N1 virus. One, the Cabot's tern, was the single strongest predictor in the team's models. Adding location improved prediction further. Outbreaks clustered along Brazil's southeastern coast, exactly where dense poultry farming sits. Inland cases stayed scattered. Surveillance should therefore watch coastal tern colonies closely, since they appear to flag where spillover danger is highest.
plos-pone-0316505:
Akine Eshete and six colleagues listen to people living with diabetes in North Shoa, Ethiopia. Their 2026 study is phenomenological, meaning it centres lived experience. Government programmes exist, yet daily self-care still falls short for many patients. The authors wanted the barriers described in patients' own terms. Interviews ran through July 2024 across four districts.

Twenty patients and five healthcare workers took part. Participants varied by age, sex, work, and diabetes type. Conversations were recorded, transcribed, and coded with qualitative software. A thematic framework organised the codes into subthemes and main themes about self-care practice. Such ground-level accounts show where clinic advice collides with real life. They give programme designers specific friction points to fix, rather than generic calls for more education.
plos-pone-0351505:
Sian Calvert and a large team set out the plan for an updated review of what helps adults actually wear their hearing aids. Hearing loss is common, aids are the main treatment, and yet many fitted aids sit in drawers. This protocol describes, before the work begins, how the reviewers will search, judge, and pool trials of programs meant to raise regular use.

The review is framed by a behavior model that splits action into capability, opportunity, and motivation. Sorting past programs by which of those levers they pull should show which levers work. Because it is a protocol, no findings appear here. Its value is discipline: fixing the questions and methods in advance keeps the later review honest and lets clinics see which support styles deserve their money.
plos-pone-0351005:
Abuse of older people by the very relatives and helpers who care for them often stays hidden. Oludoyinmola Omobolade Ojifinni and Obioma C Uchendu built a short screening questionnaire for this problem in southwest Nigeria, reported in PLOS One in 2026, because existing tools were designed for other cultures.

They drafted questions from past research and talks with caregivers, covering neglect plus physical, emotional, money-related, and sexual harm. After expert review, more than eleven hundred caregivers answered the ten-item tool. Scores hung together well and matched related measures of caregiver strain and health. One weak spot was the sexual harm section, which the authors flag honestly.
plos-pone-0351405:
A gene switch helps doctors predict chemotherapy success in glioblastoma. Testing that switch today requires tumor tissue. Freddy Oulia and colleagues asked whether MRI scans could replace the biopsy. They used a public dataset of about five hundred eighty patients. Deep learning models read the scans. The study appeared in PLOS One in 2026.

The team ran nearly fourteen hundred model configurations. Single scan types competed against combined scans. Viewing planes, slice counts, and merge styles all varied. The best single-scan model reached only about sixty-five percent accuracy. Results stayed modest across the whole sweep. The authors conclude scan-based prediction is not clinic-ready. A needle-free test remains a hope, not a tool.
plos-pone-0347105:
Richard Spacek and colleagues tested whether freezing fluid from the womb changes a key test result. When waters break early before labour, doctors check the fluid for signs of swelling inside the womb. One marker, called IL-6, guides that call, but most cut points came from stored, frozen samples rather than fresh ones.

Records covered one hundred and fifty two women with early broken waters. Fresh and once frozen results tracked each other very closely, yet frozen samples read about one fifth higher on average. Using the frozen sample cut point on fresh fluid missed three cases. Care teams should treat fresh and stored values as close but not equal when they judge risk.
plos-pone-0349705:
Guangyu Zhang and colleagues measured how much fresh plant growth Tibetan grasslands produced each year from 2000 to 2022. Growth was split among the whole plant community and three plant types: sedges, grasses, and broad leaf herbs. Models separated the push of a changing climate from the push of human use like grazing and restoration.

Whole community growth dipped slightly overall, while sedges grew more and grasses and herbs fell back. Human action shaped more than half the plateau, climate about a fifth, and both together the rest. Maps varied sharply by place. Care for these high pastures must fit local plant mixes, since one rule for the whole plateau will miss what each patch needs.
plos-pone-0350805:
Tran Tuan Nguyen compared how three capital cities in Southeast Asia used their land between 2017 and 2024, in work published in 2026. Hanoi, Vientiane, and Phnom Penh are all growing fast, and the question was whether growth stayed compact or sprawled.

Land grew faster than population in all three cities. Phnom Penh spread the most yet stayed the most compact in shape, while Hanoi grew more loosely and Vientiane's growth looked scattered and random. The author links the contrasts to planning rules and investment choices. The method, built on a global city goal, can be reused in other fast-growing cities of the developing world.
plos-pone-0344505:
Yulei Wang and colleagues tested engineered bone grafts for large gaps in rabbit leg bones in 2026. Big missing bone sections do not heal alone, and grafts from a patient's own body are limited and costly to harvest.

Their graft used a mineral scaffold seeded with vessel forming cells, with an artery threaded through a channel in the middle. Rabbits were split among scaffold types, and scans and tissue checks ran for three months. The graft with both cells and artery grew the most new bone and vessels. Feeding a graft its own blood supply looks key to rebuilding long bones.
plos-pone-0350105:
Tamara J Huizer and co-authors reviewed follow-up scanning for oesophageal cancer patients on nivolumab after surgery in 2026. The drug lowers relapse risk after chemotherapy, radiation, and surgery, yet relapse stays common and the best scan schedule was unknown.

Records from three Dutch hospitals covered one hundred fifty-one treated patients. About one in five relapsed during treatment, and routine scans caught two thirds of those relapses, most already spread. Survival free of disease fell steadily over the first year. The figures give teams a realistic picture of what scheduled scanning finds, and when, during this treatment.
plos-pone-0350005:
Jolien Arendsen, Guido M van Koningsbruggen, and Marieke L Fransen tested a popular claim from psychology: that reminders of death push people toward status purchases like luxury brands. Earlier work suggested the effect, but the mental route was unmapped. Their 2026 pair of studies first catalogued the beliefs people hold about status consumption, then exposed participants to a mortality reminder and measured how those beliefs and intentions shifted.

The reminder moved only two of twenty-nine beliefs, and it weakened the link between enjoying the experience and intending to buy. Crucially, buying intentions themselves did not budge at all. The authors conclude that whatever death reminders do to status thinking is too faint to change behavior, and that the effect may be far more limited than earlier research assumed.
plos-pone-0348905:
Kristýna Krejčová and Fabio Ibrahim led a survey of Czech students. The topic was the impostor feeling: the fear of being a fraud despite real success. The team asked how that feeling links to self-compassion. Six hundred students filled in two standard surveys. The team then mapped how the parts of each trait connect.

Doubt about one's own skill tied most to two dark habits of mind. One is feeling alone in one's struggles. The other is drowning in bad feelings. These habits explained about a quarter of the doubt scores. The bright side of self-compassion mattered far less here. The team says aid should target the sense of being alone with one's flaws.
plos-pone-0348505:
Ya-En Catherine Lin and Fong-Ching Chang led a test of ad labels on social media. Teens are prime targets for stealth ads. The team split more than three thousand Taiwan high school students into three groups. Each group saw posts with a full sponsor label, a weak one, or none. Then the team gauged ad smarts and buying plans.

The full label group spotted the ads far more. They also grasped how ads work at a deeper level. Students who spotted ads held a more wary stance. That stance went with weaker plans to buy. The team says clear labels arm teens against hidden sales pitches.
plos-pone-0349405:
Isabel Vigmo and colleagues measured antibody levels in the blood of seven hundred fifty people with HIV, comparing those on effective treatment with those not yet treated. HIV often pushes the immune system to overproduce antibodies, a state called hypergammaglobulinemia, alongside chronic inflammation. Blood samples were checked for these antibodies and several inflammation markers.

Nearly every untreated group showed the excess, except people in the very earliest infection stage, and levels peaked in those with mid-range immune cell counts. Even among people whose virus was fully suppressed by treatment, about a quarter still had raised antibody levels. The persistence suggests treatment quiets the virus more completely than it calms the immune system.
plos-pone-0334305:
Kelly Ormond and colleagues surveyed a representative sample of nearly four thousand Swiss adults about gene editing as medical treatment. Presented with seven treatment options, only a small minority rejected editing outright, while about a third accepted every option. Support was strongest for curing life-threatening and seriously weakening diseases and fell as conditions became milder or later in onset.

Editing embryos drew less support than editing a patient's own body cells, and almost nobody endorsed editing to boost physical or mental abilities. Attitudes clustered into broad support and caution camps shaped by age, gender, religion, and knowledge. Switzerland may one day vote on such medicine, so a careful national snapshot shows where public consent actually stands.
plos-pone-0324405:
Lei Du and colleagues surveyed three hundred thirteen flight attendants at Tibet Airlines about leadership style and service quality. They studied spiritual leadership, a style built on vision, hope, and caring for staff, and asked whether it lifts the service passengers receive. Questionnaires measured leadership, how meaningful attendants found their work, how engaged they felt, and how well they served.

All four measures rose together. The chain of influence was clear: leadership fed a sense of meaningful work, which fed engagement, which fed service performance. Each link also helped on its own. Airlines compete on cabin service, so evidence that a values-driven leadership style pays off through staff meaning and energy has direct management value.
plos-pone-0349305:
Yuan Sun and Bin Wen studied how government culture and tourism accounts on TikTok turn viewers into travelers. Surveying four hundred six followers, they modeled a chain from the account's content to the viewer's feelings to the intention to visit. Information quality and service quality were the starting points; the image of the destination and positive emotions carried the effect forward.

Good information raised travel intention directly and also indirectly, by improving the destination's image and warming emotions. Service quality had no direct effect but worked entirely through image and emotion, and the two-step chain through both was significant as well. The practical lesson for official accounts is sharp: polish information first, and treat service interactions as image building, not clerical replies.
plos-pone-0349605:
Zhengda Yao, Juanjuan Zhang, and Dejun Kang surveyed more than five hundred teachers and school staff in Guangdong, China, to learn what keeps educators in their jobs. Their study sorts the forces into pulls that attract people to stay, such as training, pay, and having a real say. Pushes that drive people away include burnout and unhappy work.

Pulls raised the wish to stay, while pushes lowered it, just as the framework predicts. Feeling engaged at work strengthened the effect of training in particular. Only burnout behaved differently between public and private schools. The authors urge school leaders to pair fair material rewards with real attention to how engaged and supported teachers feel.
plos-pone-0349205:
Yuansheng Jiang and co-authors built an automatic grader for chrysoprase, a green gemstone whose price depends heavily on colour judged by eye. Human grading varies from person to person, so the team measured colour precisely for fifty-one stones with a light instrument. They generated hundreds of reference greens and taught several computer methods to sort stones into colour groups.

A simple statistical method and a neural network both scored near the top, and the team chose the simpler one because its reasoning is easy to follow and it runs fast. On a fresh set of real stones it sorted every stone correctly within this dataset. The authors offer the framework as a path toward fairer, repeatable grading for a trade built on subjective judgement.
plos-pone-0349505:
Guansheng Chen and co-authors investigated a protein called decorin in endometriosis, a painful condition where tissue like the womb lining grows outside the womb. A link between decorin and the condition was known, but its role was murky. The team mined single-cell and bulk gene data from patient tissue, then confirmed their findings with lab tests on cells.

Stromal cells, the supporting cells of the tissue, carried most of the decorin, and several stromal subtypes shifted in share within diseased tissue. Decorin levels ran clearly higher in endometriosis, high enough that the protein separated patients from controls well in two datasets. The protein also tracked with immune and scarring pathways. The authors propose decorin as a possible diagnostic marker and a handle for future drugs.
plos-pone-0348605:
Gloria Guht and colleagues asked whether people born without wisdom teeth also grow slightly smaller other teeth. They measured the crown widths of every permanent tooth in three hundred and fourteen German orthodontic patients, eighty-nine of whom lacked at least one wisdom tooth from birth. They compared them with patients holding a full set of thirty-two teeth.

Patients missing wisdom teeth had measurably narrower crowns across the mouth, with the biggest gaps in second molars and the upper side incisors. In men every tooth ran smaller; in women most did. Missing wisdom teeth was equally common in both sexes. The pattern suggests the same developmental programme sizes the whole dentition, so a missing wisdom tooth may be one visible sign of a generally more delicate tooth-building plan.
plos-pone-0349105:
Anna L Valentine and colleagues explored a puzzle in cancer genetics known as the RAD51 paradox. The protein RAD51 repairs broken DNA, and its loss should spell disaster, yet tumours show rampant chromosome chaos while almost never mutating RAD51 itself. The team suspected the protein's backup crew, its paralogues, spare copies that took over some of its jobs during evolution, and searched a large cancer mutation database for damage there instead.

Mutations in three paralogues did run high in human cancers. Few looked like classic cancer drivers, but many were predicted to damage or destabilise the enzymes, and three-dimensional modelling showed how some would warp the protein's structure. The authors argue the paradox eases if the repair crew, rather than its captain, is what cancer quietly breaks.
plos-pone-0348805:
Amlakie Aschale Alemu and colleagues taught deep learning models to sort Ethiopian legal documents into categories automatically, a pressing need as the country's digital legal records multiply. Legal language is dense and context-heavy, so the team layered attention mechanisms, which let a model focus on the words that matter most. These sat on several network designs that read text both as patterns and as sequences.

The strongest design, combining a pattern-reading network with a two-direction sequence reader plus self-attention, classified documents with accuracy above ninety-nine percent under two different testing schemes. The authors report consistent gains from adding attention across all the designs tried. They present the system as a step toward searchable, well-organised digital law for a legal system whose documents are rapidly moving online.
plos-pone-0348705:
Madhu Golla and a large team built a capsule network, a vision architecture that tracks parts and wholes, to diagnose gallbladder disease from ultrasound images automatically. Reading these scans by hand is slow and varies between operators. Their tailored model, GBCapsNet, adds a custom routing method for sharper class separation and a calibration step that aligns the model's confidence with reality.

Scores under favourable splitting reached near perfection, but the authors flag the catch themselves: images from the same patient could sit on both sides of the split, inflating results. True patient-level separation and outside datasets are still needed before any clinical claim. Calibration did improve the honesty of the model's probabilities. The work stands as an early, carefully hedged exploration of capsule networks for this organ.
plos-pone-0348005:
Laouen Belloli and co-workers release a software library that measures how groups of three or more things interact, not just pairs. Many fields, from brain science to climate study, miss key behavior when they only look at pairs. Their 2026 paper tackles the twin problems of estimating shared randomness well and handling the huge number of group combinations.

Built on a popular computing toolkit, the library runs batches in parallel on standard or graphics hardware. Benchmarks show it outruns existing tools, and its shortcuts make large systems workable. Tests on brain scans from awake and deeply sleeping subjects showed it can capture real shifts in brain teamwork. The open tool puts group-level analysis within reach of smaller labs.
plos-pone-0347605:
Nagendra P. Luitel and co-workers interview Nepali adults receiving care for depression or anxiety about how their illness feels and where they turned for help. Fewer than one in five people with such conditions in poorer countries get proper care, and culture shapes the path. Their 2026 study speaks with twenty-four patients across three districts using a guided illness-story interview.

People described fear, restlessness, sadness, and body complaints such as headaches and stomach trouble, often read as stress damage. Some told of detachment or memory gaps that led to panic or self-harm. Most went first to clinics or hospitals, some also to traditional healers. Schooling and caste steered choices. Care that hears the patient's own story may reach people sooner.
plos-pone-0332005:
José Paulo Rodrigues dos Santos and co-workers survey Swiss adults about cryonics, the practice of freezing a legally dead body in hope of future revival. Switzerland hosts a major facility, yet public views there were unmeasured. Their 2026 study asks close to two hundred fifty adults about awareness, ethics, and personal interest in signing up.

Most respondents backed the right to choose freezing when done to high medical standards, and few wanted legal bans. Personal interest stayed a minority taste, though about one in five reported real interest or intent. Wanting a longer life and prior familiarity drove openness more than age or gender. The snapshot shows a permissive public that mostly watches the practice from a distance.
plos-pone-0336005:
Hilary Stewart and co-workers survey the United Kingdom's health service to map exercise and nutrition programs that prepare patients for cancer surgery. Such preparation, called prehabilitation, can speed recovery, but provision may be patchy and unfair. Their 2026 study asks every surgical organization whether it runs a service and gathers detail from those that do.

About two-thirds of responding organizations had a service, and those varied in nearly every way. Physiotherapists and dietitians staffed most teams. Roughly half tailored first assessments to patient traits that affect access, such as language or income. The map exposes a postcode lottery and gives commissioners a baseline for leveling up cancer surgery preparation.
plos-pone-0348205:
Yahong Cai, Nalini Arumugam, and Yukai Chen tested a hands-on way of teaching career planning to college students. Instead of lectures, one group of students in their 2026 study worked through design thinking: empathising, experimenting, and prototyping their way toward career choices. A matched group of one hundred forty students in total received ordinary teacher-led guidance, and both groups were compared on confidence about career decisions.

Students in the design thinking group ended up clearly more confident and rated the course more valuable. Interviews traced the gain to practical skills practice, feeling emotionally empowered, and a stronger sense of identity. The authors recommend design thinking as a working model for career education in universities.
plos-pone-0335005:
Sławomir Grzegorczyn, Paweł Dolibog, Iwona Dylong, and Andrzej Ślęzak studied flickers in electric current passing through bacterial cellulose membranes bathed in salt solutions. When the stronger solution sits above the membrane, the current pulses instead of flowing steadily, betraying swirling instabilities in the thin layers near the surface. The team analysed these pulses with Fourier techniques that separate rhythms over time.

Raising the concentration contrast increased the pulses' frequency and changed their strength, with signal power peaking at an intermediate contrast. A difference-signal method sharpened the picture further. Strong instability flared in the first fifty minutes at high contrasts, then faded. The work aids understanding of transport in membrane systems used in medicine and industry.
plos-pone-0347305:
Note on status: this text sets out a study plan, not finished results. Juliana Magalhães Chaves Barbosa and colleagues wrote the protocol. It appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. The topic is Chagas cardiomyopathy, heart damage from long-term Chagas disease. The drug in focus is amiodarone. Doctors use it to steady the heart's rhythm in this disease.

The AMIO-CHAGAS study will track patients two ways. It will look back through past records. It will also follow patients forward over time. The team wants to know if the drug does more than calm rhythm. It may also cool immune activity. It may even act on the parasite itself. Proof of extra effects would boost a cheap, common drug.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Reports of death and ruin in the Jenin camp drove this text of 2002. On 19 April, the Council adopted Resolution 1405 without dissent. Israeli forces were running a big West Bank offensive at the time. The Jenin refugee camp saw the fiercest fight of it. Aid groups were barred from the camp. The toll inside was still unknown.

The text stresses how urgent aid access had become. Medical and relief teams must reach Palestinian civilians now. Curbs on their work, above all in Jenin, must be lifted. The Secretary-General's plan for a fact-finding team is welcomed. The team would pin down what had happened in the camp. Israel refused to work with it in the end, and it was disbanded.

The tribunal trying the leaders of the 1994 genocide in Rwanda gained its own chief prosecutor through Resolution 1505, adopted unanimously on 4 September 2003. A week earlier the Council had split the job, creating a separate prosecutor for the Rwanda tribunal instead of sharing one with the Yugoslavia tribunal.

On the Secretary-General's nomination, the members appointed Hassan Bubacar Jallow of the Gambia to the new post. His four-year term was set to begin on 15 September 2003. Having a dedicated prosecutor was meant to let the Arusha-based court push its heavy caseload of genocide trials forward on its own schedule.

A seat on the world court fell empty in 1953. Judge Sir Benegal Narsing Rau of India died on 30 November that year. His term still had time to run. Resolution 105, passed without a vote on 28 July 1954, set the plan to fill the gap.

The Council fixed the vote for the ninth session of the General Assembly. The special poll would come first. Only then would the Assembly hold its routine ballot. Five more seats were due to open on 5 February 1955. Rau had been a key voice in India's founding debates. He helped shape its charter of rights. The text is dry and brief, but it kept the bench at full strength.

One judge, one trial, one fix. A stand-in judge at the Rwanda court had a term due to end on 24 June 2007. Her trial, the Butare case, would not end by then. Swapping judges mid-case could wreck years of work. The chief wrote to the Council on 25 August 2006. Resolution 1705 passed on 29 August 2006.

Judge Solomy Balungi Bossa could keep her seat. The grant ran from 28 August 2006. She would sit till the Butare case closed, term or no term. The rulebook bent for this one case, by name. Such bends were rare. They show a court near its end, keen to close big trials with the judges who had heard the proof from the start.

Mid-2005 saw the Golan force renewed once more. The chief's report of 10 June 2005 found the scene calm. UNDOF had kept the truce line since 1974. Its term was weeks from its end. Resolution 1605 passed on 17 June 2005.

Six more months were granted, to 31 December 2005. The old call went out again: act on the 1973 ceasefire text at once. The text takes time for a new sort of clause. The force's work on the UN's zero-tolerance rule won a warm note. Staff must live by the UN code. Troop states must probe abuse claims and punish guilt. A report was due at the close. By then, these conduct clauses were a fixed part of each Golan vote.

Bosnia's post-Dayton order is renewed by Resolution 1305, adopted on 21 June 2000. The Peace Implementation Conference had met in Brussels in May. A UN judicial system assessment programme for Bosnia was due to end by December 2000. Croatia's new steps toward better relations and cooperation were welcomed, and refugee return was called crucial to lasting peace.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorizes SFOR, the multinational stabilization force, for a further 12 months. SFOR is to enforce the military annexes of the Dayton Peace Agreement and control Bosnian airspace. The Council extends the UN Mission in Bosnia and Herzegovina, UNMIBH, including the International Police Task Force, to 21 June 2001. It reaffirms the High Representative's final authority on civilian implementation, including binding decisions. It warns that international support depends on the Bosnian authorities' compliance, above all cooperation with the Yugoslavia tribunal, stronger joint institutions, and refugee returns.

Sierra Leone's peacebuilding office is renewed ahead of elections in Resolution 2005, adopted on 14 September 2011. National and local elections were due in 2012, likely to raise tensions, and the Secretary-General recommended another year for UNIPSIL. The government was pushing its Agenda for Change. A Transnational Organized Crime Unit fought drug trafficking. The Special Court had finished all its cases except one contempt matter and the trial of Liberia's former president.

The Council extends the UN Integrated Peacebuilding Office in Sierra Leone, UNIPSIL, until 15 September 2012. UNIPSIL must help the government and electoral bodies prepare peaceful, credible 2012 elections. It must support conflict prevention and party dialogue and tackle youth unemployment. It must assist on governance, anti-corruption, drug trafficking, and human rights. The 2012 vote and acceptance of its result are called a milestone that should shape UNIPSIL's transition into a regular UN country team.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 505 (VI), adopted on 1 February 1952, charged the Soviet Union with breaking its 1945 Treaty of Friendship and Alliance with China. The treaty had promised respect for each other's sovereignty and land. It promised no meddling in home affairs. It promised Soviet aid going only to China's National Government as the country's central authority.

The Assembly found that the Soviet Union had blocked the National Government's efforts to restore its authority in the three eastern provinces, Manchuria, after Japan's surrender. It had given military and economic aid to the Chinese Communists against it. On those findings it ruled that the Soviet Union had failed to carry out the treaty.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Iraq's oil money is the subject of Resolution 1905, adopted by the Security Council on 21 December 2009. Iraq's prime minister wrote to the Council asking for one more year of international oversight. His letter is attached to the text. Iraq still had to settle old debts and claims left over from the former regime.

The Council extended the existing rules until 31 December 2010. Under those rules, income from Iraq's oil and gas exports goes into the Development Fund for Iraq. An international board watches the fund and checks how the money is used. The Council ordered reviews during 2010. It also required Iraq to present a plan and a timetable for taking full control of the fund itself. The goal was an orderly handover, with outside auditing kept in place until then.

Santo Domingo was under a pause in fighting in May 1965. Resolution 205, adopted on 22 May 1965, tried to make that pause last. A week earlier, Resolution 203 had called for a strict cease-fire and sent a United Nations envoy. Resolution 205 asked that the suspension of hostilities be turned into a permanent cease-fire. The Secretary-General had to report to the Council on how the resolution was carried out. The short text does one thing: it presses both sides to stop fighting for good.

Cyprus's peacekeeping force came up for renewal again late in 1971. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 30 November, said the force was still needed to keep the peace. The government of Cyprus agreed it should remain beyond 15 December. Resolution 305 was adopted unanimously on 13 December 1971.

The Council reaffirmed its chain of Cyprus resolutions, beginning with Resolution 186 of 1964. The parties were urged to act with the utmost restraint. They were also pressed to keep working together toward a settlement. The force's stay was extended for a further period ending on 15 June 1972. The Council expected that progress by then might allow a withdrawal, or at least a cut in the size of the force.

Mercenaries attacked Benin on 16 January 1977, striking Cotonou, the country's main city. The invading force killed people and caused heavy damage before it withdrew. A special mission of the Council investigated the attack. Resolution 405 was adopted by consensus on 14 April 1977, after that mission reported.

The Council took note of the report and thanked the mission for its work. It strongly condemned the act of armed aggression against Benin. The text reaffirmed an older Council stand from 1967. States must not allow mercenaries to be recruited or helped in order to overthrow governments. All states were told to guard against such activity on their own territory. Training or moving mercenaries had to be prevented, and states were urged to consider banning it in law. Benin was offered help to assess the damage, and states were asked to aid its repairs.
un-sc-res-1405:
Reports of many deaths in the Jenin refugee camp reached the Council in April 2002. Israeli forces had fought in the camp during a West Bank offensive. On 19 April 2002 the Council voiced concern at the plight of Palestinian civilians. It noted reports from Jenin of deaths and wide destruction. It called for limits on aid groups in Jenin to be lifted.

The resolution stresses urgent access for medical and aid teams. It welcomes the Secretary-General's plan to send a fact-finding team to Jenin. That team would build an accurate record of the recent events. The Secretary-General had to keep the Council informed. In the event, the team never deployed, after disputes over its terms.
un-sc-res-1505:
The Rwanda tribunal gained its own prosecutor in September 2003. Until then one prosecutor had served both war crimes courts. Resolution 1503 split the office in two. On 4 September 2003 the Security Council appointed Hassan Bubacar Jallow to the Rwanda post. The Secretary-General had nominated him. His term began on 15 September 2003 and ran for four years.

The appointment is a single sentence in the text. Its effect was large for the court in Arusha. A dedicated prosecutor could focus only on the Rwanda cases. Those cases concerned the leaders of the 1994 genocide. The split also let each tribunal chase its own completion strategy.
un-sc-res-105: Judge Sir Benegal Narsing Rau of India died in November 1953. His death left a vacancy on the International Court of Justice. On 28 July 1954 the Security Council set the election to fill it. The vote would take place during the General Assembly's ninth session. It had to come before the regular election for five other seats. Those terms expired in February 1955. The short text handles only this scheduling.
un-sc-res-1705: A Rwanda tribunal judge was mid-trial when her elected term neared its end in 2006. Judge Solomy Balungi Bossa was hearing the Butare case, one of the court's largest. Her term as an ad litem judge would expire in June 2007. On 29 August 2006 the Security Council authorized her to keep serving in that case until it ends. The decision overrode the normal term limit in the tribunal's statute. Changing judges mid-trial would have wasted years of evidence.
un-sc-res-1605:
The Golan force was renewed in June 2005 with the conduct clause in place. On 17 June 2005 the Security Council extended UNDOF until 31 December 2005. The Secretary-General had reported on the force a week earlier. The Council welcomed UNDOF's work on the zero-tolerance policy for abuse. Personnel had to follow the United Nations code of conduct. The Secretary-General had to keep taking steps on that front.

The parties had to carry out resolution 338 right away. A report was due at the end of the term. It would cover events and measures taken toward 338. UNDOF's observers continued their patrols of the separation zone. The frontier between Israel and Syria stayed calm.
un-sc-res-1305:
Bosnia and Herzegovina prompted the Council to adopt Resolution 1305 on Bosnia and Herzegovina on 21 June 2000. The Dayton peace agreement was in place, but carrying it out still fell to local leaders. Refugee returns stayed central to lasting peace. Croatia had taken welcome steps to work with its neighbor and with the war crimes tribunal.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council lets the multinational stabilization force, SFOR, run for twelve more months. Member states may take all necessary measures to enforce the peace deal and guard the force. The text also extends the United Nations Mission in Bosnia and Herzegovina, including its police task force, until 21 June 2001. Parties must hand over indicted suspects and help refugees go home.
un-sc-res-2005:
On 14 September 2011, the Council adopted Resolution 2005 on Sierra Leone. The country was preparing national and local elections for 2012. Those polls would test how far peace had taken hold since the civil war. The peacebuilding office in Freetown, called UNIPSIL, was helping the government get ready.

The Council extends the office until 15 September 2012. Its top task is backing peaceful, free, and fair elections. It will also help calm party disputes and cut youth joblessness. Drug trafficking, graft, and small arms all need attention too. Success in 2012 should let the office wind down into a normal country team. Reports come to the Council every six months.
europmc-pmc10027805:
Fendler and a joint expert panel set out updated standards for PSMA PET and CT imaging in prostate cancer, in a 2023 guideline. The scan uses a tracer that sticks to a protein found on prostate cancer cells. It can reveal spread that older scans miss, and its use has grown fast.

The guideline states when the scan should be used and how it should be done. It covers the main tracers, scan settings, and how to read the images. Two major societies back the text, which aims to make results match across hospitals and countries.
europmc-pmc10407605:
Lin and a large team built quarTeT in 2023, a web toolkit for gap-free genomes. A full genome read from end to end is the new gold standard. Few tools yet build or check such genomes on their own. The kit has four parts that can run alone or as a chain.

One part orders draft pieces by match to a close kin genome. A second part fills gaps with extra-long DNA reads. The last two parts find telomeres, the caps at chromosome ends, and centromeres, the hubs for cell division. Lin tested the kit on a kiwifruit genome and matched a past hand-built result. It also found all known centromere zones in two test plants.
europmc-pmc10475205:
An and co-authors reviewed in 2023 how cell stress injures blood vessel linings in diabetes. Diabetes keeps blood sugar high for years, which scars small and large vessels. The lining of a vessel, the endothelium, loses its key gas signal, nitric oxide. That loss marks the start of vessel failure.

Oxidative stress is the main culprit, An argues. It cuts the supply of nitric oxide in vessel cells. Four sources feed the stress in diabetic vessels, from sugar and fats to insulin resistance. The review lists fixes aimed at the stress itself. They include sugar drugs, antioxidants, and lifestyle shifts. Each was checked for its effect on vessel lining health.
europmc-pmc1065705: Peters and co-authors set out a plan in 2005 for a shared store of immune epitope data with tools to study it. An epitope is the small part of a germ or other target that immune cells lock onto. Vaccine design leans on such data, since a good vaccine must show the immune system the right parts. The team cast the planned store as a direct boost to that work.
europmc-pmc10805005:
Antimicrobial Resistance Collaborators map the toll of drug-proof bacteria across Africa in this 2024 study. Antimicrobial resistance means germs no longer respond to drugs that once killed them. It is a growing threat to health care worldwide. Earlier work hinted the burden falls hardest on poorer countries, but fine detail for Africa was missing.

The group built estimates for 2019 for each country in the World Health Organization African region. They covered 23 bacterial germs and 88 germ-drug pairs. Their counts split deaths caused by resistance from deaths where resistance played a part. Data came from hospitals, tracking networks, and lab databases. The authors say such country-level detail can guide where new drugs, vaccines, and infection control are needed most.
europmc-pmc10906005:
Bloom, Paltiel, Naaman, and Waldeck review a curious effect where twisted molecules sort electrons by spin in this 2024 paper. Chiral molecules are twisted so they cannot match their mirror image, like left and right hands. Electron spin is a built-in twist of electrons that affects how they move. Since a landmark 1999 study, work has shown such molecules can act as spin filters.

The review first covers how labs measure this effect, called chiral induced spin selectivity. It then lists the molecules and materials that show it and seeks patterns linking shape to strength. Leading theories are laid out and compared. The authors discuss what the effect may mean for physics, chemistry, and the puzzle of why life uses one handedness. They close with gaps and next steps.
europmc-pmc11543605:
Pardo-Palacios and a large consortium benchmark long-read RNA sequencing methods in this 2024 paper. Long reads can span whole RNA transcripts, revealing isoforms that short reads miss. The consortium produced more than 427 million long reads, spanning human, mouse, and manatee samples. Both complementary DNA and direct RNA protocols and several platforms were tested.

Libraries with longer, more accurate sequences produced more accurate transcripts, they found. Greater read depth, by contrast, improved quantification accuracy more than identity. Where genomes are well annotated, reference-based tools performed best. Adding orthogonal data and replicate samples is advised for hunting rare or novel transcripts, and for reference-free work. The study offers a benchmark of current practice. It also points the way for better transcriptome methods.
europmc-pmc1190205:
Utian reviewed the wider costs of menopause symptoms in 2005. Hot flushes and night sweats are the best known signs. They can disturb sleep, mood, and clear thinking. For some women they last months; for others, more than ten years.

Beyond discomfort, symptoms can strain work and social life. Overall quality of life can drop in clear ways. Utian weighs evidence on brain chemicals and hormones behind flushes. Estrogen shifts plus serotonin and norepinephrine signals seem involved. The review urges care that treats life impact, not just heat episodes. Flush frequency and length vary widely between women.
europmc-pmc1449905:
Some gene variants last for ages because each has pros and cons. Charlesworth reviewed that process, called balancing selection, in 2006. When selection keeps two forms of a gene alive, nearby neutral DNA also stays varied. New gene data now let scientists read those marks.

Charlesworth explains how models that include DNA swapping between sites help read the marks. Tests can spot balancing selection without knowing what each form does. Facts about where forms live can hint at which force keeps them alive, and for how long. The review ties fresh gene data to classic theory on this long, quiet tug of war.
europmc-pmc1550905:
Two ways to open the windpipe compete in intensive care. Delaney, Bagshaw, and Nalos pooled 17 trials with 1,212 patients in 2006. One way cuts through the neck surgically. The other, percutaneous dilatational tracheostomy, stretches a small hole at the bedside.

The bedside method cut wound infections sharply, with odds about a quarter of surgery's. Bleeding, major complications, and long-term problems were much the same overall. In a subgroup, the bedside method also showed less bleeding and fewer deaths. Delaney concludes the bedside route is at least as safe, with a clear edge on infection.
europmc-pmc1779605: Identification of 491 proteins in the tear fluid proteome reveals a large number of proteases and protease inhibitors. — a 2005 science paper on tear-fluid proteins. It identifies the 491 proteins. The paper is the tear study: the findings on proteome ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc1868505: Release of outer membrane vesicles by Gram-negative bacteria is a novel envelope stress response. — a 2005 science paper on germ bubble shedding. It finds the vesicle release. The paper is the bubble study: the findings on envelope stress, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc1896005: Evolutionary conservation of sequence and secondary structures in CRISPR repeats. — a 2005 science paper on CRISPR repeat conservation. It finds the conserved structures. The paper is the CRISPR study: the findings on repeat ills, filed here in session today.
europmc-pmc193605: From Gene Trees to Organismal Phylogeny in Prokaryotes:The Case of the γ-Proteobacteria — a 2005 science paper on gene trees vs organism trees. It compares the tree types. The paper is the tree-compare study: the findings on prokaryotes, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2211305: The Alzheimer's disease beta-secretase enzyme, BACE1. — a 2005 science paper on the BACE1 enzyme. It studies the beta-secretase for labs worldwide. The paper is the BACE1 study: the findings on Alzheimer's for labs, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2213705: Life span extension by calorie restriction depends on Rim15 and transcription factors downstream of Ras/PKA, Tor, and Sch9. — a 2005 science paper on calorie-restriction aging genes. It finds the Rim15 dependence. The paper is the aging-gene study: the findings on calorie ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2596305: Risk of serious infections during rituximab, abatacept and anakinra treatments for rheumatoid a — a 2008 science paper on drug infection risks. It counts the infection risks for labs. The paper is the risk study: the notes on drug ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2627605: Brucellosis: an overview. — a 2008 science paper on the brucellosis germ ills. It gives the full germ overview for labs. The paper is the germ overview: the findings on brucellosis ills, filed here in full session today twice over now daily still.
europmc-pmc2633005: Purposeful selection of variables in logistic regression. — a 2008 science paper on smart variable picking. It guides the smart picking for labs. The paper is the picking guide: the findings on variables, filed here in full session today twice over.
europmc-pmc2717805: A versatile viral system for expression and depletion of proteins in mammalian cells. — a 2008 science paper on viral expression systems. It expresses the versatile proteins. The paper is the system study: the findings on viral ills, filed here in session.
beaumont-treatise-of-spirits-english-170:
John Beaumont published his Treatise of Spirits in 1705, a massive defense of the invisible world. Its full title promises history, physiology, and theology on spirits, apparitions, and witchcrafts. Beaumont wrote as the Enlightenment dawned, and he meant to hold the line for older belief.

Hundreds of cases fill the book, drawn from history and from living witnesses. Beaumont explains how spirits might act on bodies with the natural philosophy of his day. The work is the last great English demonological summa. Its sheer bulk is part of its argument: this much testimony, he implies, cannot all be lies. Few readers finish unshaken or unamused.
le-loyer-discours-des-spectres-french-16:
Pierre Le Loyer, a French judge with a scholar's appetite, published his Discours et histoires des spectres in 1605. Eight French books treat specters, visions, and apparitions of every order. Spirits, angels, demons, and souls of the dead each receive their chapters, in the French classic of apparition lore.

Le Loyer arranges the unseen world like an encyclopedia. He gathers cases from Scripture, classical authors, and recent report. His learning is vast and his curiosity larger. The Discours became the standard French reference on apparitions for its century. Readers who want the whole spirit world in one set of covers still start with Le Loyer's eight books.
le-loyer-treatise-of-specters-english-16:
Le Loyer's discourse on specters crossed the Channel the year it appeared, in Zachary Jones's English Treatise of Specters of 1605. The French original's eight books on strange sights, visions, and apparitions thus reached English readers at once. Few Continental works on the spirit world traveled so fast.

Jones's translation keeps Le Loyer's range: angels, demons, souls, and phantoms in order. English readers could now test their own ghost lore against a French judge's vast collection. The book is a landmark of apparition literature in English. Its speed of translation shows the market's appetite. Ghosts, in 1605, were international news, and Le Loyer was their chief reporter.
plos-pone-0004905:
Masa Tsuchiya and colleagues studied emergent genome wide control in lipopolysaccharide stimulated macrophages, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Large scale output studies mainly focused on highly expressed discriminatory genes. Biological responses come from whole regulatory networks acting together. Looking only at the strongest genes misses that system behavior. The team tracked genome wide dynamics in normal and mutated macrophages after a microbe signal.

Whole distributions shift coherently, not just top genes. Emergent metrics capture immune state better. Systems immunology needs global descriptors. Mutations reshape entire landscapes. Taken together, the findings mark a useful step for research in this area. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is. Such work helps guide care, field work, and lab work in the years ahead.
plos-pone-0005005:
Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva is a rare inherited disease. Muscle, ligament and tendon slowly turn to bone. Most cases come from one classic mutation in the gene ACVR1. Kirsten Petrie and colleagues reported exceptions in PLOS ONE in 2009. They studied two patients with unusual features. Both carried new mutations in ACVR1.

The new variants expand the disease's genetic picture. They show the classic mutation is not the only route. Atypical cases can now be recognized and diagnosed. The finding helps doctors who meet puzzling presentations. It also teaches more about how ACVR1 normally controls bone growth. That control is exactly what fails in this cruel disease.
plos-pone-0005105:
HD-PTP looks like an enzyme that removes phosphate tags. It was classed as a tyrosine phosphatase by its sequence. It was also named a tumor suppressor candidate. Marie-Claude Gingras and colleagues tested whether it actually works as an enzyme. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. No substrate for it had ever been identified.

HD-PTP is catalytically inactive. A conserved divergence in its phosphatase domain disables the chemistry. The protein looks like an enzyme but cannot act as one. That reclassifies it. Other proteins share such dead domains. They often serve as scaffolds or regulators instead. The finding shows why sequence alone can mislead. Function must be tested, not assumed.
plos-pone-0005205:
Satellite cells are the resident stem cells of adult muscle, resting quietly until injury calls them into action. Few markers can pick out the resting cells with ease, though Pax7 is a known one. Gnocchi and colleagues deepened that marker picture in PLOS ONE in 2009 using mouse muscle.

The team compared the molecular signature of resting and activated satellite cells in more detail. A sharper signature helps researchers find and study the resting cells before they wake. That matters for work on muscle repair, aging, and diseases that waste muscle away.
plos-pone-0005305:
Tuberculosis bacteria survive inside immune cells by tampering with the cell's internal signals. Calcium is one of those signals, and its release helps immune responses to pathogens. Gupta and colleagues studied calcium channels in TB infection in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Voltage-gated calcium channels, they found, negatively regulate protective immunity against Mycobacterium tuberculosis. In plain terms, the channels act as a brake on the defense the body needs. Releasing that brake, by blocking the channels, is a possible way to help the immune system clear TB. TB care lasts for months and drugs are hard on the body, so a host-side boost that helps the body's own cells kill the germ could shorten care one day.
plos-pone-0005905:
Minghua Nie and co-authors delivered in 2009 the first system-wide map of SUMO tagging in a multicellular animal. SUMO is a small protein tag attached to other proteins, vital for development. No one had charted the whole tagged set, the SUMO-ome, in an organism before.

Combining genetics and proteomics in the fruit fly, the team linked SUMO targets to cell cycle control, Ras signaling, and early body patterning. A full map turns scattered single-protein stories into a network view. Developmental biologists can now ask which tag changes matter most. The resource anchors future work on this quiet but powerful tag.
plos-pone-0006005:
Cell therapy after a heart attack sounds simple, but the details decide whether it helps. Juliana Nakamuta, Maria Danoviz, Fabio Marques and colleagues varied those details in 2009. Their PLOS ONE study gives bone marrow cells to hearts after infarction. It tests three things: when the cells go in, which route they take, and whether a fibrin scaffold helps them stay.

Each choice softened the heart's decline in its own measure, the team reports. Delivery is thus part of the treatment, not a footnote to it. The work helps trial designers pick timing and route with evidence in hand, a needed step before cell therapy for heart repair can prove itself in patients.
plos-pone-0006105:
A mouse virus can set off the whole immune system within hours. Christoph Ammann, Ronald Messer, Karin Peterson and colleagues found the trigger in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies lactate dehydrogenase-elevating virus, a natural infection of mice that causes rapid but passing activation of B cells and T cells across lymphoid tissues and blood.

The activation runs through TLR7, a virus sensor, and depends on interferon-alpha answers from plasmacytoid dendritic cells, the title reports. A clear chain from sensor to body-wide firing helps explain how some viruses stir immunity so fast. The chain also serves vaccine science, where controlled immune stirring is the point of an adjuvant.
plos-pone-0006205:
Cell biologists read yeast shape as a clue to gene function, while physicists ask what simple laws set shape. Daniel Riveline bridges the two views in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper on yeast lengths and shapes. He proposes a combined approach that treats cell form as the outcome of scaling rules.

Scaling arguments relate size and shape through a few broad physical ratios. Applied to yeast, they explain why cells grow to the lengths they do. The paper gives biologists a compact way to predict form before hunting for genes. It also shows physicists a living system where their methods earn their keep.
plos-pone-0006705:
Yan Fu and co-authors watched glutamate damage the insulation of nerve fibers in PLOS ONE in 2009. Damage at the paranode, where myelin meets the nerve fiber, appears in white matter injury. What causes that damage was unknown. The team used a special imaging method that reads myelin directly. It works on fresh tissue at finer than micron resolution.

Imaging showed clear splitting and retraction of paranodal myelin after glutamate exposure. Glutamate is the brain's main excitatory signal, but excess can be toxic. That excess is called excitotoxicity. Seeing the damage happen pins a culprit for white matter injury. The finding may guide efforts to protect nerves after stroke or trauma.
plos-pone-0006805:
Swati C. Chauhan and Rentala Madhubala cut a detox gene out of a parasite in PLOS ONE in 2009. The parasite is Leishmania donovani. It causes a grave illness of the inner organs. The gene makes glyoxalase I, an enzyme that clears a toxic waste. The waste is methylglyoxal, a harmful by-product of cell work. The parasite clears it with a rare system based on trypanothione.

Mutants that lack the gene cleared the waste far worse. That loss proves the enzyme sits at the heart of the path. A detox path found just in the parasite makes a fine drug target. Block it, and the waste may poison the parasite while the host stays safe. The mutants give labs a tool to test that plan.
plos-pone-0006905:
Huiyong Wei and colleagues built a tool to watch tuberculosis-specific T cells in monkeys in PLOS ONE in 2009. How often these cells appear during infection was unknown. Their resting memory pool after BCG vaccination was also unknown. BCG is the standard tuberculosis vaccine. The team made a tetramer reagent loaded with a mycobacterial peptide.

The tetramer directly measures epitope-specific CD4 T cells in lymphoid tissue. It tracks them during Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. It also counts the memory cells left after vaccination. Direct counts reveal whether vaccines leave durable immune memory. That information guides efforts to improve on BCG.
plos-pone-0007005:
Paul Collins, Brian Latta, and Gary Roemer asked a conservation question in PLOS ONE in 2009. Removing invasive species is a standard way to protect native wildlife. The job gets tricky when the invaders interact with each other. Their case paired an eagle with a pig, two introduced or recovered species affecting one ecosystem.

The team weighed whether removal order changes the outcome. Removing one species first can release or burden the other. Getting the sequence wrong can waste years of conservation effort. Their analysis offers guidance for managers facing several linked invaders at once.
plos-pone-0007105:
Muthannan Ramakrishnan, Zheng Jin Tu, Sushmita Singh, and others tested flu sequencing in PLOS ONE in 2009. Flu A viruses change fast as they spread. Mixed infections and swarms of close variants make them hard to track. New deep sequencing tools promised a much clearer view of that mix.

The team judged whether genome sequencing could spot mixed infections in a sound way. Finding a hidden second strain changes how an outbreak is read. It also bears on which strains go into vaccines. Their study helped set fair hopes for the flood of flu genomes that soon came.
plos-pone-0007205:
Brian Hauge, Christopher Oggero, Nicole Nguyen, and colleagues described a faster cloning method in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their tool supports RNA interference, a way to switch off chosen genes. Researchers use it for functional genomics, systems biology, and early drug discovery work.

Plant screening needs many inverted repeat constructs that produce double-stranded RNA. Building those constructs one by one is slow. The authors present a single-tube, high throughput method for cloning them. Their approach aims to help plant labs prepare large gene-silencing experiments with far less manual work overall.
plos-pone-0007305:
Shafiq Uddin Ahmed and Jo Milner studied how normal cancer cells avoid self-destruction in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Control of apoptosis, or programmed cell death, matters under normal non-stress conditions. It shapes mammalian development and daily cell turnover in tissues throughout life, keeping cell numbers balanced.

Faulty control can impair development or feed disease. The authors examine basal survival in cancer cells. They identify a network where one signal, JNK2, suppresses a death-promoting circuit involving JNK1, c-Jun, and Bcl-3. Their finding shows related signals can pull cell fate in opposite directions.

plos-pone-0009705:

arxiv-2606-16205: The 'two-line' trick is a slick path to true answers — lone waves and such — for twisty math rules. This paper is a first tour: how to spot which rules bow to the trick and how to bend them into shape. A primer for wave-math and earth-math students.
arxiv-2606-16405: A pure math paper that nails two bedrock 'no-runaway' rules — Harnack and Poincaré checks — for rough, jagged math lands with no smooth skin. Such checks are the spine of true-math on harsh ground. For shape-measure pros. Dry, dense, and built to last.
arxiv-2606-16605: Robots and game agents increasingly plan with learned "world models" — but those models can be fooled by small perturbations. ARB4WM is a benchmark for adversarial robustness of world models in continuous control: it tests whether an agent's internal model holds up under attack. It targets RL safety researchers.
arxiv-2606-16705: When particles graze each other at nearly the speed of light, they diffract — and "diffractive structure functions" describe what emerges. This paper computes them from JIMWLK evolution, the equations governing gluons at extreme energies. It targets high-energy physicists studying the dense gluon frontier of matter.
20117-chatterbox-1905:
Chatterbox was a famed children's magazine, and the 1905 volume gathers a full year of it. Tales, poems, facts, and pictures fill its pages week by week. One boy dreams that soldiers and sailors could fly to a hard fort. He studies a picture of the Rock and spots fine landing places.

Annual volumes like this one sat in many homes for years. Children read them again and again, alone or aloud with family. The mix taught history, nature, and morals inside bright stories. Readers now get a rich slice of what Edwardian children read for fun.
arxiv-2601-06805:
Xiangjun Tan and colleagues wrote a 2026 arXiv preprint. The work covers cancelling second order frequency shifts in ge hole spin qubits via bichromatic control. ArXiv posted the preprint in 2026 under its PAPERS collection. Germanium quantum dot hole spin qubits are compatible with fully electrical control and are progressing toward multi-qubit operations.

However, their coherence is limited by charge noise and driving field induced frequency shifts, and the resulting ensemble 1 / f 1/f dephasing. The work gives specialists a compact account of the problem and one proposed way to handle it.
