arxiv-2601-07405:
An arXiv preprint from 2026 deals with design and expected performance of the ALICE ITS3 upgrade. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. During the LHC Long Shutdown 3 ALICE will replace its three innermost tracking layers by a new detector, the “ITS3”. It will be based on newly developed, wafer-scale monolithic active pixel sensors.

Which are bent into truly cylindrical layers and held in place by light mechanics made from carbon foam. Unprecedented low values of material budget (0. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-08105:
Fabian Spaeh, Tianyi Chen, Chen-Hao Chiang, and Bin Shen study how retrieval agents should handle questions they cannot ground. Their 2026 arXiv paper covers agentic retrieval-augmented generation, where tool-using agents answer from outside knowledge. When a question falls outside that knowledge, hallucination becomes a real risk.

Guardrail systems try to block out-of-scope questions before harm is done. The authors instead work on query suggestion through dynamic in-context learning. The aim is to steer users toward questions the system can answer from its sources. For builders of search assistants, the paper links question wording to safer, better-grounded answers.
arxiv-2601-08205: Taminul Islam and co-authors present FUME, a deep learning system that detects rumen acidosis from gas images. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that ruminal acidosis is common in dairy cattle. The disorder causes real economic losses and animal welfare concerns. Current diagnosis relies on invasive pH measurement, which limits continuous monitoring at scale. FUME uses dual-gas optical imaging under in vitro conditions instead. The authors call it the first deep learning approach of its kind for this task. Noninvasive checks could let farms catch acidosis earlier.
arxiv-2601-06705:
Daan de Graaf and five co-authors craft GraphAlg, a tongue for graph tasks, in a 2026 paper. Query tongues for graph stores can not state tasks like PageRank, they argue. Users must haul data out of the store at great cost to run them.

Past fixes add code packs, node-based hooks, or loops built in the query tongue. Each fix lacks some mix of range, speed, and ease, the team says. GraphAlg states graph tasks in its own small tongue for the job. It then turns those tasks into the store's own core math form. Tasks and queries can thus run in one pipe, with no haul-out. Store users stop shipping graphs out just to run known tasks. The plan aims to do graph task support the right way at last.
arxiv-2601-07605:
Space physicists rely on coordinate systems with short names like GEI and GSM, but those names hide real disagreement. Definitions and software implementations differ between sources. The authors of this 2026 preprint compare definitions across online resources, software packages, and widely cited journal articles. They also compare data providers' ephemeris values, which give positions of the Sun, Earth, and spacecraft.

The comparison shows that same-named coordinate transforms can differ significantly between implementations. Two teams using the same named system may therefore get different results from the same data. That gap threatens reproducibility across the field. The authors offer recommendations for clearer definitions and implementations. It is written for anyone who converts space measurements between frames and expects others to reproduce the numbers.
arxiv-2601-07905:
Jaroslav Haas, Pavel Kroupa, and Sergij Mazurenko describe star clusters as incubators for mid-sized black holes. Massive star clusters formed in starbursts sort their heaviest members toward the center. There, black holes of stellar mass gather into sub-clusters above ten thousand solar masses. In gas-rich settings like galactic central molecular zones, these sub-clusters likely swallow large amounts of nearby gas. Their 2026 preprint studies how that gas changes the dynamics.

Intermediate-mass black holes may be the seeds of the supermassive ones in galaxy centers. How they form is still an open question. Gas accretion can deepen a cluster's gravity well and speed black hole growth. It can also change how the black holes interact and merge. The paper serves astrophysicists tracing black hole origins. It links star cluster dynamics to the growth of the largest black holes.
arxiv-2601-08005:
Joe Kwon and Stephen Casper warn that AI regulation has a blind spot inside the companies themselves. Frontier AI rules focus mainly on systems deployed to external users. External deployment is visible and open to outside scrutiny. High-stakes uses can also occur internally, when firms deploy capable systems within their own organizations. Examples include automating research, speeding critical business processes, and handling sensitive proprietary data. Their 2026 preprint names these internal deployment gaps.

Internal systems can shape research directions and company decisions with little oversight. The same capabilities that worry regulators externally exist behind the firewall. The authors argue the gap deserves direct attention. Their analysis serves policymakers and AI governance scholars. It asks what rules should follow capability, not just customer access. The paper adds an institutional case to the AI safety debate.
arxiv-2601-08805:
Cristina Anghel and Andras Juhasz link two ways to read a knot by its braid form. A knot can be shown as a braid that is then closed in a loop. From that form, two key sums can be built. One is the Alexander sum. The next is the Jones sum. Each sum tells us a trait of the knot that does not change when the knot is bent.

The pair builds a joint view called a quantum Heegaard diagram. It lets both sums be read from one setup. They show the grade marks in the two views line up in a clean way. A reader in knot work gets a bridge. It ties a disc based view to a split surface view in one frame.
arxiv-2601-09005:
Alberto Sainz Dalda and four co-authors give a fast tool to read the heat state of the low Sun from its light. The tool is called IRIS 2+. It works on data from the IRIS space scope, which watches the Sun's edge zone. From line shapes in that light, the tool works back to heat, push, and flow at each height.

It also sums how much power the zone throws off as light. That sum is a key check on how the Sun heats its crown. The tool is built to be fast, so vast IRIS sets can be read in bulk. A reader in Sun work gets both heat maps and loss sums from one run.
arxiv-2601-09605:
Jeremiah Coholich, Justin Wit, Robert Azarcon, and Zsolt Kira help robot policies survive a change of camera. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses image-to-image translation to bridge fake and real views. Policies that steer a robot arm by sight work well in training but break when the camera moves.

Real robot data is scarce and rarely covers many viewpoints. Simulation can generate demonstrations from every angle, but its images look different from real ones. Restyling fake views to look real promises policies that hold up from new angles, learned from fixed-camera data. Such toughness would make lab-trained robots far easier to put to work.
arxiv-2601-09805:
Phuong Minh Nguyen, Tien Huu Dang, and Naoya Inoue fix faulty reasoning inside the model instead of around it. Their 2026 arXiv paper improves chain-of-thought reasoning for logic tasks with an attention-aware intervention. Most current methods wrap the model in complex frameworks that split the task into prompted subtasks.

Others lean on external solvers, adding overhead and limiting scale. The authors instead intervene where attention goes wrong during the chain of thought. Steering attention mid-reasoning promises cleaner logic with no extra machinery. The approach keeps the pipeline simple: one model, thinking more carefully.
arxiv-2601-09905:
Zackary Okun Dunivin, Mobina Noori, Seth Frey, and Curtis Atkinson study a weak spot in the use of large language models for text coding. Such models can sort large sets of texts into themes. Yet simple prompts can still yield far too many wrong labels, even when the prompts are checked with care.

The team sets out a two step plan. First, one model codes each text with a code book made by people and tuned for model use. Then a second model acts as a critic. It reads the source text and the first model's reasons, and it makes the final call on each plus label. The aim is a plain, shared way to cut coding errors.
arxiv-2601-10105:
Khushbakht Farooq and co authors guard data at the edge of the net with a chain log. Edge work puts small nodes near users. In health care, those nodes share live data fast. But the flow can leak. Fakes can slip in, and trails can be hard to trace.

The team joins a chain log with fuzzy rules for who may pass. Fuzzy rules grade trust in soft steps, not just yes or no. The gate can adapt as facts change. It aims to keep health data safe at the edge. It also keeps a trail of who did what.
arxiv-2601-10205:
Arya Shah, Himanshu Beniwal, and Mayank Singh test if search tools can match a user to the right guide text. India has over a billion people and many tongues and scripts. A good aid must fit the tongue and the life of each user. That fit is more than word match.

Past tests oft mix search with text making. They may also test just one tongue. The team asks a pure search ask. Can a tool encode if a user sketch and a guide text fit? They test low resource Indian tongues. The work shows where tools stand on this fit task.
arxiv-2601-10405:
Joseph Malinzi and co authors model two viruses used as one cure for tumors. Each virus can kill tumor cells. Used as a pair, they may do more than the sum. The pair is vesicular stomatitis virus and vaccinia virus. Their play has a back and forth form.

The team call that form a ping pong loop. Cells hit by one virus shed a shield protein. That protein blocks a host alarm. The next virus then grows more well in the tumor. The model tracks cells, viruses, and the alarm as one rig. It seeks the best gap twixt doses.
arxiv-2601-10905:
Rajat Ghosh and Debojyoti Dutta present Action Shapley, a metric for picking training data for world models. In reinforcement learning, a world model mimics the environment so an agent can practice inside it. Such models matter most when real trials are costly, dangerous, or impractical. Their quality hinges on the data they were trained on.

Action Shapley scores which training data most help the world model. Shapley values, borrowed from game theory, split credit fairly among contributors. With a fair score, builders can keep the data that teach the most and drop noise. Better data curation could make simulated practice safer and more faithful for real agents.
arxiv-2601-11705:
Henriette Elvang, Aidan Herderschee, and Roger Morales study a broad class of field theories with the most symmetry that a flat theory can have. Each theory in their set looks like super Yang-Mills theory at first order. They ask what rules the next terms in such theories must obey.

They work in the weak force case and use symmetry plus a set R-symmetry group. They also ask that tree level results split in the standard way at set poles. From these rules they find strong, non-linear limits on the four point terms. The work helps map which low energy theories can come from string theory.
arxiv-2601-12105:
Richik Chakraborty, Lawrence Liu, and Syed Hasnain build a privacy-safe frame for cohort checks in health apps. Health apps use group norms to give context, such as how a user compares with peers. Group sums of health data can leak private facts, most of all in live, long-run apps.

Their frame adds differential privacy, a strict noise rule that bounds leaks. It also models risk in a stochastic way. Users could get peer context with a firm privacy bound. The work weighs insight gains against that bound.  The risk model tracks how leaks grow with each query.
arxiv-2601-12305:
Deepak Kanneganti, Sajib Mistry, Sheik Fattah, Joshua Boland, and Aneesh Krishna build a generator for data sets to test machine learning as a service. Buyers must pick and join ML services, yet lack fair test data for that choice. Their frame makes configurable, reproducible sets for that task.

It simulates real service acts by training many model families on many real data sets. It varies data spread settings as well. Reproducible acts let teams grade vendor claims with care. The work is set for the Web Conference 2026.  Varied spreads test how picks hold when data shift.
arxiv-2601-11205:
W. Heemels, R. Postoyan, P. Bernard, K. Scheres, and R. Sanfelice study hybrid systems. Hybrid systems mix smooth flow with jumps or switches in state. Their 2026 preprint adds inputs that flow in as time goes on. Many real plants are best framed in just this way.

For systems with no inputs, the base theory is well built. What counts as a solution is clear, and tests for full runs exist. With time inputs, those same results are mostly missing. The team sets out to close that gap with care. They give solution forms and tests for when runs exist and stay complete. Such base work guides control design for switched plants.
arxiv-2601-12505:
Ashish Raj Shekhar and four co authors build a defense for exams in the age of AI. Multimodal language models can now read exam files directly and answer them. That power threatens standard tests and academic integrity. Their framework is called DoPE, for decoy oriented perturbation encapsulation. It works at the document layer, inside the exam file itself.

DoPE embeds semantic decoys into PDF or HTML assessments. The decoys exploit gaps between how a file is rendered and how a model parses it. A human sees the true exam, while a model may latch onto the decoy content. The aim is documents that stay readable for people but hostile to AI. Such tools could help schools keep take home tests meaningful.
arxiv-2601-12705:
Dipto Das and four co authors study how people who live abroad drive change in the land they left. Their case is Bangladeshis abroad in the 2024 quota reform drive, which turned into a push for open rule. From talks with those who took part, they trace how the group found its feet. Social apps and money sent home became their main tools.

The team find four phases in the work of the group. Talk online grew into real acts, and ties formed fast across lands. A boycott on money sent home turned a need of the state into a lever of power. Last, the group adapted when the state watched them and cut the net. The study shows how cash and apps link expats to home affairs.
arxiv-2601-13605:
Milad Hoseinpour, Shubhanshu Shekhar, and Vladimir Dvorkin work on spotting power grid faults fast in 2026. When part of the grid fails, traders face big money risk at once. Quick action to hedge that risk needs quick proof that a fault has in fact hit. The team builds its test on public market data, not on grid sensors.

Their method rests on quickest change detection, a branch of stats for live data streams. It weighs how well new data fits life before a fault versus after one. That ratio helps the test flag a shift as soon as the proof is strong. Fast, firm alerts could cut losses when the grid breaks.
arxiv-2601-14105:
Olesya Razuvayevskaya and Kalina Bontcheva compare how pro and crowd fact-checks persuade readers in 2026. Fact-checks use rhetoric to convince, not just facts to inform. Their study is the first large-scale comparison of persuasion techniques in both kinds. Datasets come from Community Notes, EUvsDisinfo, and the Database of Known Fakes.

They quantify the prevalence and types of persuasion techniques in each ecosystem. Community notes are written by platform users, while the other sources are professional. Knowing which styles persuade helps fight false claims in public debate. It also shows what training crowd checkers may need.
arxiv-2601-14205:
J. Staforelli-Vivanco and co-authors rebuild Chilean pollen grains in 3D without lenses in 2026. They study Gevuina avellana hazel, Conium maculatum hemlock, and Anthemis cotula chamomile pollen. Their tool is lens-free digital in-line holographic microscopy. It captures complex interference patterns from each grain.

The patterns are numerically reconstructed using the Kirchhoff-Helmholtz transform. That yields a robust 3D volumetric reconstruction of the grains. Pollen shape identifies plant species for allergy, ecology, and forensic work. A lens-free system is cheap and portable for field labs. The three grains come from plants that grow in Chile. Their shapes add to the base set for pollen work in that land.
arxiv-2601-14505:
Mohammad Shamim Ahsan and Peng Liu study a blind spot in network security in this 2026 paper. Machine learning-based network intrusion detection systems sort packets into benign and attack classes. Attacks on such systems are usually framed one way: attack packets perturbed so they are misclassified as benign. Practical issues like imbalanced data shaped that belief.

The reverse case has been largely ignored. A maliciously perturbed benign packet can be misclassified as an attack. The authors call this FPR manipulation, since it inflates the false positive rate. Their study uncovers how the attack works in industrial IoT networks. Readers get a warning about a threat that can flood defenders with fake alarms.
arxiv-2601-14605:
Weiwei Ma and a large team train medical segmentation models in this 2026 paper. In clinical practice, medical segmentation datasets are often limited and heterogeneous. They vary in modalities, protocols, and anatomical targets across institutions. Existing deep learning models struggle to jointly learn from such diverse data. They often sacrifice either generalization or domain-specific knowledge.

The team's method is U-Harmony. It enhances joint training for segmentation models with universal harmonization. Harmonization makes datasets from distinct sources work together instead of fighting. Readers get a training scheme aimed at one model that can serve many hospitals, scanners, and body parts at once.
arxiv-2601-14705:
Casimir Czworkowski, Stephen Hornish, and Alhassan S. Yasin modify a reinforcement learning algorithm in this 2026 paper. Proximal Policy Optimization, or PPO, is widely used for its stability and sample efficiency. It often suffers from premature convergence due to limited exploration. The policy settles early on a decent behavior and stops searching for better ones.

The team proposes POEM, PPO with Evolutionary Mutations. It introduces an adaptive exploration mechanism inspired by evolutionary algorithms. Mutations inject fresh variation when progress stalls. The change is small but apt. It keeps the calm pace of PPO and adds a push to roam more. The test is plain. If the push to roam is too weak or too strong, the scores will show it. Readers get a PPO variant designed to keep exploring without losing the stability that made PPO popular.
arxiv-2601-14805:
Ryuhei Mizutani studies submodular function minimization in this 2026 paper. Submodular functions are set functions with diminishing returns: adding an item helps less as the set grows. Minimizing them is a core task in optimization. This paper restricts the minimization to a family of subsets. Mizutani shows that minimization over complements of families with certain hierarchical structures can be solved in polynomial time.

That result yields a polynomial-time algorithm for several cases. They include complements of intersecting families, crossing families, and unions of lattices. Polynomial time means the task is provably tractable, not just fast in practice. Fast counts here. A task that once took days of hand work can be set up in far less time. Readers get new exact islands in a hard optimization landscape.
arxiv-2601-15605:
Baktash Ansari, Elias Martin, and Afra Mashhadi tackle toxic chat on live streams in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their system is called ToxiTwitch. Live platforms like Twitch produce fast, high-volume chat. Toxic behavior there is hard to moderate at scale. Human moderators face harassment themselves while working. Keyword filters help, but they miss context and coded language. Emotes add a whole visual dialect that plain text tools ignore.

The title names the approach: emote-aware hybrid moderation. Hybrid suggests machine tools working with human judgment, not replacing it. Reading emotes as part of the message should catch abuse that text alone hides. Live chat moves too fast for slow review. A system that keeps pace while respecting context would ease a real burden on moderation teams.
arxiv-2601-15705:
Ali Caglayan, Nevrez Imamoglu, and Toru Kouyama map land cover across Japan from radar data in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their data come from the ALOS-2 satellite's SAR sensor, in single-polarization HH mode. The task is semantic segmentation at national scale. A companion task detects water as a binary map. Their base is SAR-W-MixMAE, a self-supervised pretraining method they build on.

Radar segmentation has known failure modes. Boundaries get over-smoothed. Thin structures are missed. Rare classes degrade under long-tailed labels. The team refines a lightweight model to fight all three. They stress doing so without adding pipeline complexity. For land agencies, maps from radar matter because radar sees through clouds. Steady national maps support farming, flood, and land-use planning.
arxiv-2601-15805:
Jaakko Visuri, Maria Gritsevich, and Janne Sievinen sharpen meteor work in a 2026 arXiv paper. To find a fireball's path, its direction must be known well. Direction feeds the path and speed estimates. Errors there ripple outward. They shift the orbit found for the object before impact. They shift mass estimates too. They also change dark flight models that predict where meteorites land.

The team adds a new fix for atmospheric refraction. Refraction bends light as it crosses the air. Their fix does not depend on distance, per the title. That matters because fireballs are seen from varied ranges. The authors say the fix handles a factor the field had missed. Better paths mean better orbits and better meteorite hunts.
arxiv-2601-16005:
Pierre-Élie Larré, Claire Michel, and Nicolas Cherroret compute a speed limit for light-based superfluids in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their system is a two-dimensional binary superfluid of light. It flows past a polarization-sensitive optical obstacle. The critical speed is the fastest mean flow with no dissipation. Below it, the flow stays clean. Above it, excitations drain energy. In the weak-obstacle regime, linear-response theory sets the speed.

Landau's criterion applied to two mode families does the work. Density modes and spin modes each give a candidate limit. Saturation of the optical nonlinearity can invert which mode rules. That inversion is a neat twist of this light-based system. Superfluid analogs made of light let physicists test flow ideas on an optical bench.
arxiv-2601-15305:
Alfred Shen and Aaron Shen merge two fixes for the cost of attention in long texts. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with long-context language models. Attention grows costly as the context grows, and two lines of work attack that cost.

Sparse attention cuts the cost by letting each token attend to only a chosen few. Gated attention instead improves training stability and curbs the attention sink effect. The authors combine both lines in one design, gated sparse attention. It aims for cheap long-context runs that still train in a stable way.
arxiv-2601-16105:
Xavier Caruso and Florian Fürnsinn give code rules for key traits of hypergeometric maps. Their 2026 preprint sits in maths and code based number work. These maps show up in many parts of pure maths. One key trait is how a prime based value sizes the map. That size can be hard to work out by hand.

The pair give steps to find that size on any disk in range. The disk must sit in the zone where the map holds. Their steps run in code, not just in proof. Firm code helps teams test claims about these maps fast. The work adds tools for prime based study of such maps.
arxiv-2601-16205:
Patrick Altmeyer trains models with what if tales so they learn to give good grounds. His 2026 preprint deals with grounds for a model pick. A what if tale shows how facts would need to shift to flip a pick. Such tales are oft made post hoc for fixed models. Altmeyer puts the tales in the train loop in their place.

Train with tales aims to grow the skill to give grounds. Good grounds must be apt to the case and fit for acts. Users can then see what to change to get a new pick. The work joins train design to the worth of grounds. It seeks models that both pick well and tell why.
arxiv-2601-16905:
Andy Zhu, Rongzhe Wei, Yupu Gu, and Pan Li teach chatbots to drop taught facts on call. Such fact drops, called unlearning, serve safety and law. Past tools work for plain dense models. Mix-of-experts models route each ask to a few parts. Past tools game that route to dodge facts. The facts stay, but are just hid from view.

Their 2026 preprint, GRIP, curbs the router with shape rules. Those rules force true erasure, not mere dodges. Use loss is kept low as facts drop. Safe drops matter for private text in training sets. The tool works across drop plans, by the team's claim.
arxiv-2601-17105:
Jean-Pierre Magnot sets a frame for a wild wave rule set in bent algebra. The KP chain is a tower of linked wave rules. His 2026 preprint makes that tower noncommutative. In plain words, swap order now counts in the math. The frame turns with SU(3) group acts as one. A Lorentz-type form fits the frame as well.

That form is coded in a twisted four-part algebra. Gauge fields of hypercomplex type join the frame too. Such frames join waves, symmetry, and fields in one view. They may spark new tools for field math.
arxiv-2601-17205:
Giuseppe Arena and Maarten Marsman work on Bayesian inference for discrete Markov random fields. These models link discrete variables in a network. Each variable depends on its near neighbors. They are used when links are complex and hard to map by hand. Exact inference in such models is very hard to compute.

The core block is the partition function. It sums over all states the system could take. That sum grows fast and soon cannot be done in full. The authors use coordinate rescaling to move past that block. Their method aims to make sound inference fit for real use. It serves fields that rely on network models for discrete data.
arxiv-2601-17305:
C. G. Krishnanunni and three co-authors take a fresh look at the Ensemble Kalman Filter. The filter solves inverse problems by blending model runs with real data. It is a workhorse in weather, oil, and earth science. The team views it through a Lagrangian dual lens. They show the filter can be derived from a sample-based form of that dual.

That new base yields fresh math on how the filter behaves. It covers non-asymptotic bounds, not just large-sample claims. It also points to ways to speed convergence. A firmer base helps users trust the filter in hard cases. It may cut the runs teams need for a good answer.
arxiv-2601-17505:
M. Ladra, P. Páez-Guillán, and C. Zargeh build HNN-extensions for Lie superalgebras. An HNN-extension grows an algebra by adding a stable letter with set rules. It is a classic tool from group theory, moved to algebra. The authors prove each Lie superalgebra embeds in its extensions. No structure is lost in the growth.

As a payoff, any Lie superalgebra of at most countable dimension embeds in one with just two generators. Two-generator forms ease proofs and constructions. Superalgebras model supersymmetry in physics. Tools that shrink their description help both math and physics. The embedding result is a firm base. It tells researchers the extension is safe to use.
arxiv-2601-18005:
Gergely Bérczi, Baran Hashemi, and Jonas Klüver build a learning loop that hunts for extreme math structures. Their 2026 preprint presents FlowBoost. Finding extremal structures means searching vast, rugged landscapes. Analytic methods give little guidance there, and brute force quickly becomes hopeless. FlowBoost is a closed-loop generative frame. It learns from its own finds and steers the next round of search toward rarer, more extreme objects.

Each loop can sharpen the hunt for counterexamples and record holders. Such objects test conjectures and mark the true bounds of a theory. A tool that finds them faster could change how some fields work. The paper joins machine learning with pure math search.
arxiv-2601-18205:
Amin Aalipour and Nima Khosravi work out how to glue two different gravity theories along a shared border. Their 2026 preprint studies f(R) gravity, a family that broadens Einstein's theory. Gluing needs junction conditions: rules that say what must match where the two regions meet. The authors derive those conditions with a variational approach. They treat the general f(R) family and, for comparison, the special case of plain Einstein gravity.

A clean derivation keeps model builders from joining spacetimes in ways the math forbids. Junction rules serve work on stars, shells, and wormholes. Side-by-side treatment of both theories shows exactly where the broader theory adds new terms.
arxiv-2601-18305:
Xuan Wang, Siyuan Su, Quantong Fu, Yongxiang Hu, and Yangfan Zhou teach GUI agents to swipe like people. Their 2026 preprint presents SwipeGen. GUI agents that automate phone and computer tasks have grown strong at seeing screens. They can ground an instruction into concrete steps. But carrying the steps out has become the new bottleneck. Swiping is a case in point: a bad swipe fails even when the plan is right. SwipeGen synthesizes human-like swipes to bridge that execution gap.

Synthetic swipes can train agents without endless human demos. The aim is motion with the speed, curve, and lift of a real finger. Better low-level skills lift the whole agent stack. The work targets the unglamorous layer where many agent runs die.
arxiv-2601-18905:
Eliot Halley Vrijmoet and five co-authors report new orbits for pairs of small red stars near the Sun. Their 2026 study covers M dwarf stars that have close companions, all within a short range of Earth. The team used a speckle camera on a large telescope in Chile to take the measures.

The paper lists more than a thousand speckle measures taken over four years. Most of them split close pairs into two stars, and the set spans over two hundred pairs in all. Gaps between the stars run from very tight to a few arc seconds wide. Such orbits help astronomers weigh these faint stars and learn how pairs form.
arxiv-2601-19305:
Hsuan-Jui Su and five co-authors sense microwaves with atoms tuned to catch radio waves. Rydberg atoms, atoms puffed into high energy states, react strongly to electric fields. A microwave field splits their spectral lines in a pattern called Autler-Townes splitting, which the team reads as their signal.

From that one pattern they pull out both the field's frequency and its strength at once. Their sensor spans a broad band with high sensitivity and a wide range. Atom based sensors could one day calibrate radio gear and map fields with a standard set by atoms themselves.
arxiv-2601-19405:
Ivan Markin and three co-authors simulate mergers of a black hole with a neutron star at near equal mass. A detected event, GW230529, hinted that such pairs can be more symmetric than once thought. Even more symmetric pairs should leave fat disks of debris around the merged object.

Those disks can drive bright light shows, like kilonovae, that telescopes can chase. The team runs numerical simulations for equal and near equal mass ratios to map what happens. Their maps help observers know what light to expect when the next such merger's waves arrive.
arxiv-2601-19805:
Sofía Garzón Mora and Christian Haase study the shapes formed by tensor networks. A tensor network writes a large tensor as a web of small ones arranged along a binary tree. The set of all tensors a given network can produce forms a variety, a geometric object. Understanding these varieties is key to knowing what tensor networks can express.

Building on earlier work, the authors study which of these varieties contain others. Containment tells us when one network format can simulate another. The combinatorics of the tree drive the encoding they study. Such results guide the design of tensor methods in physics and machine learning. They also enrich the geometry of tensors, a fast-growing field.
arxiv-2601-20105:
Faezeh Hosseini, Mohammadali Yousefzadeh, and Yadollah Yaghoobzadeh study a weak spot of large language models: fixed sayings whose meaning is not literal. Their 2026 preprint presents a benchmark for Persian idioms and proverbs. Such expressions are rooted in culture, and their words do not add up to their meaning in the usual way.

The authors call the failure mode figurative hallucination, where a model treats a fixed expression as if its words were literal. Their benchmark is built to test how models handle these Persian sayings. Work like this matters because idioms are common in daily speech, and a model that misreads them will also misread the people who use them.
arxiv-2601-20205:
Tianze Jiang, Blake Bordelon, Cengiz Pehlevan, and Boris Hanin study how to carry tuning settings across model scales in mixture-of-experts networks. These networks route each token to a few expert subnetworks, which separates total size from the compute used per token. The design adds new knobs, such as router weights and the number and size of experts.

Each knob needs tuning, and tuning at full scale is costly. The authors examine how good settings found on small models transfer to large ones with expert layers. Reliable transfer rules would cut the cost of training the sparse models now common in large AI systems.
arxiv-2601-20305:
Zhenchen Tang and six colleagues address a gap in unified multimodal models, which both understand and generate images and text. Their understanding is strong, yet it often fails to guide their own generation. The authors call this the cognitive gap: the model does not know how to use what it understands to improve what it makes.

They propose endogenous reprompting, where the model writes self-aligned descriptors during generation as an explicit reasoning step. Understanding then becomes an active part of making, not a passive encoding. The idea could raise the quality of generated images without a bigger model.
arxiv-2601-18405:
Sara Solarova and three colleagues look at how well checks on big social sites work in real life. A new law in Europe sets firm rules for such sites. The rules cover how their ranking code must stay clear, how users must be kept safe, and how their data must be kept from harm.

The law tells each big site to face a check by an outside team once in a while. Yet we know little of how those checks run, or of how much good they do. The team digs into that gap, with a focus on the code that picks what each user sees. Their work aims to move past a mere tick in a box. It points toward checks that can catch real risk and push sites to mend it.
arxiv-2601-18605:
Yan Gao and Jinsong Zeng study when a kind of maths rule lives in-side a group they call a molecule. The rules are the kind that raise a count to a whole power and add a set shift. A rule counts as in a molecule when it links to a web of its kin in a set way. Groups of this kind chart how rules that bend and fold a plane sort them-selves.

The pair find a clean test for when a rule sits in a molecule. The test checks the rule's key points, the spots where its slope dies. All such points must sit in long chains of calm zones of the rule. The pair also show that two such groups never share a rule. That split keeps the chart of such rules neat and of use.
arxiv-2601-18805:
Rishabh More studies why thick mixes of grains in a fluid grow thin as they are stirred fast. Such a mix is called a dense suspension: grains crowd a fluid so thick that they brush and press as they pass. As the stir rate climbs, the mix flows with more ease. That shift is most oft blamed on how the grains line up and pack as they flow.

More runs sims that track each grain in mixes that thin by un-like tricks of push and pull. Some grains draw near, some push off, and some grip with a force that leans on the load. In all of them, one rule holds: how far grains stray from the smooth flow is set by the stir rate alone. The pack, the line-up, and the kind of push do not shift that stray.
arxiv-2601-21405:
Kailash A. Hambarde and Hugo Proença work on matching the same person across aerial and ground cameras. A drone view and a street view of one person can look wildly different. Distance and angle warp the body's shape, which breaks the usual way of scoring how alike two images are.

Most methods still trust dot-product similarity inside attention, even under huge viewpoint gaps. The authors argue that this trust is misplaced and set out to fix the warped similarity. Fair matching across views supports search and rescue, crowd safety, and tracking in public spaces, where cameras rarely share the same angle.
arxiv-2601-21505:
Diaoulé Diallo and five co-authors test whether steering a language model's inner activity can set its writing style. Steering adjusts hidden activations at run time instead of retraining the model. It is a light way to guide output toward a desired tone or form.

Earlier claims for steering rested mostly on automatic checks. The authors run a human evaluation to see if readers actually notice the intended style shift. Human judgment is the ground truth for style, since style lives in the reader's eye. Their results show what steering can and cannot do when real people grade the outcome.
arxiv-2601-21605:
Shashiwadana Nirmani, Garima Sharma, Hourieh Khalajzadeh, and Mojtaba Shahin study how app reviews talk about age. Apps now run much of daily life, from work to fun. Yet many apps serve some age groups poorly, and the reviews are where that friction surfaces first.

The authors analyze age-related discussion in user reviews. Patterns in the complaints show where older or younger users feel left out. Developers rarely test with every age group, so reviews become an early warning system. The study gives builders a way to hear age-based needs straight from the people who live with the gaps.
arxiv-2601-22305:
Bo Yuan and five co-authors put workflow building for AI agents on a firmer math footing. A workflow chains model calls, tool use, and clean-up steps into one long task. Their 2026 preprint, BayesFlow, notes that most past builders treat the task as a plain search with thin theory.

BayesFlow frames the build as a question of odds and evidence. Helper agents guide the search for a chain that fits the task. A firm frame can make built workflows more sound and easier to trust. It can also cut trial-and-error cost. The work targets teams that ship agent systems.
arxiv-2601-22605:
Falai Chen, Buyang Li, Jiajie Li, and Rong Tang speed shape design with a flow that has momentum and guards the mesh. Their 2026 preprint tackles PDE-constrained shape optimization, plus hole filling on Willmore-driven surfaces. Two pains rule the field: flat energy zones stall progress, and meshes warp as shapes move.

Their second-order inertial flow pushes through flat zones. A minimal-deformation rule keeps the mesh sound as it goes. Good shapes, reached fast, serve design from parts to implants. The work is a numerics advance with clear uses. It should travel well across fields.
arxiv-2601-22705:
Qiaoling Chen and a large team built Concur, a gatekeeper that admits agent jobs to a batch system with care. Agentic batch work piles state into the GPU key-value cache, turn by turn. Their 2026 preprint names the failure that follows: middle-phase thrashing, where cache yield collapses long before memory runs out.

Concur admits work proactively, at the agent level, to keep the cache sound. Higher yield means cheaper, faster service for agent fleets. The work spots a failure mode others had missed. Naming it is half the fix. The gate is the other half.
arxiv-2601-21705:
A classical problem in insurance and finance asks how a firm should pay dividends without going broke. In the standard model, ruin happens only when the firm's surplus first reaches zero. The 2026 preprint behind this entry adds a second, more realistic route to failure.

In the new model, default can also strike when the surplus spends too long below a distress level, even if it never hits zero. The authors call the time limit behind this rule the Omega clock. They then study the best dividend policy as a singular control problem under both risks. The setup speaks to regulators and managers who know that long distress, not only sudden ruin, kills real firms.
arxiv-2601-22105:
Yang Liu, Alexey Koshelev, Anna Tokareva, and Ziyue Zhu test whether corrections to Einstein's black hole can pile up forever. In effective field theory, the Schwarzschild solution of general relativity receives small corrections at every order of a derivative expansion. The authors focus on the region far from the horizon.

They find the dominant corrections at all orders, and their title states the punchline. The sum of corrections converges only if the underlying theory respects UV locality, a constraint from high-energy physics. Their 2026 preprint turns a formal series into a diagnostic. If future observations ever measure deviations around black holes, this work helps say which theories could produce them consistently.
arxiv-2601-22205:
Amadou Keita and Ilya Shapiro revisit a famous false conjecture, in a restricted world where it may live again. Mutually orthogonal Latin squares are grids whose symbols line up without repetition in useful ways. MacNeish's conjecture about how many such squares can coexist is known to be false in general.

The authors restrict attention to transitive families of these squares, where a symmetry group moves any symbol to any other. For the simply transitive case, they find the conjecture holds. They also give partial results toward the wider transitive case. Their 2026 preprint shows how symmetry assumptions can rescue precise structure from a conjecture that fails without them.
arxiv-2601-20805:
Lukas Koch writes about a small task that can quietly mislead: plotting data with error bars. His 2026 paper covers the common job of plotting measured y-values against fixed x-values. Each point carries an uncertainty, usually drawn as a vertical error bar. The bar may stand for a frequentist confidence interval or a Bayesian credible interval. Readers assume the bar tells the whole story.

Koch's focus is what changes when the data points are correlated. Correlation means the errors in the points move together, not on their own. A plot that ignores those links can suggest more certainty than the data hold. The paper explains how to present such data honestly. It is a practical read for anyone who makes or reads scientific plots.
arxiv-2512-01305:
Jianru Duan studies a torsion invariant for three-dimensional shapes. The invariant is built from L2 methods, which use square-summable data. Sutured decomposition cuts a shape into simpler parts. Duan asks what the invariant can tell about a shape's fibers.

He proves it detects whether a given class is fibered. That means it can tell if the shape is built from a surface swept along a loop. One case is set aside, for closed graph shapes with no curved metric of the right type. Such tests help sort shapes that look alike at first glance.
arxiv-2512-01605:
Anurag and co-authors count the cost of VQE for small molecules. VQE is a hybrid quantum-classic method to find ground-state energies. Those energies drive drug and materials design. Noise and small quantum hardware cap its use today.

The team gauges resources under distinct fermion mappings and Hamiltonian cuts. Each choice shifts qubit counts and circuit depth. Clear counts show which choices save most. That guides chemists to spend scarce quantum time on the setups most likely to yield sound energies. Small molecules are the test bed where quantum chemistry hopes to beat classic methods first, so honest costs there set the field's pace.
arxiv-2512-01805:
Caroline Piaulet-Ghorayeb and co-authors find a window for water-hydrogen demixing on warm sub-Neptunes. Sub-Neptunes are the most common planet type found. Their bulk makeup is still poorly known. Old views said only very cold planets could split volatiles into layers.

Warm, metal-rich sub-Neptunes may split as well, the team argues. Envelopes once thought fully mixed could stratify. Layering changes how heat and chemistry move inside the planet. That shift alters how observers should read spectra of the most common planets known. Metal-rich envelopes are common in the sub-Neptune census, so a demixing window there reshapes population models, not just single planet stories.
arxiv-2512-00705:
Seongyeon Park and five coauthors present FlexiWalker, a 2025 computer systems paper on random walks over graphs. Random walks hop from node to node and support many graph analysis tasks. Dynamic walks change their hop chances as the graph evolves, which makes them flexible but hard to speed up.

Most fast CPU and GPU designs rely on precomputed data, which dynamic walks break. Users are left with slow frameworks or hand-tuned code that fits one workload only. FlexiWalker is a GPU framework that adapts at runtime to varied workloads. Its goal is fast dynamic walks without rewriting kernels for each new job.
arxiv-2601-22805:
Pit Neitemeier and five co-authors study how smart sequence models choose where to split long streams of bytes. These hierarchical models learn their own segments instead of using fixed tokens. That saves compute, but it has been hard to measure where the splits fall, or to steer them.

Their tool, SOMBRERO, measures boundary placement and guides it in a planned way. Clear measures help builders see if a model spends its compute on the parts that matter most. Steering the splits could make long-text models faster without making them dumber.
arxiv-2601-22905:
Muqing Liu, Chongjie Si, and Yuheng Jia make a popular fine-tuning method more flexible. Full fine-tuning of large models costs too much memory and compute for many teams. Low-Rank Adaptation, or LoRA, trains small added matrices instead, but it fixes their rank in advance.

A fixed rank wastes capacity on some layers and starves others. FlexLoRA uses entropy, a measure of spread, to guide where rank should grow or shrink. Flexible ranks could give small teams big-model quality at a lower training bill. Entropy guides the flexibility, giving layers with richer signals more rank while trimming layers that need less capacity.
arxiv-2512-00105:
Finding interesting patterns in large numerical databases can overwhelm analysts with far too many results. Djawad Bekkoucha and co-authors present a sampling approach for interval patterns in a 2025 journal article. Instead of listing everything, sampling draws a manageable subset at random, weighted by an interestingness measure.

Measures such as frequency or hyper-volume decide which patterns are more likely to be drawn. The authors describe their method as the first sampling approach built for interval patterns in numerical data. It offers data miners a practical way to explore huge pattern spaces without drowning in output. Interval patterns describe ranges rather than single values, which suits sensor and financial data.
arxiv-2512-00605:
Combinatorial bandit problems force repeated choices under constraints, balancing learning with earning. Aurélien Delage and Romaric Gaudel study matroid bandit linear optimization in 2025, exploiting unimodality to gain efficiency. Recent approaches already achieve optimal regret, matching the known lower bound.

Time complexity remains the problem, especially for large matroids or costly membership oracles, as in recommendation systems that must ensure diversity. Unimodality, a single-peaked structure in the problem, can be leveraged to cut computation. The result aims at bandit algorithms that stay optimal in regret while finally running fast enough for real platforms. Matroids generalize independence, covering scheduling, spanning trees, and diversity constraints alike. Unimodality gives the search a peak to climb instead of a plateau to wander.
arxiv-2512-03505:
Quantum systems can show nonclassical traits in phase space. Kyu-Won Park and Jongin Jeong develop a complex entropy framework for those traits in this 2025 work. They apply it to avoided crossings in an oval quantum billiard.

For a real Wigner function, the Gibbs-Shannon functional becomes complex. Its imaginary part, tied to the Wigner-negative volume, serves as an entropy-like measure of nonclassicality. The authors add Fisher control of that negativity. Such measures help track how quantum behavior fades into classical motion. Negativity measures mark where classical pictures fail inside the billiard's phase space.
arxiv-2512-02105:
An anomaly is an obstruction: a symmetry of a quantum system that cannot be gauged or realized by a trivial state. Alexander Czajka, Roman Geiko, and Ryan Thorngren build in 2025 a rigorous topological theory of such anomalies for systems living on a lattice.

They also construct spectra of invertible states and quantum cellular automata, mathematical objects that organize these phases. With those spectra, both anomalies and symmetry-protected topological phases can be classified up to a blending equivalence. The classification tells physicists which exotic states of matter can exist on a lattice and which are forbidden in principle.
arxiv-2512-02205:
The Integrable Optics Test Accelerator at Fermilab is a small ring built to test bold plans for strong particle beams. Four authors, Banerjee, Romanov, Stancari, and Wallbank, report in 2025 on the traits and motion of proton beams in that ring.

The ring lets staff study how space charge, beam load effects, and bent optics act on each other in storage rings. These effects cap how bright a beam can be. The proton cases worked out here guide tests that could unlock brighter beams for the next machines. Such groundwork must come first, before the new optics can leave theory and run in steel.
arxiv-2512-03005:
Dawei Li and six co-authors test whether language models can mediate online flame wars instead of fueling them. Models increasingly sit inside everyday communication, drafting and smoothing messages. Their potential to foster empathy and constructive dialogue is an important frontier for responsible AI, the authors argue.

A mediator model would step into heated threads and cool them toward resolution. The study asks whether current models can serve that role at all. Evidence here guides platforms weighing AI moderation that aims higher than deletion, toward actually repairing conversations between angry users. Cool heads are scarce in a flame war. A calm third voice that both sides can hear may do what bans and blocks can not do at all.
arxiv-2512-02905:
F. Andreatta and three co-authors build technical tools for computing p-adic maps that link geometry and number theory. Their ongoing work targets explicit reciprocity laws for the group GSp4. Tools of this kind compute Abel-Jacobi maps in p-adic étale settings.

The authors define syntomic polynomial cohomology for filtered Frobenius log isocrystals. The setting covers proper, semistable schemes over a local field's integers, with smooth generic fiber and horizontal divisors. Solid foundations here underpin some of the deepest current work on L-functions and motives. Base tools earn their keep in the work they let peers skip. This set is built to be that kind of base for a hard line of proofs.
plos-pone-0010005:
Srikanth Chiliveru, Svend Birkelund, and Søren Paludan published cell work in 2010. They studied how fibroblasts sense Chlamydia pneumoniae. That bacterium lives inside host cells. Fibroblasts are common connective tissue cells. When they detect germs, they can switch on interferon-stimulated genes, a set of defense genes that slow infection.

The authors asked which sensors inside the cell detect this bacterium and trigger those defense genes. They pointed to receptors that sense nucleotides, the building blocks of DNA and RNA, inside the cell. The result helps map how the body spots a germ that hides within its own cells.
plos-pone-0010105:
The authors were Guy Lahat, Quan-Sheng Zhu, Kai-Lieh Huang, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study named vimentin as a possible cancer drug target. Vimentin is a structural filament found in many connective tissue cells. In active cells it also helps with adhesion, movement, survival, and signaling through constant rebuilding.

The team drew evidence from lab cell work and mouse tumors grown from human tissue. Soft tissue sarcomas were among the cancers in view. If vimentin can be attacked safely, cancers that depend on it might gain a new treatment option.
plos-pone-0010205:
The authors were Claudia Molins, Mark Delorey, Brook Yockey, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study compared tularemia germs in mice. The type A form of Francisella tularensis causes serious human disease. Genetic typing splits type A into three distinct groups, called clades A1a, A1b, and A2.

Human case data hinted those clades differ in how severe illness becomes. The team tested virulence, the power to cause disease, in mice for each clade. Confirmed differences would help doctors read a patient's infecting strain as a clue to likely outcomes. The report appeared in 2010.
plos-pone-0010305:
Yoshiyuki Kumada and Shuguang Zhang grew gum ligament cells in designer scaffolds in 2010. Periodontal ligament fibroblasts hold teeth in their sockets and repair gum tissue. The team built two peptide scaffolds, mesh-like gels that self-assemble, with short active motifs attached. Those motifs include RGD, a cell-gripping signal found in body proteins, to invite cells to settle.

In three-dimensional scaffolds, the human cells made large amounts of type I and type III collagen. They did so without any extra growth factors added. Their PLOS ONE result supports scaffold-only approaches for dental tissue repair.
plos-pone-0009905:
Gene studies produce sprawling datasets, and judging which analysis methods work best is hard. Christopher Cabanski and colleagues proposed a standardized score for that judging. Their method appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Different methods can give different answers from the same data.

The score is called SWISS MADE, short for Standardized Within Class Sum of Squares. It evaluates both methodologies and dataset elements on one yardstick. A shared yardstick makes comparisons between studies fairer. The tool helps analysts pick methods that truly fit their data. Fair scores keep method fights honest.
